abstract: Linsker has reported the development of centre---surround receptive fields and oriented receptive fields in simulations of a Hebb-type equation in a linear network. The dynamics of the learning rule are analysed in terms of the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix of cell activities. Analytic and computational results for Linsker's covariance matrices, and some general theorems, lead to an expla(cid:173) nation of the emergence of centre---surround and certain oriented structures. Linsker [Linsker, 1986, Linsker, 1988] has studied by simulation the evolution of weight vectors under a Hebb-type teacherless learning rule in a feed-forward linear network. The equation for the evolution of the weight vector w of a single neuron, derived by ensemble averaging the Hebbian rule over the statistics of the input patterns, is:! a at Wi = k! + L(Qij + k 2 )wj subject to -Wmax ~ Wi < Wmax

paragraphs: This paper explains patterns that appeared in Linsker's simulations of learning in a linear neural network. Those simulations produced receptive fields with center-surround organization and sensitivity to orientation. The question is how a teacherless Hebbian rule can generate these structured responses from the statistical relationships among cell activities.

The authors analyze learning through the eigenvectors of the activity covariance matrix. A covariance matrix describes how activities vary together, while its eigenvectors identify particular patterns within those relationships. Expressing the weight dynamics in these terms connects the observed receptive fields to the input statistics that drive adaptation. The analyzed learning equation also constrains weights to remain within fixed bounds.

Analytical calculations, computational results for Linsker's covariance matrices, and general theorems explain the emergence of center-surround fields and certain oriented structures. This turns a simulation observation into an account of why particular forms can develop. The result links the organization of learned connections to the mathematical structure of correlated activity under the specified learning rule.
summary.tldr: Covariance eigenvectors help explain why Hebbian learning produces center-surround and certain orientation-sensitive receptive fields.

title: Analysis of Linsker's Simulations of Hebbian Rules

abstract: (1) The outputs of a typical multi-output classification network do not satisfy the axioms of probability; probabilities should be positive and sum to one. This problem can be solved by treating the trained network as a preprocessor that produces a feature vector that can be further processed, for instance by classical statistical estimation techniques. (2) We present a method for computing the first two moments ofthe probability distribution indicating the range of outputs that are consistent with the input and the training data. It is particularly useful to combine these two ideas: we implement the ideas of section 1 using Parzen windows, where the shape and relative size of each window is computed using the ideas of section 2. This allows us to make contact between important theoretical ideas (e.g. the ensemble formalism) and practical techniques (e.g. back-prop). Our results also shed new light on and generalize the well-known "soft max" scheme. 1 Distribution of Categories in Output Space In many neural-net applications, it is crucial to produce a set of C numbers that serve as estimates of the probability of C mutually exclusive outcomes. For exam(cid:173) ple, in speech recognition, these numbers represent the probability of C different phonemes; the probabilities of successive segments can be combined using a Hidden Markov Model. Similarly, in an Optical Character Recognition ("OCR") applica(cid:173) tion, the numbers represent C possible characters. Probability information for the "best guess" category (and probable runner-up categories) is combined with con(cid:173) text, cost information, etcetera, to produce recognition of multi-character strings.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the gap between classification-network outputs and valid probabilities. Typical output values need not be positive or sum to one. The proposed approach treats a trained network as a feature-producing preprocessor, then applies statistical estimation to its output vector to obtain probability information for mutually exclusive categories.

A second contribution computes the first two moments of a distribution describing outputs consistent with the input and training data. These moments summarize the distribution's location and spread. The authors combine this uncertainty information with Parzen-window estimation, using it to determine each window's shape and relative size rather than choosing those properties independently.

This combination connects theoretical treatment of distributions with practical backpropagation networks and generalizes the familiar softmax scheme. Its practical motivation is that recognition systems often need more than a winning label: probabilities for several categories can be combined with context or cost information. The paper therefore links learned features, probability estimation, and variation in plausible outputs within a single postprocessing approach.
summary.tldr: Statistical postprocessing turns network outputs into probability estimates using Parzen windows shaped by information about plausible output variation.

title: Transforming Neural-Net Output Levels to Probability Distributions

These results and additional experiments demonstrate that RBF networks can be successfully incorporated in hybrid recognizers and sug(cid:173) gest that they may be capable of good performance with fewer parameters than required by Gaussian mixture classifiers. A global parameter opti(cid:173) mization method designed to minimize the overall word error rather than the frame recognition error failed to reduce the error rate. 1 HMM/RBF HYBRID RECOGNIZER A hybrid isolated-word speech recognizer was developed which combines neural network and Hidden Markov Model (HMM) approaches. paragraphs: This paper combines hidden Markov models with radial basis function networks to recognize isolated spoken words from different speakers. The division of labor is deliberate: the neural network supplies static pattern classification, while HMM decoding handles the temporal alignment needed to interpret speech as a sequence.

Radial basis function networks were chosen because they offered classification performance comparable to other networks and could be trained rapidly through a one-pass matrix inversion method. On a speaker-independent E-set database, the hybrid system achieved an error rate of 11.5%, compared with 15.7% for the unimodal Gaussian HMM system on which it was based.

Additional experiments suggest that radial basis networks may achieve good performance with fewer parameters than Gaussian mixture classifiers. The paper also reports an unsuccessful extension: global parameter optimization aimed directly at overall word error did not reduce the error rate. The evidence therefore supports the hybrid architecture's improvement in this evaluation while separating that success from the attempted change in optimization objective.
summary.tldr: An HMM–radial basis network hybrid reduced isolated-word recognition error from 15.7% to 11.5% in the reported speaker-independent evaluation.

title: Improved Hidden Markov Model Speech Recognition Using Radial Basis Function Networks

abstract: The planar thallium-201 myocardial perfusion scintigram is a widely used diagnostic technique for detecting and estimating the risk of coronary artery disease. Neural networks learned to interpret 100 thallium scinti(cid:173) grams as determined by individual expert ratings. Standard error back(cid:173) propagation was compared to standard LMS, and LMS combined with one layer of RBF units. Using the "leave-one-out" method, generaliza(cid:173) tion was tested on all 100 cases. Training time was determined automati(cid:173) cally from cross-validation perfonnance. Best perfonnance was attained by the RBF/LMS network with three hidden units per view and compares favorably with human experts.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether neural networks can learn expert interpretations of heart perfusion images. The images are planar thallium scintigrams, which the abstract describes as a diagnostic technique for assessing coronary artery disease. Training uses 100 cases with ratings supplied by individual experts, so the learning target is their interpretation of the images.

The authors compare standard backpropagation, a standard least mean squares method, and least mean squares combined with a layer of radial basis function units. They evaluate generalization using leave-one-out testing across all 100 cases. In this procedure, each case takes a turn being excluded from the examples used to fit the model.

Training duration is chosen automatically using cross-validation performance. The strongest reported configuration combines radial basis functions with least mean squares and uses three hidden units per image view. Its performance compares favorably with human experts. The result concerns learning expert image assessments in this collection, with both the network design and the choice of training duration contributing to the evaluation.
summary.tldr: A radial basis function network achieved the best reported performance when learning expert interpretations of 100 cardiac scintigrams.

title: A Neural Network that Learns to Interpret Myocardial Planar Thallium Scintigrams

abstract: Reinforcement learning addresses the problem of learning to select actions in order to maximize one's performance in unknown environments. To scale reinforcement learning to complex real-world tasks, such as typically studied in AI, one must ultimately be able to discover the structure in the world, in order to abstract away the myriad of details and to operate in more tractable problem spaces. This paper presents the SKILLS algorithm. SKILLS discovers skills, which are partially defined action policies that arise in the context of multiple, related tasks. Skills collapse whole action sequences into single operators. They are learned by minimizing the com(cid:173) pactness of action policies, using a description length argument on their representation. Empirical results in simple grid navigation tasks illustrate the successful discovery of structure in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how reinforcement learning can discover useful structure across related tasks. Choosing individual actions in an unknown environment becomes difficult when many details must be considered. The proposed SKILLS algorithm learns reusable pieces of behavior that allow sequences of actions to be treated as single operators in a more manageable problem space.

A skill is a partially specified action policy that appears in the context of multiple related tasks. The learning principle uses description length to favor compact policy representations. When a reusable behavior helps describe several policies economically, it provides a candidate abstraction. This ties skill discovery to regularities shared across tasks rather than requiring every useful behavior to be specified beforehand.

Experiments in simple grid-navigation tasks demonstrate successful discovery of such structure. Their significance is that action abstraction can itself be learned: the learner identifies useful behavioral units while working across tasks. The reported evidence concerns these navigation settings, while the broader motivation is to make reinforcement learning more tractable by reducing how much low-level detail each decision must handle.
summary.tldr: SKILLS uses compact policy descriptions to discover reusable action sequences across related reinforcement-learning tasks.

title: Finding Structure in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We explain how the training data can be separated into clean informa(cid:173) tion and unexplainable noise. Analogous to the data, the neural network is separated into a time invariant structure used for forecasting, and a noisy part. We propose a unified theory connecting the optimization al(cid:173) gorithms for cleaning and learning together with algorithms that control the data noise and the parameter noise. The combined algorithm allows a data-driven local control of the liability of the network parameters and therefore an improvement in generalization. The approach is proven to be very useful at the task of forecasting the German bond market. 1 Introduction: The Observer-Observation Dilemma Human beings believe that they are able to solve a psychological version of the Observer(cid:173) Observation Dilemma. On the one hand, they use their observations to constitute an under(cid:173) standing of the laws of the world, on the other hand, they use this understanding to evaluate the correctness of the incoming pieces of information. Of course, as everybody knows, human beings are not free from making mistakes in this psychological dilemma. We en(cid:173) counter a similar situation when we try to build a mathematical model using data. Learning relationships from the data is only one part of the model building process. Overrating this part often leads to the phenomenon of overfitting in many applications (especially in eco(cid:173) nomic forecasting). In practice, evaluation of the data is often done by external knowledge, i. e. by optimizing the model under constraints of smoothness and regularization [7]. If we assume, that our model summerizes the best knowledge of the system to be identified, why should we not use the model itself to evaluate the correctness of the data? One approach to do this is called Clearning [11]. In this paper, we present a unified approach of the interac(cid:173) tion between the data and a neural network (see also [8]). It includes a new symmetric view on the optimization algorithms, here learning and cleaning, and their control by parameter and data noise. The Observer-Observation Dilemma in Neuro-Forecasting 993

paragraphs: The paper addresses a circular problem in forecasting: data are used to learn a model, yet the model can also help judge which parts of the data are informative. The authors separate training data into clean information and unexplained noise. They make a corresponding separation in the network between a time-invariant forecasting structure and a noisy component.

Their proposed theory connects data cleaning, network learning, and control of noise in both data and parameters. These operations are treated as parts of one optimization framework. This allows the learned model to participate in evaluating observations while observations continue to shape the model, rather than treating cleaning as an entirely external preparation step.

The combined algorithm provides local, data-driven control over network parameters, which the authors connect to improved generalization. They report that the approach is useful for forecasting the German bond market. The contribution is a coordinated treatment of uncertainty in observations and in the model, aimed at preserving forecastable structure while reducing overfitting.
summary.tldr: A unified forecasting framework jointly cleans data, learns network structure, and controls noise in observations and parameters.

title: The Observer-Observation Dilemma in Neuro-Forecasting

abstract: We describe an extension of the Markov decision process model in which a continuous time dimension is included in the state space. This allows for the representation and exact solution of a wide range of problems in which transitions or rewards vary over time. We examine problems based on route planning with public trans(cid:173) portation and telescope observation scheduling.
originalAbstract: We describe an extension of the Markov decision process model in which a continuous time dimension is included in the state space. This allows for the representation and exact solution of a wide range of problems in which transitions or rewards vary over time. We examine problems based on route planning with public trans(cid:173) portation and telescope observation scheduling.

paragraphs: Decision problems can depend on when an action is taken, because its possible consequences or rewards change over time. This paper extends the Markov decision process model by adding a continuous time coordinate to the state. Time thereby becomes an explicit part of the information used to describe the decision situation.

The extension allows the representation and exact solution of a wide range of problems with time-varying transitions or rewards. Including time in the state makes it possible to distinguish otherwise similar situations occurring at different moments. The exact-solution claim concerns the problems accommodated by the proposed framework, rather than every conceivable time-dependent decision problem.

The authors examine applications based on public-transport route planning and telescope observation scheduling. These provide two concrete settings for studying decisions whose timing affects the problem being solved. The contribution joins a modeling extension with exact solution capability, showing how continuous time can be incorporated directly into a Markov decision formulation for these kinds of planning tasks.
summary.tldr: Adding continuous time to an MDP's state enables exact solutions for a broad range of time-dependent planning problems.

title: Exact Solutions to Time-Dependent MDPs

abstract: People can understand complex auditory and visual information, often using one to disambiguate the other. Automated analysis, even at a low(cid:173) level, faces severe challenges, including the lack of accurate statistical models for the signals, and their high-dimensionality and varied sam(cid:173) pling rates. Previous approaches [6] assumed simple parametric models for the joint distribution which, while tractable, cannot capture the com(cid:173) plex signal relationships. We learn the joint distribution of the visual and auditory signals using a non-parametric approach. First, we project the data into a maximally informative, low-dimensional subspace, suitable for density estimation. We then model the complicated stochastic rela(cid:173) tionships between the signals using a nonparametric density estimator. These learned densities allow processing across signal modalities. We demonstrate, on synthetic and real signals, localization in video of the face that is speaking in audio, and, conversely, audio enhancement of a particular speaker selected from the video.

paragraphs: The paper learns relationships between sound and video so that one signal can help interpret the other. This is difficult because the signals have many dimensions, can be sampled at different rates, and have complicated statistical dependencies. Simple parametric joint models may be tractable, but the authors argue that they cannot capture the relationships needed here.

The approach first projects the observations into a low-dimensional subspace chosen to retain as much information as possible. It then estimates the joint distribution using a nonparametric density model. These stages work together: the projection makes density estimation more manageable, while the flexible estimator models stochastic relationships between the auditory and visual signals.

The learned distributions support processing in both directions. On synthetic and real signals, the authors demonstrate locating the speaking face in video using audio, and enhancing a particular speaker's audio after selecting that person visually. The contribution is a shared statistical representation that allows information from either modality to guide a task involving the other.
summary.tldr: A learned nonparametric audio-visual distribution supports locating speakers in video and enhancing the audio of a visually selected speaker.

title: Learning Joint Statistical Models for Audio-Visual Fusion and Segregation

abstract: We present a sequential Monte Carlo method applied to additive noise compensation for robust speech recognition in time-varying noise. The method generates a set of samples according to the prior distribution given by clean speech models and noise prior evolved from previous estimation. An explicit model representing noise effects on speech features is used, so that an extended Kalman filter is constructed for each sample, generating the updated continuous state estimate as the estimation of the noise parameter, and prediction likelihood for weighting each sample. Minimum mean square error (MMSE) inference of the time-varying noise parameter is carried out over these samples by fusion the estimation of samples according to their weights. A residual resampling selection step and a Metropolis-Hastings smoothing step are used to improve calculation efficiency. Experiments were conducted on speech recognition in simulated non-stationary noises, where noise power changed artificially, and highly non-stationary Machinegun noise. In all the experiments carried out, we observed that the method can have significant recognition performance improvement, over that achieved by noise compensation with stationary noise assumption.

paragraphs: The paper develops noise compensation for speech recognition when additive noise changes over time. A sequential Monte Carlo method draws samples using clean-speech models and a noise prior carried forward from previous estimates. This lets the noise estimate evolve as observations arrive instead of treating the noise as stationary.

An explicit model describes how noise affects speech features. For each sample, an extended Kalman filter updates the continuous noise-state estimate and produces a prediction likelihood used to weight that sample. Combining the estimates according to their weights yields a minimum mean square error estimate of the changing noise parameter.

Residual resampling and Metropolis-Hastings smoothing are included to improve computational efficiency. Experiments use both simulated noise with artificially changing power and highly non-stationary machinegun noise. Across the experiments, the authors report that the method can significantly improve recognition over compensation based on a stationary-noise assumption. The findings support adapting noise estimates over time in the changing-noise conditions they tested.
summary.tldr: Sequential sampling and per-sample Kalman filtering track changing noise and improve speech recognition over stationary-noise compensation in the reported experiments.

title: Sequential Noise Compensation by Sequential Monte Carlo Method

abstract: In this paper, we explore the use of Random Forests (RFs) in the struc- tured language model (SLM), which uses rich syntactic information in predicting the next word based on words already seen. The goal in this work is to construct RFs by randomly growing Decision Trees (DTs) us- ing syntactic information and investigate the performance of the SLM modeled by the RFs in automatic speech recognition. RFs, which were originally developed as classiﬁers, are a combination of decision tree classiﬁers. Each tree is grown based on random training data sampled independently and with the same distribution for all trees in the forest, and a random selection of possible questions at each node of the decision tree. Our approach extends the original idea of RFs to deal with the data sparseness problem encountered in language modeling. RFs have been studied in the context of n-gram language modeling and have been shown to generalize well to unseen data. We show in this paper that RFs using syntactic information can also achieve better performance in both perplexity (PPL) and word error rate (WER) in a large vocabulary speech recognition system, compared to a baseline that uses Kneser-Ney smoothing.

paragraphs: The paper explores random forests within a structured language model that uses syntactic information to predict the next word. The goal is to use information about language structure in randomly grown decision trees and assess the resulting model in automatic speech recognition. The approach extends random forests to address sparse observations in language modeling.

The forest combines decision trees built with randomness in both training-data selection and the questions available at each node. Here, syntactic information supplies material for those trees. This brings the forest approach into a model whose predictions depend on richer linguistic structure than the preceding words alone as an unstructured sequence.

The authors report improvements over a Kneser–Ney-smoothed baseline in both perplexity and word error rate within a large-vocabulary speech-recognition system. Perplexity assesses the language model's predictive performance, while word error rate reflects recognition output. Improvements in both connect the modeling change to the downstream speech task in the reported evaluation, supporting the use of syntactic random forests in this setting.
summary.tldr: Syntactic random forests improve structured language modeling and speech-recognition word error rate over the reported Kneser–Ney baseline.

title: Using Random Forests in the Structured Language Model

abstract: Finding maximally sparse representations from overcomplete feature dictionaries frequently involves minimizing a cost function composed of a likelihood (or data fit) term and a prior (or penalty function) that favors sparsity. While typically the prior is factorial, here we examine non-factorial alternatives that have a number of desirable properties relevant to sparse estimation and are easily implemented using an efficient, globally-convergent reweighted $\ell_1$ minimization procedure. The first method under consideration arises from the sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) framework. Although based on a highly non-convex underlying cost function, in the context of canonical sparse estimation problems, we prove uniform superiority of this method over the Lasso in that, (i) it can never do worse, and (ii) for any dictionary and sparsity profile, there will always exist cases where it does better. These results challenge the prevailing reliance on strictly convex penalty functions for finding sparse solutions. We then derive a new non-factorial variant with similar properties that exhibits further performance improvements in empirical tests. For both of these methods, as well as traditional factorial analogs, we demonstrate the effectiveness of reweighted $\ell_1$-norm algorithms in handling more general sparse estimation problems involving classification, group feature selection, and non-negativity constraints. As a byproduct of this development, a rigorous reformulation of sparse Bayesian classification (e.g., the relevance vector machine) is derived that, unlike the original, involves no approximation steps and descends a well-defined objective function.
originalAbstract: Finding maximally sparse representations from overcomplete feature dictionaries frequently involves minimizing a cost function composed of a likelihood (or data fit) term and a prior (or penalty function) that favors sparsity. While typically the prior is factorial, here we examine non-factorial alternatives that have a number of desirable properties relevant to sparse estimation and are easily implemented using an efficient, globally-convergent reweighted $\ell_1$ minimization procedure. The first method under consideration arises from the sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) framework. Although based on a highly non-convex underlying cost function, in the context of canonical sparse estimation problems, we prove uniform superiority of this method over the Lasso in that, (i) it can never do worse, and (ii) for any dictionary and sparsity profile, there will always exist cases where it does better. These results challenge the prevailing reliance on strictly convex penalty functions for finding sparse solutions. We then derive a new non-factorial variant with similar properties that exhibits further performance improvements in empirical tests. For both of these methods, as well as traditional factorial analogs, we demonstrate the effectiveness of reweighted $\ell_1$-norm algorithms in handling more general sparse estimation problems involving classification, group feature selection, and non-negativity constraints. As a byproduct of this development, a rigorous reformulation of sparse Bayesian classification (e.g., the relevance vector machine) is derived that, unlike the original, involves no approximation steps and descends a well-defined objective function.

paragraphs: Sparse estimation seeks an explanation that uses few features from a possibly overcomplete dictionary. Common methods balance data fit against a penalty that acts separately on each coefficient. This paper studies non-factorial priors, which allow the sparsity preference to depend jointly on coefficients, and implements them through efficient, globally convergent reweighted l1 minimization.

For a method derived from sparse Bayesian learning, the authors prove a strong comparison with Lasso in canonical sparse estimation problems. Within that setting, the method cannot do worse, and for every dictionary and sparsity profile there are cases where it does better. This is a scoped theoretical result, despite the underlying objective being highly nonconvex.

A new non-factorial variant has similar properties and further improves performance in empirical tests. The paper also applies reweighted l1 methods to classification, group feature selection, and non-negativity constraints. It derives a reformulation of sparse Bayesian classification that avoids approximation steps and decreases a well-defined objective, providing a clearer optimization foundation for that formulation.
summary.tldr: Non-factorial sparse priors yield theoretical advantages over Lasso in canonical problems and support broader estimation through reweighted l1 optimization.

title: Sparse Estimation Using General Likelihoods and Non-Factorial Priors

abstract: In this paper, we propose to learn a Mahalanobis distance to perform alignment of multivariate time series. The learning examples for this task are time series for which the true alignment is known. We cast the alignment problem as a structured prediction task, and propose realistic losses between alignments for which the optimization is tractable. We provide experiments on real data in the audio-to-audio context, where we show that the learning of a similarity measure leads to improvements in the performance of the alignment task. We also propose to use this metric learning framework to perform feature selection and, from basic audio features, build a combination of these with better alignment performance.

We provide experiments on real data in the audio-to-audio context, where we show that the learning of a similarity measure leads to improvements in the performance of the alignment task. We also propose to use this metric learning framework to perform feature selection and, from basic audio features, build a combination of these with better alignment performance.

paragraphs: Aligning multivariate time series means identifying which positions in one sequence correspond to positions in another. The quality of that alignment depends on how differences between observations are measured. This paper learns a Mahalanobis distance from training sequences whose correct alignments are known, using supervision to adapt the similarity measure to the task.

The authors formulate alignment as structured prediction, treating the correspondence between sequences as the output to be learned. They propose losses that measure errors between alignments while keeping optimization tractable. This connects the learned distance to the quality of the resulting sequence alignment, rather than leaving similarity as a fixed input to the procedure.

Experiments on real audio-to-audio data show improved alignment performance from learning the similarity measure. The paper also uses the framework for feature selection, combining basic audio features into a representation with better alignment performance. These findings support learning both how observations are compared and which features contribute to that comparison from examples of correct temporal correspondence.
summary.tldr: Learning a distance from known temporal alignments improves audio sequence alignment and supports feature selection.

title: Metric Learning for Temporal Sequence Alignment

abstract: We study accelerated mirror descent dynamics in continuous and discrete time. Combining the original continuous-time motivation of mirror descent with a recent ODE interpretation of Nesterov's accelerated method, we propose a family of continuous-time descent dynamics for convex functions with Lipschitz gradients, such that the solution trajectories are guaranteed to converge to the optimum at a $O(1/t^2)$ rate. We then show that a large family of first-order accelerated methods can be obtained as a discretization of the ODE, and these methods converge at a $O(1/k^2)$ rate. This connection between accelerated mirror descent and the ODE provides an intuitive approach to the design and analysis of accelerated first-order algorithms.

We then show that a large family of first-order accelerated methods can be obtained as a discretization of the ODE, and these methods converge at a $O(1/k^2)$ rate. paragraphs: Accelerated optimization methods are usually described as sequences of updates. This paper studies them through a complementary picture: a point moving continuously toward an optimum according to a differential equation. It combines the continuous-time motivation behind mirror descent with an ordinary differential equation interpretation of Nesterov acceleration.

For convex functions with Lipschitz gradients, the authors propose a family of continuous-time descent dynamics with a guaranteed O(1/t²) convergence rate. The smoothness assumption controls how quickly gradients can change. Within this setting, the result gives a precise relationship between elapsed time and progress toward the optimum.

The authors then connect these continuous trajectories to implementable algorithms by discretizing the differential equation. A large family of first-order accelerated methods emerges this way, with O(1/k²) convergence in the number of iterations. The value of the connection is methodological as well as theoretical: one continuous-time description provides an intuitive route to designing and analyzing multiple accelerated algorithms, rather than treating each update rule as an isolated construction.
summary.tldr: Continuous-time mirror descent dynamics provide a unified route to accelerated first-order algorithms with O(1/k²) convergence for the studied convex problems.

title: Accelerated Mirror Descent in Continuous and Discrete Time

abstract: As datasets capturing human choices grow in richness and scale, particularly in online domains, there is an increasing need for choice models flexible enough to handle data that violate traditional choice-theoretic axioms such as regularity, stochastic transitivity, or Luce's choice axiom. In this work we introduce the Pairwise Choice Markov Chain (PCMC) model of discrete choice, an inferentially tractable model that does not assume these traditional axioms while still satisfying the foundational axiom of uniform expansion, which can be viewed as a weaker version of Luce's axiom. We show that the PCMC model significantly outperforms the Multinomial Logit (MNL) model in prediction tasks on two empirical data sets known to exhibit violations of Luce's axiom. Our analysis also synthesizes several recent observations connecting the Multinomial Logit model and Markov chains; the PCMC model retains the Multinomial Logit model as a special case.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Pairwise Choice Markov Chains, a model for predicting discrete choices. Its motivation is that rich human-choice datasets can violate familiar assumptions used by traditional models. The proposed model does not require regularity, stochastic transitivity, or Luce's choice axiom, allowing it to represent behavior outside those restrictions.

The model remains tractable for inference and retains a weaker structural requirement called uniform expansion. The abstract describes this as a weaker version of Luce's axiom. It also contains Multinomial Logit as a special case, so the new framework extends that established model while preserving its availability within the larger family.

On two empirical datasets known to violate Luce's axiom, the proposed approach significantly outperformed Multinomial Logit in prediction tasks. These results support the practical value of relaxing traditional choice assumptions in settings where they are violated. The analysis also brings together connections between Multinomial Logit and Markov chains, placing the broader choice model in a framework that includes the conventional one.
summary.tldr: Pairwise Choice Markov Chains relax traditional choice assumptions and outperform Multinomial Logit on two datasets exhibiting violations of Luce's axiom.

title: Pairwise Choice Markov Chains

abstract: We describe Swapout, a new stochastic training method, that outperforms ResNets of identical network structure yielding impressive results on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Swapout samples from a rich set of architectures including dropout, stochastic depth and residual architectures as special cases. When viewed as a regularization method swapout not only inhibits co-adaptation of units in a layer, similar to dropout, but also across network layers. We conjecture that swapout achieves strong regularization by implicitly tying the parameters across layers. When viewed as an ensemble training method, it samples a much richer set of architectures than existing methods such as dropout or stochastic depth. We propose a parameterization that reveals connections to exiting architectures and suggests a much richer set of architectures to be explored. We show that our formulation suggests an efficient training method and validate our conclusions on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 matching state of the art accuracy. Remarkably, our 32 layer wider model performs similar to a 1001 layer ResNet model.

paragraphs: Swapout is a stochastic training method that samples from a broad collection of network architectures. Dropout, stochastic depth, and residual architectures appear as special cases within its formulation. The method therefore trains through architectural variation, giving an ensemble interpretation to the networks encountered during learning.

The authors also explain Swapout as regularization. It discourages units from depending too strongly on one another both within a layer and across layers. They conjecture that implicit parameter tying across layers helps explain the strong regularization; this proposed explanation is not presented as an established result. Their parameterization exposes connections among existing architectures and suggests additional structures to explore.

On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the paper reports improvements over ResNets with identical network structure and accuracy matching the state of the art. A wider 32-layer model performs similarly to a 1001-layer ResNet in the reported comparison. These findings support the proposed efficient training formulation and show that sampled architectural variation can be useful without relying solely on greater depth.
summary.tldr: Swapout trains through a rich set of sampled architectures, providing regularization and strong reported image-classification performance.

title: Swapout: Learning an ensemble of deep architectures

abstract: Optical imaging methods using calcium indicators are critical for monitoring the activity of large neuronal populations in vivo. Imaging experiments typically generate a large amount of data that needs to be processed to extract the activity of the imaged neuronal sources. While deriving such processing algorithms is an active area of research, most existing methods require the processing of large amounts of data at a time, rendering them vulnerable to the volume of the recorded data, and preventing real-time experimental interrogation. Here we introduce OnACID, an Online framework for the Analysis of streaming Calcium Imaging Data, including i) motion artifact correction, ii) neuronal source extraction, and iii) activity denoising and deconvolution. Our approach combines and extends previous work on online dictionary learning and calcium imaging data analysis, to deliver an automated pipeline that can discover and track the activity of hundreds of cells in real time, thereby enabling new types of closed-loop experiments. We apply our algorithm on two large scale experimental datasets, benchmark its performance on manually annotated data, and show that it outperforms a popular offline approach.

paragraphs: Calcium imaging produces large streams of images that must be processed to recover neuronal activity. Methods that operate on large batches can struggle with the volume of recordings and delay access to results. This paper introduces OnACID to process incoming imaging data online, supporting analysis while an experiment is taking place.

The pipeline combines motion correction, neuronal source extraction, and activity denoising and deconvolution. These stages address movement in the images, identify the neuronal sources, and recover cleaner activity signals. The framework combines and extends earlier work in online dictionary learning and calcium-imaging analysis to discover and track hundreds of cells in real time.

The authors apply OnACID to two large experimental datasets, evaluate it against manually annotated data, and report that it outperforms a popular offline approach. Real-time processing also creates opportunities for closed-loop experiments, where ongoing measurements can inform experimental actions. The contribution is an automated streaming pipeline that connects the necessary processing stages closely enough to make that interaction possible.
summary.tldr: OnACID processes streaming calcium images to discover and track hundreds of neurons in real time, enabling closed-loop experimental workflows.

title: OnACID: Online Analysis of Calcium Imaging Data in Real Time

abstract: Bayesian optimization has shown success in global optimization of expensive-to-evaluate multimodal objective functions. However, unlike most optimization methods, Bayesian optimization typically does not use derivative information. In this paper we show how Bayesian optimization can exploit derivative information to find good solutions with fewer objective function evaluations. In particular, we develop a novel Bayesian optimization algorithm, the derivative-enabled knowledge-gradient (dKG), which is one-step Bayes-optimal, asymptotically consistent, and provides greater one-step value of information than in the derivative-free setting. dKG accommodates noisy and incomplete derivative information, comes in both sequential and batch forms, and can optionally reduce the computational cost of inference through automatically selected retention of a single directional derivative. We also compute the dKG acquisition function and its gradient using a novel fast discretization-free technique. We show dKG provides state-of-the-art performance compared to a wide range of optimization procedures with and without gradients, on benchmarks including logistic regression, deep learning, kernel learning, and k-nearest neighbors.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization seeks good solutions when evaluating an objective is expensive and the objective may have multiple peaks or valleys. It typically does not use derivatives, even though derivatives provide information about how the objective changes. This paper develops derivative-enabled knowledge-gradient, or dKG, to exploit that information and reduce the number of objective evaluations needed.

The algorithm supports noisy or incomplete derivatives and can choose evaluations sequentially or in batches. An optional mechanism automatically retains a single directional derivative to reduce inference costs. The authors also introduce a fast technique for computing the acquisition function, which guides evaluation choices, and its gradient without discretization.

The theoretical results establish one-step Bayes optimality, asymptotic consistency, and greater one-step information value than in the derivative-free setting. The one-step qualification concerns the immediate decision criterion rather than an unrestricted guarantee about every sequence of evaluations. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance against methods with and without gradients on benchmarks spanning logistic regression, deep learning, kernel learning, and nearest-neighbor models.
summary.tldr: Derivative-enabled knowledge-gradient incorporates noisy or incomplete gradients into Bayesian optimization to find good solutions with fewer evaluations.

title: Bayesian Optimization with Gradients

abstract: We address the problem of dueling bandits defined on partially ordered sets, or posets. In this setting, arms may not be comparable, and there may be several (incomparable) optimal arms. We propose an algorithm, UnchainedBandits, that efficiently finds the set of optimal arms, or Pareto front, of any poset even when pairs of comparable arms cannot be a priori distinguished from pairs of incomparable arms, with a set of minimal assumptions. This means that UnchainedBandits does not require information about comparability and can be used with limited knowledge of the poset. To achieve this, the algorithm relies on the concept of decoys, which stems from social psychology. We also provide theoretical guarantees on both the regret incurred and the number of comparison required by UnchainedBandits, and we report compelling empirical results.

paragraphs: Dueling bandits learn about choices through comparisons between pairs. This paper considers a setting where those choices form a partial order, meaning that some pairs cannot be ranked against each other. Consequently, the best outcome may be a set of mutually incomparable options rather than one universally superior choice.

The proposed algorithm, UnchainedBandits, seeks this set of optimal choices, called the Pareto front. A central challenge is that it is not told which pairs are comparable. Under a set of minimal assumptions, it can find the optimal set for any partial order despite that missing information. Its approach uses decoys, a concept drawn from social psychology, to address the comparison problem.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for both the regret incurred and the number of comparisons required, alongside empirical results supporting the method. These two guarantees address different costs of learning: the quality sacrificed while exploring and the amount of comparison work needed. The contribution extends comparison-based learning to problems where incomplete ordering is part of the structure.
summary.tldr: UnchainedBandits identifies optimal options in partial orders without prior knowledge of which pairs can be compared.

title: Bandits Dueling on Partially Ordered Sets

abstract: In this paper we study differentially private Empirical Risk Minimization(ERM) in different settings. For smooth (strongly) convex loss function with or without (non)-smooth regularization, we give algorithms which achieve either optimal or near optimal utility bound with less gradient complexity compared with previous work. For ERM with smooth convex loss function in high-dimension($p\gg n$) setting, we give an algorithm which achieves the upper bound with less gradient complexity than previous ones. At last, we generalize the expected excess empirical risk from convex to Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition and give a tighter upper bound of the utility comparing with the result in \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/ZhangZMW17}.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization fits a model by reducing its loss on training data. This paper studies algorithms that perform this optimization with differential privacy. Its central concern is achieving strong utility guarantees while reducing gradient complexity, meaning the amount of gradient computation needed by the algorithm.

For smooth convex and strongly convex losses, the authors give algorithms with optimal or nearly optimal utility bounds and lower gradient complexity than previous work. Their treatment includes settings with no regularizer and settings with smooth or nonsmooth regularization. They also address smooth convex problems where the number of features greatly exceeds the number of observations, again reducing gradient complexity while attaining the stated upper bound.

The final contribution extends expected excess empirical risk analysis from convex objectives to objectives satisfying the Polyak–Lojasiewicz condition. In that setting, the paper provides a tighter utility upper bound than the cited earlier result. These are guarantees for specified optimization settings: the broader scope comes from covering additional objective conditions while improving the computational requirements of private learning.
summary.tldr: The paper reduces gradient complexity for private empirical risk minimization and extends utility guarantees to Polyak–Lojasiewicz objectives.

title: Differentially Private Empirical Risk Minimization Revisited: Faster and More General

abstract: Recent attempts to achieve fairness in predictive models focus on the balance between fairness and accuracy. In sensitive applications such as healthcare or criminal justice, this trade-off is often undesirable as any increase in prediction error could have devastating consequences. In this work, we argue that the fairness of predictions should be evaluated in context of the data, and that unfairness induced by inadequate samples sizes or unmeasured predictive variables should be addressed through data collection, rather than by constraining the model. We decompose cost-based metrics of discrimination into bias, variance, and noise, and propose actions aimed at estimating and reducing each term. Finally, we perform case-studies on prediction of income, mortality, and review ratings, confirming the value of this analysis. We find that data collection is often a means to reduce discrimination without sacrificing accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper argues that unfair predictions should be examined in the context of the data used to train and evaluate a model. Inadequate sample sizes and missing predictive variables can contribute to discrimination. When those are the causes, the authors advocate addressing them through data collection rather than relying on constraints imposed on the model.

The proposed analysis decomposes cost-based discrimination metrics into bias, variance, and noise. The authors then suggest actions for estimating and reducing each component. This makes the observed discrimination something to investigate by source, helping connect a measured disparity with a possible intervention instead of treating every disparity as the same modeling problem.

Case studies involving income, mortality, and review-rating prediction support the value of the analysis. The authors find that collecting data can often reduce discrimination without sacrificing accuracy. That qualified finding matters in sensitive settings where additional prediction errors can have serious consequences. The contribution is a way to diagnose data-related causes of unfairness and identify opportunities to improve fairness and accuracy together.
summary.tldr: Decomposing discrimination into bias, variance, and noise can reveal data-collection opportunities that reduce unfairness without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Why Is My Classifier Discriminatory?

abstract: Recommender systems have attracted much attention during the past decade. Many attack detection algorithms have been developed for better recommendations, mostly focusing on shilling attacks, where an attack organizer produces a large number of user profiles by the same strategy to promote or demote an item. This work considers another different attack style: unorganized malicious attacks, where attackers individually utilize a small number of user profiles to attack different items without organizer. This attack style occurs in many real applications, yet relevant study remains open. We formulate the unorganized malicious attacks detection as a matrix completion problem, and propose the Unorganized Malicious Attacks detection (UMA) algorithm, based on the alternating splitting augmented Lagrangian method. We verify, both theoretically and empirically, the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Much attack-detection work focuses on coordinated shilling, where an organizer creates many profiles following a common strategy to promote or demote an item. This paper examines a different pattern: independent attackers use small numbers of profiles against different items without a shared organizer.

The authors formulate detection of these unorganized malicious attacks as a matrix completion problem. They then propose the UMA algorithm, using an alternating splitting augmented Lagrangian method to solve the resulting optimization task. This formulation makes the unorganized attack setting the direct focus of the detection procedure.

The paper reports both theoretical and empirical verification of the approach's effectiveness. Its contribution is to extend attention beyond a coordinated attack pattern that dominates much of the existing work. Because the studied attackers act independently and target different items, the problem captures a distinct kind of manipulation that the authors identify as occurring in real applications. UMA provides a concrete algorithmic response to that setting.
summary.tldr: UMA formulates detection of independent, small-profile attacks on recommender systems as matrix completion and receives theoretical and empirical support.

title: Unorganized Malicious Attacks Detection

abstract: We study the fundamental problems of identity testing (goodness of fit), and closeness testing (two sample test) of distributions over $k$ elements, under differential privacy. While the problems have a long history in statistics, finite sample bounds for these problems have only been established recently. In this work, we derive upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of both the problems under $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy. We provide optimal sample complexity algorithms for identity testing problem for all parameter ranges, and the first results for closeness testing. Our closeness testing bounds are optimal in the sparse regime where the number of samples is at most $k$. Our upper bounds are obtained by privatizing non-private estimators for these problems. The non-private estimators are chosen to have small sensitivity. We propose a general framework to establish lower bounds on the sample complexity of statistical tasks under differential privacy. We show a bound on differentially private algorithms in terms of a coupling between the two hypothesis classes we aim to test. By constructing carefully chosen priors over the hypothesis classes, and using Le Cam's two point theorem we provide a general mechanism for proving lower bounds. We believe that the framework can be used to obtain strong lower bounds for other statistical tasks under privacy.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many samples are needed to compare discrete probability distributions while satisfying differential privacy. It studies identity testing, which checks agreement with a specified distribution, and closeness testing, which compares two sampled distributions. Both problems concern distributions over k possible elements, and the analysis accounts for the privacy parameters ε and δ.

The authors derive upper and lower sample-complexity bounds. For identity testing, their algorithms are optimal across all parameter ranges. For closeness testing, they provide the first results under this privacy formulation, with optimal bounds in the sparse regime where the sample count is at most k. Their algorithms privatize existing estimators chosen for low sensitivity to changes in the data.

It connects private testing to couplings between competing hypothesis classes, then combines carefully selected priors with Le Cam’s two-point theorem. This framework explains why certain sample costs cannot be avoided. The authors suggest it may also yield strong lower bounds for other private statistical tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal private identity-testing sample complexity and sparse-regime closeness-testing bounds, alongside a general lower-bound framework.

title: Differentially Private Testing of Identity and Closeness of Discrete Distributions

abstract: Zero-shot learning (ZSL) aims to recognize unseen object classes without any training samples, which can be regarded as a form of transfer learning from seen classes to unseen ones. This is made possible by learning a projection between a feature space and a semantic space (e.g. attribute space). Key to ZSL is thus to learn a projection function that is robust against the often large domain gap between the seen and unseen classes. In this paper, we propose a novel ZSL model termed domain-invariant projection learning (DIPL). Our model has two novel components: (1) A domain-invariant feature self-reconstruction task is introduced to the seen/unseen class data, resulting in a simple linear formulation that casts ZSL into a min-min optimization problem. Solving the problem is non-trivial, and a novel iterative algorithm is formulated as the solver, with rigorous theoretic algorithm analysis provided. (2) To further align the two domains via the learned projection, shared semantic structure among seen and unseen classes is explored via forming superclasses in the semantic space. Extensive experiments show that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art alternatives by significant margins.
originalAbstract: Zero-shot learning (ZSL) aims to recognize unseen object classes without any training samples, which can be regarded as a form of transfer learning from seen classes to unseen ones. This is made possible by learning a projection between a feature space and a semantic space (e.g. attribute space). Key to ZSL is thus to learn a projection function that is robust against the often large domain gap between the seen and unseen classes. In this paper, we propose a novel ZSL model termed domain-invariant projection learning (DIPL). Our model has two novel components: (1) A domain-invariant feature self-reconstruction task is introduced to the seen/unseen class data, resulting in a simple linear formulation that casts ZSL into a min-min optimization problem. Solving the problem is non-trivial, and a novel iterative algorithm is formulated as the solver, with rigorous theoretic algorithm analysis provided. (2) To further align the two domains via the learned projection, shared semantic structure among seen and unseen classes is explored via forming superclasses in the semantic space. Extensive experiments show that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art alternatives by significant margins.

paragraphs: Zero-shot recognition uses knowledge about seen object classes to recognize classes without training examples. A common bridge is a learned projection between visual features and semantic descriptions, such as attributes. The difficulty is that seen and unseen classes can differ substantially, so a projection learned for one group may transfer poorly.

Domain-invariant projection learning addresses this gap with two components. First, it introduces a feature self-reconstruction task involving seen and unseen class data. This gives a linear formulation with a min-min optimization objective. The authors develop an iterative solver for that objective and provide theoretical analysis of the algorithm.

Second, the method groups classes into superclasses in semantic space, using shared semantic structure to further align the seen and unseen domains through the projection. The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art alternatives in extensive experiments. The findings support combining reconstruction and shared class structure to learn a projection that transfers more effectively across the class divide.
summary.tldr: Feature reconstruction and shared semantic superclasses improve the transfer of a learned projection to unseen object classes.

title: Domain-Invariant Projection Learning for Zero-Shot Recognition

abstract: Many neurons in the brain, such as place cells in the rodent hippocampus, have localized receptive fields, i.e., they respond to a small neighborhood of stimulus space. What is the functional significance of such representations and how can they arise? Here, we propose that localized receptive fields emerge in similarity-preserving networks of rectifying neurons that learn low-dimensional manifolds populated by sensory inputs. Numerical simulations of such networks on standard datasets yield manifold-tiling localized receptive fields. More generally, we show analytically that, for data lying on symmetric manifolds, optimal solutions of objectives, from which similarity-preserving networks are derived, have localized receptive fields. Therefore, nonnegative similarity-preserving mapping (NSM) implemented by neural networks can model representations of continuous manifolds in the brain.

paragraphs: Many biological neurons respond only to a small neighborhood of possible stimuli. The paper asks what purpose these localized receptive fields might serve and how they could emerge through learning. Its proposal is that they arise in networks of rectifying neurons trained to preserve similarities among sensory inputs lying on low-dimensional manifolds.

The authors study nonnegative similarity-preserving mapping, a representation that retains relationships among inputs while using nonnegative neural outputs. Numerical simulations on standard datasets produce localized receptive fields that collectively tile the input manifold. This connects a network-level learning objective with an organized pattern of individual neuron responses.

The analytical result applies to data on symmetric manifolds: optimal solutions of the objectives underlying these networks have localized receptive fields. That symmetry condition defines the scope of the stated proof, while the simulations provide complementary evidence of the behavior. summary.tldr: Similarity-preserving networks produce localized receptive fields in simulations, with optimality proved for data on symmetric manifolds.

title: Manifold-tiling Localized Receptive Fields are Optimal in Similarity-preserving Neural Networks

abstract: Recent advances in generative modeling have led to an increased interest in the study of statistical divergences as means of model comparison. Commonly used evaluation methods, such as the Frechet Inception Distance (FID), correlate well with the perceived quality of samples and are sensitive to mode dropping. However, these metrics are unable to distinguish between different failure cases since they only yield one-dimensional scores. We propose a novel definition of precision and recall for distributions which disentangles the divergence into two separate dimensions. The proposed notion is intuitive, retains desirable properties, and naturally leads to an efficient algorithm that can be used to evaluate generative models. We relate this notion to total variation as well as to recent evaluation metrics such as Inception Score and FID. To demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed approach we perform an empirical study on several variants of Generative Adversarial Networks and Variational Autoencoders. In an extensive set of experiments we show that the proposed metric is able to disentangle the quality of generated samples from the coverage of the target distribution.

paragraphs: Evaluating a generative model involves at least two questions: whether its samples are good and whether they represent the variety in the target distribution. A single score can respond to both issues without revealing which one causes a poor result. The paper identifies this ambiguity in commonly used evaluation measures, including FID.

The authors define precision and recall for probability distributions to separate these aspects of comparison. Their definition gives two dimensions of assessment and leads to an efficient evaluation algorithm. They also connect it mathematically to total variation and relate it to established measures such as Inception Score and FID.

An empirical study of several GAN and variational autoencoder variants tests the usefulness of this separation. Across an extensive collection of experiments, the proposed measure distinguishes generated-sample quality from coverage of the target distribution. The practical contribution is a more informative diagnosis: comparisons can expose different failure patterns that would otherwise be compressed into one number, making the nature of a model's performance easier to interpret.
summary.tldr: Distributional precision and recall separate the quality of generated samples from coverage of the target distribution.

title: Assessing Generative Models via Precision and Recall

abstract: Progress in natural language processing (NLP) models that estimate representations of word sequences has recently been leveraged to improve the understanding of language processing in the brain. However, these models have not been specifically designed to capture the way the brain represents language meaning. We hypothesize that fine-tuning these models to predict recordings of brain activity of people reading text will lead to representations that encode more brain-activity-relevant language information. We demonstrate that a version of BERT, a recently introduced and powerful language model, can improve the prediction of brain activity after fine-tuning. We show that the relationship between language and brain activity learned by BERT during this fine-tuning transfers across multiple participants. We also show that, for some participants, the fine-tuned representations learned from both magnetoencephalography (MEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) are better for predicting fMRI than the representations learned from fMRI alone, indicating that the learned representations capture brain-activity-relevant information that is not simply an artifact of the modality. While changes to language representations help the model predict brain activity, they also do not harm the model's ability to perform downstream NLP tasks. Our findings are notable for research on language understanding in the brain.

This paper tests whether fine-tuning a language model to predict recorded brain activity can make its representations more informative about how the brain processes language meaning.

The authors fine-tune a version of BERT and find improved prediction of brain activity. The learned relationship between language and brain responses also transfers across multiple participants. This transfer matters because it shows that the adaptation captures information useful beyond the participant-specific setting in which a relationship was learned.

summary.tldr: Fine-tuning BERT on brain recordings improves brain-activity prediction, transfers across participants, and preserves reported downstream NLP performance.

title: Inducing brain-relevant bias in natural language processing models

abstract: We consider the problem of learning to play a repeated multi-agent game with an unknown reward function. Single player online learning algorithms attain strong regret bounds when provided with full information feedback, which unfortunately is unavailable in many real-world scenarios. Bandit feedback alone, i.e., observing outcomes only for the selected action, yields substantially worse performance. In this paper, we consider a natural model where, besides a noisy measurement of the obtained reward, the player can also observe the opponents' actions. This feedback model, together with a regularity assumption on the reward function, allows us to exploit the correlations among different game outcomes by means of Gaussian processes (GPs). We propose a novel confidence-bound based bandit algorithm GP-MW, which utilizes the GP model for the reward function and runs a multiplicative weight (MW) method. We obtain novel kernel-dependent regret bounds that are comparable to the known bounds in the full information setting, while substantially improving upon the existing bandit results. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of GP-MW in random matrix games, as well as real-world problems of traffic routing and movie recommendation. In our experiments, GP-MW consistently outperforms several baselines, while its performance is often comparable to methods that have access to full information feedback.

The proposed GP-MW algorithm models rewards with a Gaussian process and combines confidence bounds with a multiplicative-weights method. The model provides a way to use observed outcomes when reasoning about related outcomes. This creates an information advantage over treating every unobserved reward as unrelated to the observations already collected.

Both the theory and experiments depend on the richer feedback model rather than reward-only observations.
summary.tldr: GP-MW exploits correlated rewards and observed opponent actions to improve learning guarantees and empirical performance in unknown repeated games.

title: No-Regret Learning in Unknown Games with Correlated Payoffs

abstract: Distance Metric Learning aims to learn an appropriate metric that faithfully measures the distance between two data points. Traditional metric learning methods usually calculate the pairwise distance with fixed distance functions (\emph{e.g.,}\ Euclidean distance) in the projected feature spaces. However, they fail to learn the underlying geometries of the sample space, and thus cannot exactly predict the intrinsic distances between data points. To address this issue, we first reveal that the traditional linear distance metric is equivalent to the cumulative arc length between the data pair's nearest points on the learned straight measurer lines. After that, by extending such straight lines to general curved forms, we propose a Curvilinear Distance Metric Learning (CDML) method, which adaptively learns the nonlinear geometries of the training data. By virtue of Weierstrass theorem, the proposed CDML is equivalently parameterized with a 3-order tensor, and the optimization algorithm is designed to learn the tensor parameter. Theoretical analysis is derived to guarantee the effectiveness and soundness of CDML. Extensive experiments on the synthetic and real-world datasets validate the superiority of our method over the state-of-the-art metric learning models.

paragraphs: Distance metric learning seeks a measure of separation that reflects the structure of data. Conventional approaches often project data into a feature space and apply a fixed distance function there. This paper argues that such methods fail to capture the underlying geometry needed to represent intrinsic distances, and proposes learning curved measuring structures instead.

The starting point is a reinterpretation of linear distance metrics. The authors show an equivalence with accumulated arc lengths between the nearest points on learned straight measuring lines. They then extend these lines to curves, creating Curvilinear Distance Metric Learning. The curves allow the learned measure to adapt to nonlinear geometry in the training data.

Using the Weierstrass theorem, the authors express the method through a third-order tensor and develop an algorithm to learn its parameters. They provide theoretical analysis supporting the formulation and report better performance than state-of-the-art metric-learning models on synthetic and real datasets. The contribution makes the geometry of the measuring structure itself part of what is learned.
summary.tldr: Curvilinear Distance Metric Learning replaces straight measuring structures with learned curves to capture nonlinear data geometry.

title: Curvilinear Distance Metric Learning

abstract: We consider the issue of biases in scholarly research, specifically, in peer review. There is a long standing debate on whether exposing author identities to reviewers induces biases against certain groups, and our focus is on designing tests to detect the presence of such biases. Our starting point is a remarkable recent work by Tomkins, Zhang and Heavlin which conducted a controlled, large-scale experiment to investigate existence of biases in the peer reviewing of the WSDM conference. We present two sets of results in this paper. The first set of results is negative, and pertains to the statistical tests and the experimental setup used in the work of Tomkins et al. We show that the test employed therein does not guarantee control over false alarm probability and under correlations between relevant variables, coupled with any of the following conditions, with high probability can declare a presence of bias when it is in fact absent: (a) measurement error, (b) model mismatch, (c) reviewer calibration. Moreover, we show that the setup of their experiment may itself inflate false alarm probability if (d) bidding is performed in non-blind manner or (e) popular reviewer assignment procedure is employed. Our second set of results is positive, in that we present a general framework for testing for biases in (single vs. double blind) peer review. We then present a hypothesis test with guaranteed control over false alarm probability and non-trivial power even under conditions (a)--(c). Conditions (d) and (e) are more fundamental problems that are tied to the experimental setup and not necessarily related to the test.

paragraphs: Testing whether revealing author identities causes peer-review bias requires separating actual bias from statistical artifacts. This paper examines both the hypothesis test and experimental design used in an earlier controlled conference study. Its negative results concern the reliability of detecting bias, rather than establishing that bias is absent.

The authors show that the earlier test does not guarantee control of false alarms. When relevant variables are correlated, measurement error, model mismatch, or reviewer calibration can each contribute to a high probability of declaring bias when none exists. The bidding and assignment problems remain more fundamental design issues, not necessarily defects a different statistical test can fix. The contribution clarifies which problems require better inference and which require changes to how the experiment is organized.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies false-alarm risks in peer-review bias studies and proposes a test robust to several statistical problems while distinguishing experimental-design issues.

title: On Testing for Biases in Peer Review

abstract: Deep learning relies on good initialization schemes and hyperparameter choices prior to training a neural network. Random weight initializations induce random network ensembles, which give rise to the trainability, training speed, and sometimes also generalization ability of an instance. In addition, such ensembles provide theoretical insights into the space of candidate models of which one is selected during training. The results obtained so far rely on mean field approximations that assume infinite layer width and that study average squared signals. We derive the joint signal output distribution exactly, without mean field assumptions, for fully-connected networks with Gaussian weights and biases, and analyze deviations from the mean field results. For rectified linear units, we further discuss limitations of the standard initialization scheme, such as its lack of dynamical isometry, and propose a simple alternative that overcomes these by initial parameter sharing.

paragraphs: The paper examines neural networks before training, when randomly chosen weights and biases define a collection of possible models. These initialization choices affect how trainable individual networks are and how quickly training proceeds. Understanding this starting distribution can therefore reveal properties of the models from which learning selects a solution.

Earlier analyses use mean-field approximations that assume infinitely wide layers and examine average squared signals. The authors instead derive the exact joint distribution of signal outputs for fully connected networks with Gaussian weights and biases. This allows them to analyze departures from mean-field predictions while retaining information about the output distribution beyond an average squared quantity.

For ReLU networks, the paper then examines shortcomings of the standard initialization, including its failure to provide dynamical isometry. The proposed alternative uses parameter sharing at initialization to overcome these limitations. The contribution links a more exact description of random networks to an initialization design, under the stated fully connected Gaussian setting for the distributional analysis.
summary.tldr: An exact analysis of Gaussian-initialized networks motivates initial parameter sharing to address standard ReLU initialization's lack of dynamical isometry.

title: Initialization of ReLUs for Dynamical Isometry

abstract: We consider the problem of detecting anomalies in a large dataset. We propose a framework called Partial Identification which captures the intuition that anomalies are easy to distinguish from the overwhelming majority of points by relatively few attribute values. Formalizing this intuition, we propose a geometric anomaly measure for a point that we call PIDScore, which measures the minimum density of data points over all subcubes containing the point. We present PIDForest: a random forest based algorithm that finds anomalies based on this definition. We show that it performs favorably in comparison to several popular anomaly detection methods, across a broad range of benchmarks. PIDForest also provides a succinct explanation for why a point is labelled anomalous, by providing a set of features and ranges for them which are relatively uncommon in the dataset.
