paragraphs: An unusual data point may stand out because of only a few of its attributes. PIDForest builds anomaly detection around this intuition: a small amount of information can distinguish an anomaly from the overwhelming majority of a dataset. The paper calls this principle partial identification and turns it into a geometric definition of unusualness.

Its measure, PIDScore, looks at subcubes containing a point and takes the minimum density of data points across them. In plain terms, the score asks whether the point belongs to a particularly sparsely occupied region defined through attribute ranges. The authors then introduce a random-forest-based algorithm that detects anomalies using this definition.

Across a broad range of benchmarks, PIDForest compares favorably with several popular anomaly-detection methods. It also supplies a compact explanation for each anomaly by identifying features and ranges that occur relatively rarely in the dataset. This makes the reason for a detection concrete: the method can point to an uncommon combination of attribute values as well as flagging the observation.
summary.tldr: PIDForest detects anomalies through sparse attribute-defined regions and explains detections using uncommon feature ranges.

title: PIDForest: Anomaly Detection via Partial Identification

abstract: Strong theoretical guarantees of robustness can be given for ensembles of classifiers generated by input randomization. Specifically, an $\ell_2$ bounded adversary cannot alter the ensemble prediction generated by an additive isotropic Gaussian noise, where the radius for the adversary depends on both the variance of the distribution as well as the ensemble margin at the point of interest. We build on and considerably expand this work across broad classes of distributions. In particular, we offer adversarial robustness guarantees and associated algorithms for the discrete case where the adversary is $\ell_0$ bounded. Moreover, we exemplify how the guarantees can be tightened with specific assumptions about the function class of the classifier such as a decision tree. We empirically illustrate these results with and without functional restrictions across image and molecule datasets.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing builds an ensemble prediction by applying a classifier to randomly perturbed inputs. Existing Gaussian-noise results can certify that an adversary with a bounded l_2 perturbation cannot change that ensemble prediction. The certified radius depends on the noise variance and the ensemble's prediction margin at the input being evaluated.

This paper extends that line of work across broader classes of randomization distributions. A central contribution covers discrete inputs and adversaries bounded in l_0, where the constraint concerns how many input components can be changed. The authors provide both robustness guarantees and associated algorithms for that setting, extending certification beyond the Gaussian, l_2 formulation.

The paper also shows how additional assumptions about the classifier's function class, such as being a decision tree, can tighten the guarantees. Such improvements use known classifier structure to sharpen what can be certified. Experiments on image and molecule datasets illustrate the results with and without functional restrictions, linking the general certification framework to both unrestricted and structurally constrained classifiers.
summary.tldr: The paper broadens randomized-smoothing robustness certificates to discrete perturbations and shows how classifier structure can tighten guarantees.

title: Tight Certificates of Adversarial Robustness for Randomly Smoothed Classifiers

abstract: We study the sample complexity of private synthetic data generation over an unbounded sized class of statistical queries, and show that any class that is privately proper PAC learnable admits a private synthetic data generator (perhaps non-efficient). A differentially private synthetic generator is an algorithm that receives an IID data and publishes synthetic data that is indistinguishable from the true data w.r.t a given fixed class of statistical queries. The synthetic data set can then be used by a data scientist without compromising the privacy of the original data set. Previous work on synthetic data generators focused on the case that the query class $\D$ is finite and obtained sample complexity bounds that scale logarithmically with the size $|\D|$. Here we construct a private synthetic data generator whose sample complexity is independent of the domain size, and we replace finiteness with the assumption that $\D$ is privately PAC learnable (a formally weaker task, hence we obtain equivalence between the two tasks). Our proof relies on a new type of synthetic data generator, Sequential Synthetic Data Generators, which we believe may be of interest of their own right. A sequential SDG is defined by a sequential game between a generator that proposes synthetic distributions and a discriminator that tries to distinguish between real and fake distributions. We characterize the classes that admit a sequential-SDG and show that they are exactly Littlestone classes. Given the online nature of the sequential setting, it is natural that Littlestone classes arise in this context. Nevertheless, the characterization of sequential--SDGs by Littlestone classes turns out to be technically challenging, and to the best of the author's knowledge, does not follow via simple reductions to online prediction.

paragraphs: A private synthetic-data generator takes independent samples and releases artificial data that preserves answers to a specified class of statistical queries while providing differential privacy. This paper studies the amount of data needed when that query class need not be finite, extending beyond bounds expressed through the number of queries.

The authors show that every privately proper PAC-learnable class admits a private synthetic-data generator, although the generator may be computationally inefficient. Their construction has sample complexity independent of domain size. By replacing a finite-query requirement with private learnability, the result establishes an equivalence between learning and synthetic generation in the setting considered.

A generator proposes synthetic distributions, and a discriminator attempts to distinguish them from the real distribution through a sequential game. The authors characterize the classes admitting such generators as exactly the Littlestone classes. This connects private synthetic-data generation to a class structure associated with online learning, while the possible computational inefficiency separates the existence result from a promise of a practical fast implementation.
summary.tldr: Private proper PAC learnability implies private synthetic-data generation, potentially inefficiently, through a sequential framework characterized by Littlestone classes.

title: Synthetic Data Generators -- Sequential and Private

abstract: Recent studies have shown that introducing communication between agents can significantly improve overall performance in cooperative Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). However, existing communication schemes often require agents to exchange an excessive number of messages at run-time under a reliable communication channel, which hinders its practicality in many real-world situations. In this paper, we present \textit{Temporal Message Control} (TMC), a simple yet effective approach for achieving succinct and robust communication in MARL. TMC applies a temporal smoothing technique to drastically reduce the amount of information exchanged between agents. Experiments show that TMC can significantly reduce inter-agent communication overhead without impacting accuracy. Furthermore, TMC demonstrates much better robustness against transmission loss than existing approaches in lossy networking environments.

This paper addresses both issues in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the usefulness of communication must be balanced against the conditions of the network carrying it.

Its central design choice concerns communication over time: the method uses that temporal structure to make messaging more succinct. abstract: In this paper we provide a new efficient algorithm for approximately computing the profile maximum likelihood (PML) distribution, a prominent quantity in symmetric property estimation. We provide an algorithm which matches the previous best known efficient algorithms for computing approximate PML distributions and improves when the number of distinct observed frequencies in the given instance is small. We achieve this result by exploiting new sparsity structure in approximate PML distributions and providing a new matrix rounding algorithm, of independent interest. Leveraging this result, we obtain the first provable computationally efficient implementation of PseudoPML, a general framework for estimating a broad class of symmetric properties. Additionally, we obtain efficient PML-based estimators for distributions with small profile entropy, a natural instance-based complexity measure. Further, we provide a simpler and more practical PseudoPML implementation that matches the best-known theoretical guarantees of such an estimator and evaluate this method empirically.

paragraphs: Profile maximum likelihood, or PML, is an important ingredient in estimating symmetric properties of distributions. This paper develops an efficient approximation algorithm whose performance can benefit from the structure of the observed instance. It matches the previous best efficient algorithms and improves when the observations contain only a small number of distinct frequencies.

The algorithm exploits a newly identified sparsity structure in approximate PML distributions. It also uses a new matrix rounding algorithm, which the authors present as independently useful. These ingredients provide the first provably computationally efficient implementation of PseudoPML, a general framework for estimating a broad class of symmetric properties.

The authors further obtain efficient PML-based estimators for distributions with small profile entropy, using that quantity as an instance-based complexity measure. They also develop a simpler, more practical PseudoPML implementation that matches the best known theoretical guarantees for such an estimator and evaluate it empirically. The overall contribution is to connect computational efficiency with specific structure in the estimation problem, rather than treating all instances identically.
summary.tldr: New sparsity and rounding techniques make approximate PML computation more efficient on structured instances and enable provably efficient PseudoPML.

title: Instance Based Approximations to Profile Maximum Likelihood

abstract: Probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) and dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs) are widely used sequence models with complementary strengths and limitations. While PCFGs allow for nested hierarchical dependencies (tree structures), their latent variables (non-terminal symbols) have to be discrete. In contrast, DBNs allow for continuous latent variables, but the dependencies are strictly sequential (chain structure). Therefore, neither can be applied if the latent variables are assumed to be continuous and also to have a nested hierarchical dependency structure. In this paper, we present Recursive Bayesian Networks (RBNs), which generalise and unify PCFGs and DBNs, combining their strengths and containing both as special cases. RBNs define a joint distribution over tree-structured Bayesian networks with discrete or continuous latent variables. The main challenge lies in performing joint inference over the exponential number of possible structures and the continuous variables. We provide two solutions: 1) For arbitrary RBNs, we generalise inside and outside probabilities from PCFGs to the mixed discrete-continuous case, which allows for maximum posterior estimates of the continuous latent variables via gradient descent, while marginalising over network structures. 2) For Gaussian RBNs, we additionally derive an analytic approximation of the marginal data likelihood (evidence) and marginal posterior distribution, allowing for robust parameter optimisation and Bayesian inference. The capacity and diverse applications of RBNs are illustrated on two examples: In a quantitative evaluation on synthetic data, we demonstrate and discuss the advantage of RBNs for segmentation and tree induction from noisy sequences, compared to change point detection and hierarchical clustering. In an application to musical data, we approach the unsolved problem of hierarchical music analysis from the raw note level and compare our results to expert annotations.

summary.tldr: Recursive Bayesian Networks unify grammar-like hierarchies and continuous latent sequence models, with inference methods for their combined structure.

title: Recursive Bayesian Networks: Generalising and Unifying Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars and Dynamic Bayesian Networks

abstract: We propose a novel framework for multi-person 3D motion trajectory prediction. Our key observation is that a human's action and behaviors may highly depend on the other persons around. Thus, instead of predicting each human pose trajectory in isolation, we introduce a Multi-Range Transformers model which contains of a local-range encoder for individual motion and a global-range encoder for social interactions. The Transformer decoder then performs prediction for each person by taking a corresponding pose as a query which attends to both local and global-range encoder features. Our model not only outperforms state-of-the-art methods on long-term 3D motion prediction, but also generates diverse social interactions. More interestingly, our model can even predict 15-person motion simultaneously by automatically dividing the persons into different interaction groups. Project page with code is available at https://jiashunwang.github.io/MRT/.

paragraphs: Predicting a person's future movement can require understanding the people around them. This paper treats multi-person three-dimensional motion prediction as a task that combines each individual's movement with social interactions. Its motivation is that separate predictions for each person can miss dependencies between their actions and the behavior of others.

The Multi-Range Transformers model uses two encoders with different responsibilities. A local-range encoder captures individual motion, while a global-range encoder captures social interactions. For each person, the decoder uses a corresponding pose as a query and attends to features from both encoders. Each prediction can therefore draw on personal motion history and the wider interaction context represented by the model.

The authors report better long-term 3D motion prediction than state-of-the-art methods, along with generation of diverse social interactions. They also demonstrate simultaneous prediction for 15 people, with the model automatically separating them into interaction groups. These findings support combining local and global information in a shared prediction framework, including scenes where multiple groups of people may interact differently.
summary.tldr: Multi-Range Transformers combine individual motion and social context to predict the 3D movements of multiple people together.

title: Multi-Person 3D Motion Prediction with Multi-Range Transformers

abstract: Evidence that visual communication preceded written language and provided a basis for it goes back to prehistory, in forms such as cave and rock paintings depicting traces of our distant ancestors. Emergent communication research has sought to explore how agents can learn to communicate in order to collaboratively solve tasks. Existing research has focused on language, with a learned communication channel transmitting sequences of discrete tokens between the agents. In this work, we explore a visual communication channel between agents that are allowed to draw with simple strokes. Our agents are parameterised by deep neural networks, and the drawing procedure is differentiable, allowing for end-to-end training. In the framework of a referential communication game, we demonstrate that agents can not only successfully learn to communicate by drawing, but with appropriate inductive biases, can do so in a fashion that humans can interpret. We hope to encourage future research to consider visual communication as a more flexible and directly interpretable alternative of training collaborative agents.

paragraphs: Research on emergent communication asks how agents can develop ways to exchange information while solving tasks together. Much of that work uses sequences of discrete tokens as the communication channel. This paper investigates an alternative: agents communicate through drawings made from simple strokes, making the message itself a visual object.

The agents are neural networks, and their drawing procedure is differentiable. That allows training to connect the success of communication back to the process that creates the strokes. The authors study this setup through a referential communication game, where drawings carry information needed for the agents to refer successfully to the intended target.

The agents learn to communicate through drawing. With appropriate inductive biases, their drawings are also interpretable to humans. That qualification matters: successful communication between trained agents does not by itself establish human readability. The findings show that visual messages can support learned cooperation and, with suitable design choices, become accessible to people as well. The work motivates further study of drawing as a flexible communication channel for collaborative agents.
summary.tldr: Neural agents learn to communicate through simple drawings that humans can interpret when suitable inductive biases are used.

title: Learning to Draw: Emergent Communication through Sketching

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptive classifcation intends to improve the classifcation performance on unlabeled target domain. To alleviate the adverse effect of domain shift, many approaches align the source and target domains in the feature space. However, a feature is usually taken as a whole for alignment without explicitly making domain alignment proactively serve the classifcation task, leading to sub-optimal solution. In this paper, we propose an effective Task-oriented Alignment (ToAlign) for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). We study what features should be aligned across domains and propose to make the domain alignment proactively serve classifcation by performing feature decomposition and alignment under the guidance of the prior knowledge induced from the classifcation task itself. Particularly, we explicitly decompose a feature in the source domain into a task-related/discriminative feature that should be aligned, and a task-irrelevant feature that should be avoided/ignored, based on the classifcation meta-knowledge. Extensive experimental results on various benchmarks (e.g., Offce-Home, Visda-2017, and DomainNet) under different domain adaptation settings demonstrate the effectiveness of ToAlign which helps achieve the state-of-the-art performance. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/UDA.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation aims to improve classification in a target domain without target labels. A common strategy aligns source and target feature representations to reduce the effect of differences between domains. ToAlign questions whether aligning an entire feature representation is the right objective, since some of that representation may have little relevance to classification.

The method uses knowledge induced by the classification task to guide feature decomposition. It separates a source feature into a discriminative, task-related component and a task-irrelevant component. Alignment then focuses on the component that supports classification, while the irrelevant component is ignored. This makes the choice of what to align part of the task-solving process itself.

The distinction matters because domain similarity alone does not ensure that the aligned information helps distinguish classes. ToAlign explicitly directs alignment toward that purpose. Experiments across Office-Home, Visda-2017, and DomainNet, under different adaptation settings, demonstrate effectiveness and help achieve state-of-the-art performance. The reported results support using classification knowledge to select alignment targets rather than treating every part of a learned feature as equally useful.
summary.tldr: ToAlign improves unsupervised domain adaptation by aligning the classification-relevant portion of source features while ignoring task-irrelevant information.

title: ToAlign: Task-Oriented Alignment for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: Progressively applying Gaussian noise transforms complex data distributions to approximately Gaussian. Reversing this dynamic defines a generative model. When the forward noising process is given by a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE), Song et al (2021) demonstrate how the time inhomogeneous drift of the associated reverse-time SDE may be estimated using score-matching. A limitation of this approach is that the forward-time SDE must be run for a sufficiently long time for the final distribution to be approximately Gaussian. In contrast, solving the Schrödinger Bridge (SB) problem, i.e. an entropy-regularized optimal transport problem on path spaces, yields diffusions which generate samples from the data distribution in finite time. We present Diffusion SB (DSB), an original approximation of the Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) procedure to solve the SB problem, and provide theoretical analysis along with generative modeling experiments. The first DSB iteration recovers the methodology proposed by Song et al. (2021), with the flexibility of using shorter time intervals, as subsequent DSB iterations reduce the discrepancy between the final-time marginal of the forward (resp. backward) SDE with respect to the prior (resp. data) distribution. Beyond generative modeling, DSB offers a widely applicable computational optimal transport tool as the continuous state-space analogue of the popular Sinkhorn algorithm (Cuturi, 2013).

paragraphs: Diffusion generative models progressively add Gaussian noise to data and learn how to reverse that process. In the approach discussed here, the forward process must run long enough for its final distribution to become approximately Gaussian. This requirement motivates a different way to connect a data distribution with a simple prior.

The paper uses the Schrödinger Bridge problem, an entropy-regularized transport problem over entire paths. Its solution yields diffusions connecting distributions in finite time. The proposed Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge method approximates an iterative proportional fitting procedure to solve this problem, with theoretical analysis and generative modeling experiments.

The first iteration recovers the existing score-based methodology. Further iterations reduce the mismatch between the forward endpoint and the prior, and between the backward endpoint and the data. This gives the method flexibility to use shorter time intervals while refining those matches. Beyond generation, the authors position the method as a continuous-state counterpart of the Sinkhorn algorithm for computational optimal transport.
summary.tldr: Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge iteratively refines forward and backward diffusions to connect data and prior distributions over shorter time intervals.

title: Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge with Applications to Score-Based Generative Modeling

abstract: We study the problem of active learning with the added twist that the learner is assisted by a helpful teacher. We consider the following natural interaction protocol: At each round, the learner proposes a query asking for the label of an instance $x^q$, the teacher provides the requested label $\{x^q, y^q\}$ along with explanatory information to guide the learning process. In this paper, we view this information in the form of an additional contrastive example ($\{x^c, y^c\}$) where $x^c$ is picked from a set constrained by $x^q$ (e.g., dissimilar instances with the same label). Our focus is to design a teaching algorithm that can provide an informative sequence of contrastive examples to the learner to speed up the learning process. We show that this leads to a challenging sequence optimization problem where the algorithm's choices at a given round depend on the history of interactions. We investigate an efficient teaching algorithm that adaptively picks these contrastive examples. We derive strong performance guarantees for our algorithm based on two problem-dependent parameters and further show that for specific types of active learners (e.g., a generalized binary search learner), the proposed teaching algorithm exhibits strong approximation guarantees. Finally, we illustrate our bounds and demonstrate the effectiveness of our teaching framework via two numerical case studies.

paragraphs: An active learner chooses an example and asks for its label. This paper adds a helpful teacher who supplies both that label and an additional contrastive example. The extra example must come from a set constrained by the learner's query, such as dissimilar instances sharing the same label. Its purpose is to guide learning more efficiently.

Choosing these examples creates a sequence optimization problem. A useful teaching decision depends on the preceding interactions, so selecting an informative example requires accounting for the learner's evolving situation. The authors investigate an efficient adaptive teaching algorithm that chooses contrastive examples as the interaction unfolds, aiming to accelerate the overall learning process.

They derive performance guarantees in terms of two problem-dependent parameters and obtain strong approximation guarantees for particular active learners, including generalized binary search. Two numerical case studies illustrate the bounds and demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The work shows how explanatory examples can be treated as a structured teaching resource, with theoretical guarantees tied to the problem and learner rather than a universal claim that every additional example improves learning.
summary.tldr: An adaptive teacher can accelerate active learning by selecting query-constrained contrastive examples, with guarantees depending on the problem and learner.

title: Teaching an Active Learner with Contrastive Examples

abstract: Network quantization has gained increasing attention with the rapid growth of large pre-trained language models~(PLMs). However, most existing quantization methods for PLMs follow quantization-aware training~(QAT) that requires end-to-end training with full access to the entire dataset. Therefore, they suffer from slow training, large memory overhead, and data accessibility issues. In this paper, we study post-training quantization~(PTQ) of PLMs, and propose module-wise quantization error minimization~(MREM), an efficient solution to mitigate these issues. By partitioning the PLM into multiple modules, we minimize the reconstruction error incurred by quantization for each module. In addition, we design a new model parallel training strategy such that each module can be trained locally on separate computing devices without waiting for preceding modules, which brings nearly the theoretical training speed-up (e.g., $4\times$ on $4$ GPUs). Experiments on GLUE and SQuAD benchmarks show that our proposed PTQ solution not only performs close to QAT, but also enjoys significant reductions in training time, memory overhead, and data consumption.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces the numerical precision used by a neural network. For pretrained language models, many methods require end-to-end quantization-aware training with the full dataset, creating substantial time, memory, and data-access demands. This paper develops a post-training approach intended to reduce those costs.

Module-wise reconstruction error minimization divides the language model into multiple modules and minimizes the reconstruction error caused by quantization within each one. The authors also design a parallel training strategy that lets modules train locally on separate devices without waiting for preceding modules. This organization makes the adaptation process less dependent on sequential computation through the whole model.

On GLUE and SQuAD, the proposed method performs close to quantization-aware training while substantially reducing training time, memory overhead, and data consumption. Its parallel strategy achieves nearly the theoretical speedup, with roughly fourfold acceleration on four GPUs given as an example. The results support module-level reconstruction as a practical way to retain much of the predictive performance while making quantization substantially cheaper.
summary.tldr: Module-wise post-training quantization approaches quantization-aware training performance while reducing time, memory, and data needs in language-model evaluations.

title: Towards Efficient Post-training Quantization of Pre-trained Language Models

abstract: In neural network literature, angular similarity between feature vectors is frequently used for interpreting or re-using learned representations. However, the inner product in neural networks partially disperses information over the scales and angles of the involved input vectors and weight vectors. Therefore, when using only angular similarity on representations trained with the inner product, information loss occurs in downstream methods, which limits their performance. In this paper, we proposed the $\textit{spherization layer}$ to represent all information on angular similarity. The layer 1) maps the pre-activations of input vectors into the specific range of angles, 2) converts the angular coordinates of the vectors to Cartesian coordinates with an additional dimension, and 3) trains decision boundaries from hyperplanes, without bias parameters, passing through the origin. This approach guarantees that representation learning always occurs on the hyperspherical surface without the loss of any information unlike other projection-based methods. Furthermore, this method can be applied to any network by replacing an existing layer. We validate the functional correctness of the proposed method in a toy task, retention ability in well-known image classification tasks, and effectiveness in word analogy test and few-shot learning. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/GIST-IRR/spherization_layer

paragraphs: Learned feature vectors are often compared using their angles, even though ordinary neural network computations can encode information in both direction and magnitude. Using only angular similarity may then discard useful information. This paper introduces a spherization layer designed to place representation information into angular relationships during learning.

The layer maps pre-activation values into a specified angular range, converts the resulting angular coordinates into Cartesian coordinates with one additional dimension, and learns decision boundaries using bias-free hyperplanes through the origin. This construction keeps representation learning on a hyperspherical surface. The authors establish information preservation for the construction, distinguishing it from projection-based approaches that can lose information.

The layer can replace an existing layer in a network. Evaluations examine functional correctness on a toy task, information retention in image classification, and effectiveness in word analogy and few-shot learning. These tests address different aspects of the proposal: whether the mapping behaves as intended, whether representations retain useful content, and whether angular representations support downstream use.
summary.tldr: The spherization layer learns information-preserving representations on a hypersphere so that information is expressed through angles.

title: Spherization Layer: Representation Using Only Angles

abstract: Adder Neural Network (AdderNet) provides a new way for developing energy-efficient neural networks by replacing the expensive multiplications in convolution with cheaper additions (i.e., L1-norm). To achieve higher hardware efficiency, it is necessary to further study the low-bit quantization of AdderNet. Due to the limitation that the commutative law in multiplication does not hold in L1-norm, the well-established quantization methods on convolutional networks cannot be applied on AdderNets. Thus, the existing AdderNet quantization techniques propose to use only one shared scale to quantize both the weights and activations simultaneously. Admittedly, such an approach can keep the commutative law in the L1-norm quantization process, while the accuracy drop after low-bit quantization cannot be ignored. To this end, we first thoroughly analyze the difference on distributions of weights and activations in AdderNet and then propose a new quantization algorithm by redistributing the weights and the activations. Specifically, the pre-trained full-precision weights in different kernels are clustered into different groups, then the intra-group sharing and inter-group independent scales can be adopted. To further compensate the accuracy drop caused by the distribution difference, we then develop a lossless range clamp scheme for weights and a simple yet effective outliers clamp strategy for activations. Thus, the functionality of full-precision weights and the representation ability of full-precision activations can be fully preserved. The effectiveness of the proposed quantization method for AdderNet is well verified on several benchmarks, e.g., our 4-bit post-training quantized adder ResNet-18 achieves an 66.5% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet with comparable energy efficiency, which is about 8.5% higher than that of the previous AdderNet quantization methods. Code will be available at https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/AdderQuant.
originalAbstract: Adder Neural Network (AdderNet) provides a new way for developing energy-efficient neural networks by replacing the expensive multiplications in convolution with cheaper additions (i.e., L1-norm). To achieve higher hardware efficiency, it is necessary to further study the low-bit quantization of AdderNet. Due to the limitation that the commutative law in multiplication does not hold in L1-norm, the well-established quantization methods on convolutional networks cannot be applied on AdderNets. Thus, the existing AdderNet quantization techniques propose to use only one shared scale to quantize both the weights and activations simultaneously. Admittedly, such an approach can keep the commutative law in the L1-norm quantization process, while the accuracy drop after low-bit quantization cannot be ignored. To this end, we first thoroughly analyze the difference on distributions of weights and activations in AdderNet and then propose a new quantization algorithm by redistributing the weights and the activations. Specifically, the pre-trained full-precision weights in different kernels are clustered into different groups, then the intra-group sharing and inter-group independent scales can be adopted. To further compensate the accuracy drop caused by the distribution difference, we then develop a lossless range clamp scheme for weights and a simple yet effective outliers clamp strategy for activations. Thus, the functionality of full-precision weights and the representation ability of full-precision activations can be fully preserved. The effectiveness of the proposed quantization method for AdderNet is well verified on several benchmarks, e.g., our 4-bit post-training quantized adder ResNet-18 achieves an 66.5% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet with comparable energy efficiency, which is about 8.5% higher than that of the previous AdderNet quantization methods. Code will be available at https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/AdderQuant.

paragraphs: AdderNet replaces costly convolution multiplications with addition-based L1 computations to improve energy efficiency. Using low-bit representations could further improve hardware efficiency, but standard convolutional quantization methods do not transfer directly. Existing AdderNet approaches use one shared scale for weights and activations, which can cause substantial accuracy loss at low precision.

The paper analyzes differences between weight and activation distributions and introduces a redistribution-based quantization method. It clusters pretrained full-precision kernels into groups, sharing a scale within each group while allowing separate scales across groups. It also adds a lossless range clamp for weights and an outlier-clamping strategy for activations to compensate for distribution differences.

Experiments on several benchmarks support the method’s effectiveness. A four-bit post-training quantized adder ResNet-18 reaches 66.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, reported as about 8.5% higher than previous AdderNet quantization methods at comparable energy efficiency. The result shows that adapting scales and ranges to AdderNet’s particular computation can materially improve low-bit accuracy.
summary.tldr: Grouped scales and tailored range clamping improve low-bit AdderNet accuracy while retaining comparable energy efficiency.

title: Redistribution of Weights and Activations for AdderNet Quantization

abstract: Human vision possesses a special type of visual processing systems called peripheral vision. Partitioning the entire visual field into multiple contour regions based on the distance to the center of our gaze, the peripheral vision provides us the ability to perceive various visual features at different regions. In this work, we take a biologically inspired approach and explore to model peripheral vision in deep neural networks for visual recognition. We propose to incorporate peripheral position encoding to the multi-head self-attention layers to let the network learn to partition the visual field into diverse peripheral regions given training data. We evaluate the proposed network, dubbed PerViT, on ImageNet-1K and systematically investigate the inner workings of the model for machine perception, showing that the network learns to perceive visual data similarly to the way that human vision does. The performance improvements in image classification over the baselines across different model sizes demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

This paper uses that spatial organization as inspiration for a visual recognition network. Its central question is whether a Transformer can learn useful distinctions between peripheral regions when deciding how to combine image information.

The proposed Peripheral Vision Transformer, or PerViT, adds peripheral position encoding to multi-head self-attention layers. This encoding lets the model learn a partition of the visual field into diverse peripheral regions from training data. The approach places the biological inspiration inside the attention mechanism, where spatial organization can influence how the network processes visual features.

Evaluation on ImageNet-1K reports image-classification improvements over baselines across different model sizes. The authors also inspect the model's internal workings and find visual processing patterns resembling aspects of human vision. These analyses support the proposed peripheral organization as useful for machine perception. The reported resemblance concerns learned processing behavior, while the classification comparisons provide the direct evidence of improved task performance.
summary.tldr: PerViT adds learnable peripheral spatial organization to Transformer attention, improving ImageNet classification across model sizes.

title: Peripheral Vision Transformer

abstract: We propose an analysis in fair learning that preserves the utility of the data while reducing prediction disparities under the criteria of group sufficiency. We focus on the scenario where the data contains multiple or even many subgroups, each with limited number of samples. As a result, we present a principled method for learning a fair predictor for all subgroups via formulating it as a bilevel objective. Specifically, the subgroup specific predictors are learned in the lower-level through a small amount of data and the fair predictor. In the upper-level, the fair predictor is updated to be close to all subgroup specific predictors. We further prove that such a bilevel objective can effectively control the group sufficiency and generalization error. We evaluate the proposed framework on real-world datasets. Empirical evidence suggests the consistently improved fair predictions, as well as the comparable accuracy to the baselines.

paragraphs: Learning fair predictions becomes challenging when data contains many subgroups and each subgroup has few examples. The paper seeks to reduce prediction disparities under the criterion of group sufficiency while retaining the predictive usefulness of the data. Its focus is on learning a shared predictor that accounts for all of these subgroups.

The method uses an objective with two linked levels. At the lower level, each subgroup gets a predictor learned from its limited data together with the shared fair predictor. At the upper level, the shared predictor is updated to stay close to the subgroup-specific predictors. The two levels connect subgroup adaptation with the construction of a common model.

The authors prove that this objective can control both group sufficiency and generalization error. Evaluations on real-world datasets suggest consistently improved fairness with accuracy comparable to the baselines. The approach therefore offers a principled way to connect fairness and predictive performance when subgroup data is scarce, with empirical findings supporting that balance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A bilevel learning objective connects subgroup-specific predictors to a shared model, improving reported fairness while maintaining comparable accuracy.

title: On Learning Fairness and Accuracy on Multiple Subgroups

abstract: Uncertainty quantification is a key component of machine learning models targeted at safety-critical systems such as in healthcare or autonomous vehicles. We study this problem in the context of meta learning, where the goal is to quickly adapt a predictor to new tasks. In particular, we propose a novel algorithm to construct \emph{PAC prediction sets}, which capture uncertainty via sets of labels, that can be adapted to new tasks with only a few training examples. These prediction sets satisfy an extension of the typical PAC guarantee to the meta learning setting; in particular, the PAC guarantee holds with high probability over future tasks. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on four datasets across three application domains: mini-ImageNet and CIFAR10-C in the visual domain, FewRel in the language domain, and the CDC Heart Dataset in the medical domain. In particular, our prediction sets satisfy the PAC guarantee while having smaller size compared to other baselines that also satisfy this guarantee.

paragraphs: A predictor can express uncertainty by returning a set of plausible labels instead of committing to one label. This paper studies how to construct such prediction sets in meta-learning, where a model must adapt quickly to new tasks. The challenge is to retain a meaningful statistical guarantee when only a few examples are available for adaptation.

The authors introduce an algorithm for producing probably approximately correct, or PAC, prediction sets in this setting. Their guarantee extends the usual PAC formulation to account for future tasks: it holds with high probability over those tasks. This makes uncertainty across tasks part of the formal target, alongside adapting the predictor from limited task-specific data.

Experiments cover mini-ImageNet and CIFAR10-C for vision, FewRel for language, and the CDC Heart Dataset for medicine. The resulting sets satisfy the PAC guarantee while being smaller than those of comparison methods that also satisfy it. Smaller sets provide more selective outputs, so the reported advantage concerns informativeness while retaining the stated statistical protection.
summary.tldr: A meta-learning algorithm adapts compact prediction sets from few examples with PAC guarantees that extend across future tasks.

title: PAC Prediction Sets for Meta-Learning

abstract: Labeling training data is a critical and expensive step in producing high accuracy ML models, whether training from scratch or fine-tuning. To make labeling more efficient, two major approaches are programmatic weak supervision (WS) and semi-supervised learning (SSL). More recent works have either explicitly or implicitly used techniques at their intersection, but in various complex and ad hoc ways. In this work, we define a simple, modular design space to study the use of SSL techniques for WS more systematically. Surprisingly, we find that fairly simple methods from our design space match the performance of more complex state-of-the-art methods, averaging a 3 p.p. increase in accuracy/F1-score across 8 standard WS benchmarks. Further, we provide practical guidance on when different components are worth their added complexity and training costs. Contrary to current understanding, we find using SSL is not necessary to obtain the best performance on most WS benchmarks but is more effective when: (1) end models are smaller, and (2) WS provides labels for only a small portion of training examples.

paragraphs: Programmatic weak supervision and semi-supervised learning both address the expense of labeling training data. Weak supervision supplies labels programmatically, while semi-supervised learning makes use of unlabeled examples alongside labeled ones. Their combination has produced increasingly complicated methods, making it difficult to determine which components actually justify their additional training cost.

The paper introduces a simple, modular design space for studying these combinations systematically. Within that space, relatively simple methods match the performance of more complex state-of-the-art approaches. Across eight standard weak-supervision benchmarks, the authors report an average three-percentage-point increase in accuracy or F1 score, alongside guidance about when additional components are worthwhile.

A central finding is that semi-supervised learning is unnecessary for attaining the best performance on most of the benchmarks examined. It becomes more useful when the final predictive model is smaller or when weak supervision labels only a small fraction of examples. These findings make model size and label coverage practical considerations when deciding whether added training complexity is beneficial.
summary.tldr: Simple weak-supervision methods can match complex alternatives, with semi-supervised learning especially useful for smaller models and sparse label coverage.

title: Characterizing the Impacts of Semi-supervised Learning for Weak Supervision

abstract: The accurate predictions and principled uncertainty measures provided by GP regression incur $O(n^3)$ cost which is prohibitive for modern-day large-scale applications. This has motivated extensive work on computationally efficient approximations. We introduce a new perspective by exploring robustness properties and limiting behaviour of GP nearest-neighbour (GPnn) prediction. We demonstrate through theory and simulation that as the data-size $n$ increases, accuracy of estimated parameters and GP model assumptions become increasingly irrelevant to GPnn predictive accuracy. Consequently, it is sufficient to spend small amounts of work on parameter estimation in order to achieve high MSE accuracy, even in the presence of gross misspecification. In contrast, as $n \rightarrow \infty$, uncertainty calibration and NLL are shown to remain sensitive to just one parameter, the additive noise-variance; but we show that this source of inaccuracy can be corrected for, thereby achieving both well-calibrated uncertainty measures and accurate predictions at remarkably low computational cost. We exhibit a very simple GPnn regression algorithm with stand-out performance compared to other state-of-the-art GP approximations as measured on large UCI datasets. It operates at a small fraction of those other methods' training costs, for example on a basic laptop taking about 30 seconds to train on a dataset of size $n = 1.6 \times 10^6$.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression provides predictions and uncertainty estimates, but its standard cubic computational cost becomes prohibitive for large datasets. This paper examines nearest-neighbor Gaussian process prediction, focusing on how its behavior changes as the amount of data grows. The central question is how much careful model fitting remains necessary at that scale.

Theory and simulations show that parameter-estimation accuracy and model assumptions become increasingly unimportant for predictive accuracy as dataset size increases. This supports spending little effort on parameter estimation while retaining low mean squared error, even under substantial model misspecification. Uncertainty behaves differently: in the large-data limit, calibration and negative log-likelihood remain sensitive to the additive noise variance.

The authors show how to correct that remaining source of uncertainty error and present a simple regression algorithm. On large UCI datasets, it reports strong performance at a small fraction of competing methods' training costs. One example trains on 1.6 million observations in about 30 seconds on a basic laptop, illustrating the computational benefit of the approach.
summary.tldr: Nearest-neighbor Gaussian process regression can need little parameter fitting at large scale, while correcting noise variance supports calibrated uncertainty.

title: Leveraging Locality and Robustness to Achieve Massively Scalable Gaussian Process Regression

abstract: Quantifying uncertainty is important for actionable predictions in real-world applications. A crucial part of predictive uncertainty quantification is the estimation of epistemic uncertainty, which is defined as an integral of the product between a divergence function and the posterior. Current methods such as Deep Ensembles or MC dropout underperform at estimating the epistemic uncertainty, since they primarily consider the posterior when sampling models. We suggest Quantification of Uncertainty with Adversarial Models (QUAM) to better estimate the epistemic uncertainty. QUAM identifies regions where the whole product under the integral is large, not just the posterior. Consequently, QUAM has lower approximation error of the epistemic uncertainty compared to previous methods. Models for which the product is large correspond to adversarial models (not adversarial examples!). Adversarial models have both a high posterior as well as a high divergence between their predictions and that of a reference model. Our experiments show that QUAM excels in capturing epistemic uncertainty for deep learning models and outperforms previous methods on challenging tasks in the vision domain.

paragraphs: Epistemic uncertainty concerns uncertainty associated with the predictive model. In the formulation studied here, estimating it requires integrating a product: how plausible a model is under the posterior and how much its predictions diverge from a reference. The paper argues that methods focused primarily on posterior sampling can inadequately estimate this combined quantity.

QUAM searches for regions where the full product is large. The resulting adversarial models have both high posterior support and substantial predictive disagreement with the reference model. The word adversarial refers to alternative models, rather than altered input examples. Their role is to expose plausible disagreement that contributes strongly to the uncertainty integral.

By targeting the quantity actually being integrated, QUAM achieves lower approximation error than the previous approaches discussed in the paper. Vision experiments report stronger epistemic uncertainty estimation and better performance on challenging tasks. The central contribution is a change in how models are sought for uncertainty estimation: predictive disagreement participates directly in the search alongside posterior plausibility.
summary.tldr: QUAM estimates epistemic uncertainty by seeking plausible models that also strongly disagree with a reference model.

title: Quantification of Uncertainty with Adversarial Models

abstract: Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes have been successfully commercialized in communication systems due to their strong error correction capabilities and simple decoding process. However, the error-floor phenomenon of LDPC codes, in which the error rate stops decreasing rapidly at a certain level, presents challenges for achieving extremely low error rates and deploying LDPC codes in scenarios demanding ultra-high reliability. In this work, we propose training methods for neural min-sum (NMS) decoders to eliminate the error-floor effect. First, by leveraging the boosting learning technique of ensemble networks, we divide the decoding network into two neural decoders and train the post decoder to be specialized for uncorrected words that the first decoder fails to correct. Secondly, to address the vanishing gradient issue in training, we introduce a block-wise training schedule that locally trains a block of weights while retraining the preceding block. Lastly, we show that assigning different weights to unsatisfied check nodes effectively lowers the error-floor with a minimal number of weights. By applying these training methods to standard LDPC codes, we achieve the best error-floor performance compared to other decoding methods. The proposed NMS decoder, optimized solely through novel training methods without additional modules, can be integrated into existing LDPC decoders without incurring extra hardware costs. The source code is available at https://github.com/ghy1228/LDPC_Error_Floor.

title: Boosting Learning for LDPC Codes to Improve the Error-Floor Performance

abstract: We design replicable algorithms in the context of statistical clustering under the recently introduced notion of replicability from Impagliazzo et al. [2022]. According to this definition, a clustering algorithm is replicable if, with high probability, its output induces the exact same partition of the sample space after two executions on different inputs drawn from the same distribution, when its internal randomness is shared across the executions. We propose such algorithms for the statistical $k$-medians, statistical $k$-means, and statistical $k$-centers problems by utilizing approximation routines for their combinatorial counterparts in a black-box manner. In particular, we demonstrate a replicable $O(1)$-approximation algorithm for statistical Euclidean $k$-medians ($k$-means) with $\operatorname{poly}(d)$ sample complexity. We also describe an $O(1)$-approximation algorithm with an additional $O(1)$-additive error for statistical Euclidean $k$-centers, albeit with $\exp(d)$ sample complexity. In addition, we provide experiments on synthetic distributions in 2D using the $k$-means++ implementation from sklearn as a black-box that validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Replicable clustering asks for a stronger form of consistency than simply obtaining similar clustering costs. Under the definition used here, two runs on independently drawn inputs from the same distribution should, with high probability, induce exactly the same partition of the sample space. The runs share their internal randomness, making that shared randomness part of the guarantee.

The authors construct algorithms for statistical k-medians, k-means, and k-centers by using approximation routines for the corresponding combinatorial problems as black boxes. For Euclidean k-medians and k-means, they obtain constant-factor approximation guarantees with sample complexity polynomial in dimension. This connects replicability to existing clustering procedures without requiring each underlying approximation routine to be redesigned.

For Euclidean k-centers, the result includes a constant additive error as well as a constant approximation factor, and the sample complexity is exponential in dimension. Experiments on synthetic two-dimensional distributions, using sklearn's k-means++ implementation as a component, validate the theoretical results. The differing dimension dependence distinguishes the strength of the guarantees across the clustering objectives.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs clustering algorithms that reproduce the same population partition with high probability when runs share randomness.

title: Replicable Clustering

abstract: In an effort to further advance semi-supervised generative and classification tasks, we propose a simple yet effective training strategy called *dual pseudo training* (DPT), built upon strong semi-supervised learners and diffusion models. DPT operates in three stages: training a classifier on partially labeled data to predict pseudo-labels; training a conditional generative model using these pseudo-labels to generate pseudo images; and retraining the classifier with a mix of real and pseudo images. Empirically, DPT consistently achieves SOTA performance of semi-supervised generation and classification across various settings. In particular, with one or two labels per class, DPT achieves a Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) score of 3.08 or 2.52 on ImageNet $256\times256$. Besides, DPT outperforms competitive semi-supervised baselines substantially on ImageNet classification tasks, *achieving top-1 accuracies of 59.0 (+2.8), 69.5 (+3.0), and 74.4 (+2.0)* with one, two, or five labels per class, respectively. Notably, our results demonstrate that diffusion can generate realistic images with only a few labels (e.g., $<0.1$%) and generative augmentation remains viable for semi-supervised classification. Our code is available at *https://github.com/ML-GSAI/DPT*.

paragraphs: Dual pseudo training connects semi-supervised classification with conditional image generation. The aim is to make both tasks work better when only a few examples have labels. A classifier supplies predicted labels for training a generative model, and the resulting generated images then provide additional training material for the classifier.

The strategy has three stages. First, a classifier learns from partially labeled data and assigns pseudo-labels. Second, a conditional diffusion model learns using those labels and generates pseudo images. Third, the classifier is retrained on a mixture of real and generated images. The two kinds of model therefore contribute different forms of additional supervision.

The authors report leading generation and classification results across the evaluated settings. On ImageNet at 256 by 256 resolution, generation reaches FID scores of 3.08 and 2.52 with one and two labels per class. Classification reaches top-1 accuracies of 59.0%, 69.5%, and 74.4% with one, two, and five labels per class. These results demonstrate that generated-image augmentation can remain useful under extremely limited labeling.
summary.tldr: Dual pseudo training lets a semi-supervised classifier and a diffusion generator improve each other through predicted labels and generated images.

title: Diffusion Models and Semi-Supervised Learners Benefit Mutually with Few Labels

abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs) have been proven useful for learning non-linear dynamics of arbitrary trajectories. However, current NODE methods capture variations across trajectories only via the initial state value or by auto-regressive encoder updates. In this work, we introduce Modulated Neural ODEs (MoNODEs), a novel framework that sets apart dynamics states from underlying static factors of variation and improves the existing NODE methods. In particular, we introduce *time-invariant modulator variables* that are learned from the data. We incorporate our proposed framework into four existing NODE variants. We test MoNODE on oscillating systems, videos and human walking trajectories, where each trajectory has trajectory-specific modulation. Our framework consistently improves the existing model ability to generalize to new dynamic parameterizations and to perform far-horizon forecasting. In addition, we verify that the proposed modulator variables are informative of the true unknown factors of variation as measured by $R^2$ scores.

Different trajectories can also have underlying characteristics that remain fixed throughout each trajectory. This paper introduces Modulated Neural ODEs, or MoNODEs, to separate those static factors from the changing dynamical state.

The framework learns time-invariant modulator variables from data. These variables provide a distinct way to represent trajectory-specific variation, beyond encoding it only in an initial state or through autoregressive encoder updates. The authors incorporate the framework into four existing neural ODE variants, showing how the same separation can extend several model designs.

Tests cover oscillating systems, videos, and human walking trajectories with trajectory-specific modulation. Across these evaluations, MoNODE improves generalization to new dynamic parameterizations and forecasting farther into the future. Measurements using R² also show that the learned modulators contain information about the true unknown variation factors. Together, the results support explicitly representing persistent trajectory differences when learning changing behavior.
summary.tldr: MoNODE separates fixed trajectory factors from evolving states, improving generalization and long-range forecasting in the evaluated neural ODE models.

title: Modulated Neural ODEs

abstract: Pretrained vision-language models, such as CLIP, have demonstrated strong generalization capabilities, making them promising tools in the realm of zero-shot visual recognition. Visual relation detection (VRD) is a typical task that identifies relationship (or interaction) types between object pairs within an image. However, naively utilizing CLIP with prevalent class-based prompts for zero-shot VRD has several weaknesses, e.g., it struggles to distinguish between different fine-grained relation types and it neglects essential spatial information of two objects. To this end, we propose a novel method for zero-shot VRD: RECODE, which solves RElation detection via COmposite DEscription prompts. Specifically, RECODE first decomposes each predicate category into subject, object, and spatial components. Then, it leverages large language models (LLMs) to generate description-based prompts (or visual cues) for each component. Different visual cues enhance the discriminability of similar relation categories from different perspectives, which significantly boosts performance in VRD. To dynamically fuse different cues, we further introduce a chain-of-thought method that prompts LLMs to generate reasonable weights for different visual cues. Extensive experiments on four VRD benchmarks have demonstrated the effectiveness and interpretability of RECODE.

Using a vision-language model such as CLIP with simple category prompts can struggle to distinguish closely related interactions and overlook the objects’ spatial arrangement. RECODE addresses these weaknesses through more detailed descriptions of the visual evidence for each relation.

The method splits each relation category into subject, object, and spatial components. A large language model generates descriptive prompts for those components, providing complementary cues that distinguish similar categories from different perspectives. A further prompting procedure asks the language model to reason about suitable weights for combining the cues, allowing their contributions to vary.

Experiments on four visual-relation benchmarks support RECODE’s effectiveness and interpretability. Its central contribution is a way to translate relation categories into structured descriptions that better match the visual distinctions the task requires. The findings show the value of composite prompts and weighted cues for the evaluated zero-shot setting, where relation recognition draws on pretrained models rather than relying only on category names.
summary.tldr: RECODE improves zero-shot visual relation detection using language-model-generated subject, object, and spatial descriptions with weighted cue fusion.

title: Zero-shot Visual Relation Detection via Composite Visual Cues from Large Language Models

abstract: Federated learning has a significant advantage in protecting information privacy. Many scholars proposed various secure learning methods within the framework of federated learning but the study on secure federated unsupervised learning especially clustering is limited. We in this work propose a secure kernelized factorization method for federated spectral clustering on distributed dataset. The method is non-trivial because the kernel or similarity matrix for spectral clustering is computed by data pairs, which violates the principle of privacy protection. Our method implicitly constructs an approximation for the kernel matrix on distributed data such that we can perform spectral clustering under the constraint of privacy protection. We provide a convergence guarantee of the optimization algorithm, reconstruction error bounds of the Gaussian kernel matrix, and the sufficient condition of correct clustering of our method. We also present some results of differential privacy. Numerical results on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed method is efficient and accurate in comparison to the baselines.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering groups data using a matrix of pairwise similarities. In a federated setting, those pairs may span data held in different locations, making direct similarity computation conflict with privacy constraints. This paper addresses that obstacle for unsupervised learning, where secure federated methods have received less attention than other learning tasks.

The proposed kernelized factorization method implicitly constructs an approximation to the similarity matrix for the distributed dataset. This approximation enables spectral clustering while respecting the method’s privacy constraints. The central idea is to reconstruct the information needed for clustering without directly building the full matrix from exposed cross-location data pairs.

The paper supplies several forms of theoretical support: convergence of the optimization algorithm, reconstruction-error bounds for a Gaussian kernel matrix, and a sufficient condition for correct clustering. It also presents differential-privacy results. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show efficient and accurate performance relative to the evaluated baselines. These findings connect the quality of the reconstructed similarities to clustering behavior, with correctness established under a sufficient condition rather than claimed for every dataset.
summary.tldr: Secure kernel approximation enables spectral clustering across distributed data, supported by convergence, reconstruction, and conditional clustering guarantees.

title: Federated Spectral Clustering via Secure Similarity Reconstruction

abstract: Unlike traditional statistical models depending on hand-specified priors, neural processes (NPs) have recently emerged as a class of powerful neural statistical models that combine the strengths of neural networks and stochastic processes. NPs can define a flexible class of stochastic processes well suited for highly non-trivial functions by encoding contextual knowledge into the function space. However, noisy context points introduce challenges to the algorithmic stability that small changes in training data may significantly change the models and yield lower generalization performance. In this paper, we provide theoretical guidelines for deriving stable solutions with high generalization by introducing the notion of algorithmic stability into NPs, which can be flexible to work with various NPs and achieves less biased approximation with theoretical guarantees. To illustrate the superiority of the proposed model, we perform experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, and the results demonstrate that our approach not only helps to achieve more accurate performance but also improves model robustness.

paragraphs: Neural processes combine neural networks with stochastic processes to model flexible families of functions. They use context observations to shape those functions, allowing contextual knowledge to inform predictions. However, noisy context points can make the learned model sensitive: a small change in training data may produce a large model change and reduce generalization.

The paper brings algorithmic stability into neural processes to address this sensitivity. It provides theoretical guidance for obtaining stable solutions with strong generalization and describes an approach that can work with various neural process models. The analysis also supports a less biased approximation, connecting stability considerations with the quality of the model's approximation.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show improvements in accuracy and robustness. These results support treating sensitivity to training-data changes as a design concern for neural processes, alongside their ability to represent complex functions. The contribution combines theoretical guidance with empirical evidence that controlling this sensitivity can improve the reliability of predictions built from noisy context.
summary.tldr: The paper incorporates algorithmic stability into neural processes, providing theoretical guidance and empirical improvements in accuracy and robustness.

title: Neural Processes with Stability

abstract: Community detection is an essential tool for unsupervised data exploration and revealing the organisational structure of networked systems. With a long history in network science, community detection typically relies on objective functions, optimised with custom-tailored search algorithms, but often without leveraging recent advances in deep learning. Recently, first works have started incorporating such objectives into loss functions for deep graph clustering and pooling. We consider the map equation, a popular information-theoretic objective function for unsupervised community detection, and express it in differentiable tensor form for optimisation through gradient descent. Our formulation turns the map equation compatible with any neural network architecture, enables end-to-end learning, incorporates node features, and chooses the optimal number of clusters automatically, all without requiring explicit regularisation. Applied to unsupervised graph clustering tasks, we achieve competitive performance against state-of-the-art deep graph clustering baselines in synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Community detection finds groups within networks and helps expose their organizational structure without labeled examples. Many traditional methods optimize a specialized objective using a custom search algorithm. This paper brings one established information-theoretic objective, the map equation, into neural learning by rewriting it in a differentiable tensor form.

The reformulation allows gradient descent to optimize the map equation and makes it compatible with neural-network architectures. It supports end-to-end learning and the inclusion of node features, connecting information about individual nodes with the network clustering objective. The authors also state that the formulation automatically selects the optimal number of clusters without requiring explicit regularization.

On synthetic and real-world graph-clustering tasks, the approach achieves competitive performance against leading deep graph-clustering baselines. The finding supports integrating a traditional community-detection objective into modern neural training, rather than establishing superiority across all evaluated methods. The broader contribution is a reusable differentiable formulation that allows network-flow-based community detection to benefit from learned representations and node attributes.
summary.tldr: A differentiable map equation enables end-to-end neural graph clustering with node features and automatic selection of the number of clusters.

title: The Map Equation Goes Neural: Mapping Network Flows with Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Generative models trained at scale can now produce novel text, video, and more recently, scientific data such as crystal structures. The ultimate goal for materials discovery, however, goes beyond generation: we desire a fully automated system that proposes, generates, and verifies crystal structures given a high-level user instruction. In this work, we formulate end-to-end language-to-structure generation as a multi-objective optimization problem, and propose Generative Hierarchical Materials Search (GenMS) for controllable generation of crystal structures. GenMS consists of (1) a language model that takes high-level natural language as input and generates intermediate textual information about a crystal (e.g., chemical formulae), and (2) a diffusion model that takes intermediate information as input and generates low-level continuous value crystal structures. GenMS additionally uses a graph neural network to predict properties (e.g., formation energy) from the generated crystal structures. During inference, GenMS leverages all three components to conduct a forward tree search over the space of possible structures. Experiments show that GenMS outperforms other alternatives both in satisfying user request and in generating low-energy structures. GenMS is able to generate complex structures such as double perovskites (or elpasolites), layered structures, and spinels, solely from natural language input.

paragraphs: Generative Hierarchical Materials Search, or GenMS, turns natural-language requests into candidate crystal structures. The paper treats this as a multi-objective search problem: a candidate should satisfy the user's description while also having desirable predicted material properties. Producing a structure is therefore one stage in a larger process of proposing and assessing possibilities.

A language model first converts the request into intermediate textual information, such as a chemical formula. A diffusion model uses that information to generate continuous-valued crystal structures. A graph neural network predicts properties of those structures, including formation energy. During inference, a forward tree search coordinates all three components to explore possible candidates.

summary.tldr: GenMS combines language, diffusion, and property-prediction models in a search process that generates crystals from natural-language requests.

title: Generative Hierarchical Materials Search

abstract: 3D particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) is a key technique for analyzing turbulent flow, one of the most challenging computational problems of our century. At the core of 3D PTV is the dual-frame fluid motion estimation algorithm, which tracks particles across two consecutive frames. Recently, deep learning-based methods have achieved impressive accuracy in dual-frame fluid motion estimation; however, they heavily depend on large volumes of labeled data. In this paper, we introduce a new method that is **completely self-supervised and notably outperforms its fully-supervised counterparts while requiring only 1\% of the training samples (without labels) used by previous methods.** Our method features a novel zero-divergence loss that is specific to the domain of turbulent flow. Inspired by the success of splat operation in high-dimensional filtering and random fields, we propose a splat-based implementation for this loss which is both efficient and effective. The self-supervised nature of our method naturally supports test-time optimization, leading to the development of a tailored Dynamic Velocimetry Enhancer (DVE) module. We demonstrate that strong cross-domain robustness is achieved through test-time optimization on unseen leave-one-out synthetic domains and real physical/biological domains. Code, data and models are available at [https://github.com/Forrest-110/FluidMotionNet](https://github.com/Forrest-110/FluidMotionNet).

Deep learning methods have achieved strong accuracy for this task but depend heavily on labeled training data. The authors introduce a fully self-supervised approach and report that it exceeds fully supervised counterparts using only 1% as many training samples, without labels.

A central component is a zero-divergence loss tailored to turbulent flow. This provides a domain-specific constraint for learning from the observations themselves. The paper introduces a splat-based implementation designed to make that loss efficient and effective, connecting the physical training objective to a practical computational procedure.

Because its learning objective does not require labels, the method can also optimize on test data. A dedicated Dynamic Velocimetry Enhancer module supports this adaptation. Experiments report strong cross-domain robustness on held-out synthetic domains and real physical and biological domains. The findings connect reduced dependence on labeled data with the ability to adjust motion estimates to unfamiliar conditions at inference.
summary.tldr: A self-supervised fluid motion estimator combines zero-divergence loss with test-time optimization, outperforming supervised counterparts with 1% as many training samples.

title: Dual-frame Fluid Motion Estimation with Test-time Optimization and Zero-divergence Loss

abstract: This paper aims at developing novel shuffling gradient-based methods for tackling two classes of minimax problems: nonconvex-linear and nonconvex-strongly concave settings. The first algorithm addresses the nonconvex-linear minimax model and achieves the state-of-the-art oracle complexity typically observed in nonconvex optimization. It also employs a new shuffling estimator for the ``hyper-gradient'', departing from standard shuffling techniques in optimization. The second method consists of two variants: semi-shuffling and full-shuffling schemes. These variants tackle the nonconvex-strongly concave minimax setting. We establish their oracle complexity bounds under standard assumptions, which, to our best knowledge, are the best-known for this specific setting. Numerical examples demonstrate the performance of our algorithms and compare them with two other methods. Our results show that the new methods achieve comparable performance with SGD, supporting the potential of incorporating shuffling strategies into minimax algorithms.
