paragraphs: Reasoning models can produce self-reflection that does not reliably check whether their answers are correct. RISE addresses this by training problem solving and self-verification together within one online reinforcement learning process. The goal is to make checking a learned capability alongside solution generation.

During each iteration, the model first produces solutions and then critiques those same solutions generated under its current policy. An outcome verifier provides verifiable rewards for both activities, and both trajectories contribute to the policy update. This connects verification training to the model’s own current behavior, allowing feedback on both its answers and its assessment of those answers.

Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks, RISE consistently improves problem-solving accuracy while strengthening self-verification. The authors also find benefits from online verification and additional verification computation. Trained models check their reasoning more frequently and more accurately. These results support explicitly rewarding verification within reasoning training as a way to make self-checking more dependable in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: RISE jointly rewards solution generation and self-verification, improving mathematical reasoning accuracy and the reliability of models’ self-checks.

title: Trust, But Verify: A Self-Verification Approach to Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

abstract: Process reward model (PRM) has been proven effective in test-time scaling of LLM on challenging reasoning tasks. However, the reward hacking induced by PRM hinders its successful applications in reinforcement fine-tuning. We find the primary cause of reward hacking induced by PRM is that: the canonical summation-form credit assignment in reinforcement learning (RL), i.e. cumulative gamma-decayed future rewards, causes the LLM to hack steps with high rewards. Therefore, to unleashing the power of PRM in training-time, we propose PURE: Process sUpervised Reinforcement lEarning. The core of PURE is the min-form credit assignment that defines the value function as the minimum future rewards. This method unifies the optimization objective with respect to process rewards during test-time and training-time, and significantly alleviates reward hacking due to the limits on the range of values of value function and more rational assignment of advantages. Through extensively experiments on 3 base models, we achieve similar reasoning performance using PRM-based approach compared with verifiable reward-based approach if enabling min-form credit assignment. In contrast, the canonical sum-form credit assignment even collapses training at the beginning. Moreover, when we incorporate 1/10th verifiable rewards to auxiliary the PRM-based fine-tuning, it further alleviate reward hacking and results in the best fine-tuned model based on Qwen2.5-Math-7B with 82.5% accuracy on AMC23 and 53.3% average accuracy across 5 benchmarks. Furthermore, we summary the reward hacking cases we encountered during training and analysis the cause of training collapse.

paragraphs: Process reward models score intermediate reasoning steps, but using those scores for reinforcement fine-tuning can encourage reward hacking. This paper identifies summing discounted future rewards as the primary cause in its analysis: a model can exploit highly rewarded steps without producing reliably sound reasoning. PURE changes how these step-level rewards determine training credit.

Its value function uses the minimum future reward, making the weakest future score central to evaluation. The authors argue that this aligns training with how process rewards are used at test time, limits value ranges, and assigns advantages more rationally. Across three base models, this approach achieves reasoning performance similar to training with verifiable rewards, whereas conventional summation causes early training collapse.

Adding one-tenth verifiable rewards further reduces reward hacking. The best reported Qwen2.5-Math-7B-based model reaches 82.5% accuracy on AMC23 and 53.3% average accuracy across five benchmarks. The paper also analyzes encountered hacking cases and collapse. Its findings show that the way step rewards are combined can strongly affect whether process supervision supports useful training.
summary.tldr: PURE uses minimum future process rewards for credit assignment, substantially reducing reward hacking in the reported reasoning experiments.

title: Stop Summation: Min-Form Credit Assignment Is All Process Reward Model Needs for Reasoning

abstract: Autoregressive models (ARMs) show strong capabilities in many domains but face challenges with planning and complex reasoning due to their sequential generation. Masked diffusion models (MDMs) address these issues by enabling controllable, any-order, and parallel generation but encounter training difficulties as token prediction complexity varies with unmasked token positions. This work identifies two key characteristics of efficient MDM sampling paths: prioritizing tokens near unmasked ones and generating subsequence earlier in reasoning. We propose the Simple Path Masked Diffusion Model (SPMDM), which partitions sequences into fixed-length, non-overlapping subsequences and applies varying noise scales to learn token-level and cross-subsequence dependencies. Experiments on synthetic data and tasks like Countdown and Sudoku show SPMDM captures structural rules effectively, significantly outperforming existing MDMs and ARMs, with competitive results on broader reasoning benchmarks.

This work identifies two key characteristics of efficient MDM sampling paths: prioritizing tokens near unmasked ones and generating subsequence earlier in reasoning. paragraphs: Masked diffusion models allow tokens to be generated in different orders and in parallel, offering flexibility beyond sequential generation. Their training is complicated by the fact that predicting a token can become easier or harder depending on which other positions are already visible. SPMDM addresses this variation through a more structured sampling path.

The paper identifies two useful characteristics: favoring tokens close to already unmasked tokens and generating subsequences earlier in reasoning. It divides sequences into fixed-length, non-overlapping subsequences and applies different noise scales. This design is intended to teach both dependencies among individual tokens and dependencies across the larger subsequence units.

On synthetic data and tasks including Countdown and Sudoku, SPMDM captures structural rules effectively and significantly outperforms the evaluated masked diffusion and autoregressive models. It also achieves competitive results on broader reasoning benchmarks. The findings support structuring the generation path as a way to make masked diffusion learning more effective, with the strongest reported advantages appearing in the stated structured tasks.
summary.tldr: SPMDM structures masked diffusion generation around fixed-length subsequences, improving rule learning and performance on tasks including Countdown and Sudoku.

title: SPMDM: Enhancing Masked Diffusion Models through Simplifying Sampling Path

abstract: We study the problem of differentially private second moment estimation and present a new algorithm that achieve strong privacy-utility trade-offs even for worst-case inputs under subsamplability assumptions on the data. We call an input $(m,\alpha,\beta)$-subsamplable if a random subsample of size $m$ (or larger) preserves w.p $\geq 1-\beta$ the spectral structure of the original second moment matrix up to a multiplicative factor of $1\pm \alpha$. Building upon subsamplability, we give a recursive algorithmic framework similar to Kamath et al (2019) that abides zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy (zCDP) while preserving w.h.p the accuracy of the second moment estimation upto an arbitrary factor of $(1\pm\gamma)$. We then show how to apply our algorithm to approximate the second moment matrix of a distribution $\mathcal{D}$, even when a noticeable fraction of the input are outliers.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate a second-moment matrix while protecting the privacy of individual data points. Such a matrix summarizes how the magnitudes and directions of data vary together. The goal is to preserve its spectral structure, meaning its behavior along different directions, even for difficult inputs that satisfy a specified sampling condition.

That condition is subsamplability: a sufficiently large random subset must preserve the original matrix's spectral structure within a chosen multiplicative tolerance, with a specified probability. Building on this assumption, the authors develop a recursive estimation framework satisfying zero-concentrated differential privacy. They establish high-probability accuracy within an arbitrary multiplicative tolerance, expressed as one plus or minus gamma.

The result therefore connects private estimation to a concrete structural property of the data rather than claiming accuracy for every unrestricted input. The authors also show how to apply the algorithm to a distribution's second-moment matrix when a noticeable fraction of observations are outliers. Together, these results provide a route to private matrix estimation with both multiplicative accuracy and outlier tolerance under the stated framework.
summary.tldr: A recursive private estimator preserves second-moment structure with high probability under a subsamplability assumption, with an application to data containing outliers.

title: A Private Approximation of the 2nd-Moment Matrix of Any Subsamplable Input

abstract: Trust in a decision-making system requires both safety guarantees and the ability to interpret and understand its behavior. This is particularly important for learned systems, whose decision-making processes are often highly opaque. Shielding is a prominent model-based technique for enforcing safety in reinforcement learning. However, because shields are automatically synthesized using rigorous formal methods, their decisions are often similarly difficult for humans to interpret. Recently, decision trees became customary to represent controllers and policies. However, since shields are inherently non-deterministic, their decision tree representations become too large to be explainable in practice. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach for explainable safe RL that enhances trust by providing human-interpretable explanations of the shield's decisions. Our method represents the shielding policy as a hierarchy of decision trees, offering top-down, case-based explanations. At design time, we use a world model to analyze the safety risks of executing actions in given states. Based on this risk analysis, we construct both the shield and a high-level decision tree that classifies states into risk categories (safe, critical, dangerous, unsafe), providing an initial explanation of why a given situation may be safety-critical. At runtime, we generate localized decision trees that explain which actions are allowed and why others are deemed unsafe. Altogether, our method facilitates the explainability of the safety aspect in the safe-by-shielding reinforcement learning. Our framework requires no additional information beyond what is already used for shielding, incurs minimal overhead, and can be readily integrated into existing shielded RL pipelines. In our experiments, we compute explanations using decision trees that are several orders of magnitude smaller than the original shield.

paragraphs: A safety shield restricts which actions a reinforcement-learning system may take, using a model and formal safety analysis. Although this can enforce safety, the shield's own decisions can be difficult to understand. Representing the whole shield as one decision tree can become unwieldy because a shield may permit multiple actions in a given situation.

This paper organizes explanations into a hierarchy of decision trees. During design, a world model is used to assess the safety risks of actions in different states. That analysis produces both the shield and a high-level tree assigning states to safe, critical, dangerous, or unsafe categories. At runtime, smaller local trees explain which actions are allowed and why alternatives are considered unsafe.

The hierarchy separates understanding the current risk from understanding the available action choices. It uses information already required for shielding and is reported to add minimal overhead, making integration into existing pipelines straightforward. In experiments, the explanation trees are several orders of magnitude smaller than the original shield. The contribution makes the safety mechanism's decisions more accessible through localized, case-based explanations.
summary.tldr: A hierarchy of compact decision trees explains the risk categories and action restrictions imposed by reinforcement-learning safety shields.

title: Explainably Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models have garnered significant attention for generating high-quality images aligned with text prompts. However, rapid T2I model advancements reveal limitations in early benchmarks, lacking comprehensive evaluations, especially for text rendering and style. Notably, recent state-of-the-art models, with their rich knowledge modeling capabilities, show potential in reasoning-driven image generation, yet existing evaluation systems have not adequately addressed this frontier. To systematically address these gaps, we introduce $\textbf{OneIG-Bench}$, a meticulously designed comprehensive benchmark framework for fine-grained evaluation of T2I models across multiple dimensions, including subject-element alignment, text rendering precision, reasoning-generated content, stylization, and diversity. By structuring the evaluation, this benchmark enables in-depth analysis of model performance, helping researchers and practitioners pinpoint strengths and bottlenecks in the full pipeline of image generation. Our codebase and dataset are now publicly available to facilitate reproducible evaluation studies and cross-model comparisons within the T2I research community.

paragraphs: Text-to-image systems need evaluation that reflects more than the overall appearance of their outputs. The paper argues that earlier benchmarks provide incomplete coverage, particularly for rendered text, style, and image generation requiring reasoning. OneIG-Bench is designed to examine these capabilities through a more comprehensive and finely separated evaluation framework.

Its dimensions include alignment with requested subjects and elements, precision of text rendering, reasoning-dependent content, stylization, and diversity. Separating these dimensions helps reveal where a model succeeds and where it encounters difficulties. A model’s ability to create attractive imagery can therefore be assessed alongside its handling of the specific content and constraints expressed in a prompt.

The contribution is an evaluation resource for analyzing strengths and bottlenecks across image generation. Its structured coverage supports more detailed comparisons between models and helps researchers investigate capabilities that older evaluation systems did not adequately address. The authors make the code and dataset publicly available to support reproducible studies and cross-model comparisons; the abstract does not announce a winning model.
summary.tldr: OneIG-Bench evaluates image generators across content alignment, text rendering, reasoning, style, and diversity.

title: OneIG-Bench: Omni-dimensional Nuanced Evaluation for Image Generation

abstract: We introduce a proximal version of the stochastic dual coordinate ascent method and show how to accelerate the method using an inner-outer iteration procedure. We analyze the runtime of the framework and obtain rates that improve state-of-the-art results for various key machine learning optimization problems including SVM, logistic regression, ridge regression, Lasso, and multiclass SVM. Experiments validate our theoretical findings.
originalAbstract: We introduce a proximal version of the stochastic dual coordinate ascent method and show how to accelerate the method using an inner-outer iteration procedure. We analyze the runtime of the framework and obtain rates that improve state-of-the-art results for various key machine learning optimization problems including SVM, logistic regression, ridge regression, Lasso, and multiclass SVM. Experiments validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: The paper develops an optimization framework for regularized loss minimization, a formulation shared by several major machine learning methods. Its starting point is stochastic dual coordinate ascent. The contribution concerns how to solve these learning problems more efficiently, with the same framework covering several different objectives.

The authors introduce a proximal version of the method and then accelerate it through an inner–outer iteration procedure. This places the underlying optimization method inside a larger iterative scheme. The two contributions are connected: the proximal formulation supplies the method to be accelerated, while the nested procedure supplies the acceleration mechanism analyzed in the paper.

Runtime analysis yields improved rates over the stated state of the art for SVMs, logistic regression, ridge regression, Lasso, and multiclass SVMs. Experiments validate the theoretical findings. The breadth of this list matters because it spans several regularized learning formulations, making the result a reusable optimization framework rather than an improvement confined to a single prediction model.
summary.tldr: A proximal dual coordinate ascent framework uses nested iterations to improve runtime rates for several standard learning problems.

title: Accelerated Proximal Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent for Regularized Loss Minimization

abstract: We analyze the problem of linear bandits under heavy tailed noise. Most of of the work on linear bandits has been based on the assumption of bounded or sub-Gaussian noise. However, this assumption is often violated in common scenarios such as financial markets. We present two algorithms to tackle this problem: one based on dynamic truncation and one based on a median of means estimator. We show that, when the noise admits admits only a 1 + εmoment, these algorithms are still able to achieve regret in \widetildeO(T^\frac2 + ε2(1 + ε)) and \widetildeO(T^\frac1+ 2ε1 + 3 ε) respectively. In particular, they guarantee sublinear regret as long as the noise has finite variance. We also present empirical results showing that our algorithms achieve a better performance than the current state of the art for bounded noise when the L_∞bound on the noise is large yet the 1 + εmoment of the noise is small.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear bandits when reward noise has heavy tails. Much prior work assumes bounded or sub-Gaussian noise, but the authors point out that these assumptions can fail in settings such as financial markets. The question is whether a learner can still control its cumulative decision-making loss under weaker noise conditions.

The authors propose two algorithms: one uses dynamic truncation, and the other uses a median-of-means estimator. Both are designed to handle noise through methods that are robust to unusually large observations. They derive regret bounds when the noise has only a finite moment of order one plus epsilon, making the relationship between tail behavior and learning performance explicit.

In particular, both algorithms guarantee sublinear regret when the noise has finite variance. This means regret per decision decreases over time under that sufficient condition. Experiments also show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art bounded-noise methods when the maximum noise bound is large but the relevant moment remains small, supporting the practical value of the weaker noise formulation.
summary.tldr: Two robust linear-bandit algorithms handle heavy-tailed noise and guarantee sublinear regret when the noise has finite variance.

title: No-Regret Algorithms for Heavy-Tailed Linear Bandits

abstract: In this paper we argue for the fundamental importance of the value distribution: the distribution of the random return received by a reinforcement learning agent. This is in contrast to the common approach to reinforcement learning which models the expectation of this return, or value. Although there is an established body of literature studying the value distribution, thus far it has always been used for a specific purpose such as implementing risk-aware behaviour. We begin with theoretical results in both the policy evaluation and control settings, exposing a significant distributional instability in the latter. We then use the distributional perspective to design a new algorithm which applies Bellman’s equation to the learning of approximate value distributions. We evaluate our algorithm using the suite of games from the Arcade Learning Environment. We obtain both state-of-the-art results and anecdotal evidence demonstrating the importance of the value distribution in approximate reinforcement learning. Finally, we combine theoretical and empirical evidence to highlight the ways in which the value distribution impacts learning in the approximate setting.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can represent future rewards by their average, but that average leaves out how possible returns are distributed. This paper argues that learning the distribution itself matters for reinforcement learning more broadly, beyond specific uses such as choosing actions according to risk preferences.

The authors study this perspective theoretically in both policy evaluation and control. Policy evaluation assesses an existing policy, while control involves learning which actions to take. Their analysis identifies a significant distributional instability in the control setting. They also develop an algorithm that uses Bellman’s equation to learn approximate return distributions, turning the distributional viewpoint into a concrete learning method.

On games from the Arcade Learning Environment, the algorithm achieves results reported as state of the art. The authors combine these experiments with theory and anecdotal evidence to examine how return distributions affect approximate learning. The contribution therefore includes both a successful algorithm and an account of why distributional information can influence learning, alongside an identified theoretical difficulty in control.
summary.tldr: Learning distributions of future returns yields a successful reinforcement learning algorithm while revealing distributional instability in control.

title: A Distributional Perspective on Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Representation learning and option discovery are two of the biggest challenges in reinforcement learning (RL). Proto-value functions (PVFs) are a well-known approach for representation learning in MDPs. In this paper we address the option discovery problem by showing how PVFs implicitly define options. We do it by introducing eigenpurposes, intrinsic reward functions derived from the learned representations. The options discovered from eigenpurposes traverse the principal directions of the state space. They are useful for multiple tasks because they are discovered without taking the environment’s rewards into consideration. Moreover, different options act at different time scales, making them helpful for exploration. We demonstrate features of eigenpurposes in traditional tabular domains as well as in Atari 2600 games.

paragraphs: An agent learning through reinforcement needs both a useful representation of its surroundings and useful behaviors that extend across multiple steps. This paper connects those challenges through proto-value functions, an existing representation-learning approach. It shows how these representations implicitly define options: extended behaviors that the agent can use while interacting with an environment.

The connection comes from eigenpurposes, intrinsic reward functions derived from the learned representation. These rewards encourage options that traverse principal directions of the state space. Instead of building each behavior around the environment’s task reward, the method extracts behaviors from the structure represented by the proto-value functions.

That separation from task rewards makes the discovered options useful across multiple tasks. The options also operate over different durations, giving exploration behaviors at different time scales. The paper demonstrates features of eigenpurposes in tabular environments and Atari 2600 games. Its contribution is a framework linking representation learning to reusable behavior discovery, with demonstrations across these two settings.
summary.tldr: Eigenpurposes turn learned state representations into task-independent, multistep behaviors useful for exploration.

title: A Laplacian Framework for Option Discovery in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: It is one typical and general topic of learning a good embedding model to efficiently learn the representation coefficients between two spaces/subspaces. To solve this task, $L_{1}$ regularization is widely used for the pursuit of feature selection and avoiding overfitting, and yet the sparse estimation of features in $L_{1}$ regularization may cause the underfitting of training data. $L_{2}$ regularization is also frequently used, but it is a biased estimator. In this paper, we propose the idea that the features consist of three orthogonal parts, namely sparse strong signals, dense weak signals and random noise, in which both strong and weak signals contribute to the fitting of data. To facilitate such novel decomposition, MSplit LBI is for the first time proposed to realize feature selection and dense estimation simultaneously. We provide theoretical and simulational verification that our method exceeds $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ regularization, and extensive experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in the few-shot and zero-shot learning.

paragraphs: Learning an embedding involves estimating how representations in two spaces relate. Regularization helps control this estimation, but familiar choices have drawbacks: L1 regularization selects features through sparsity and can underfit, while L2 regularization produces biased estimates. The paper asks how to select important features without discarding weaker information that also helps fit the data.

Its proposed view separates features into three orthogonal components: a sparse set of strong signals, a dense collection of weak signals, and random noise. Both signal components contribute to explaining the data. MSplit LBI is designed around this decomposition so that feature selection and dense estimation can happen together.

The authors report theoretical and simulation evidence that their method exceeds L1 and L2 regularization, along with state-of-the-art experimental performance in few-shot and zero-shot learning. The conceptual contribution is the distinction between weak signal and noise. Under the proposed decomposition, selecting strong features need not mean removing all remaining contributions, which creates room to combine interpretive selection with a richer fit to the data.
summary.tldr: MSplit LBI jointly selects strong features and estimates dense weak signals, with reported benefits for few-shot and zero-shot learning.

title: MSplit LBI: Realizing Feature Selection and Dense Estimation Simultaneously in Few-shot and Zero-shot Learning

abstract: We develop the first general semi-bandit algorithm that simultaneously achieves $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ regret for stochastic environments and $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret for adversarial environments without knowledge of the regime or the number of rounds $T$. The leading problem-dependent constants of our bounds are not only optimal in some worst-case sense studied previously, but also optimal for two concrete instances of semi-bandit problems. Our algorithm and analysis extend the recent work of (Zimmert & Seldin, 2019) for the special case of multi-armed bandits, but importantly requires a novel hybrid regularizer designed specifically for semi-bandit. Experimental results on synthetic data show that our algorithm indeed performs well uniformly over different environments. We finally provide a preliminary extension of our results to the full bandit feedback.

paragraphs: The paper develops a semi-bandit algorithm that adapts to two different kinds of environments. In stochastic environments, outcomes follow a statistical pattern; in adversarial environments, the learner must withstand strategically unfavorable outcomes. The algorithm does not need advance knowledge of which setting it faces or how many rounds it will run.

Its guarantees describe regret, the cumulative cost of learning compared with a reference choice. Regret grows logarithmically with the number of rounds in stochastic settings and at a square-root rate in adversarial settings. Achieving both with one algorithm avoids requiring the learner to select a regime in advance. The construction extends a multi-armed bandit approach using a new hybrid regularizer specifically designed for semi-bandit learning.

The results also address the leading constants in these bounds, establishing their optimality for two concrete semi-bandit problems as well as a worst-case criterion. Synthetic experiments support good performance across different environments. The paper additionally offers a preliminary extension to full bandit feedback; this extension is presented less definitively than the main semi-bandit results.
summary.tldr: A single semi-bandit algorithm achieves strong stochastic and adversarial regret guarantees without knowing the environment type or time horizon.

title: Beating Stochastic and Adversarial Semi-bandits Optimally and Simultaneously

abstract: Adaptive data analysis is frequently criticized for its pessimistic generalization guarantees. The source of these pessimistic bounds is a model that permits arbitrary, possibly adversarial analysts that optimally use information to bias results. While being a central issue in the field, still lacking are notions of natural analysts that allow for more optimistic bounds faithful to the reality that typical analysts aren’t adversarial. In this work, we propose notions of natural analysts that smoothly interpolate between the optimal non-adaptive bounds and the best-known adaptive generalization bounds. To accomplish this, we model the analyst’s knowledge as evolving according to the rules of an unknown dynamical system that takes in revealed information and outputs new statistical queries to the data. This allows us to restrict the analyst through different natural control-theoretic notions. One such notion corresponds to a recency bias, formalizing an inability to arbitrarily use distant information. Another complementary notion formalizes an anchoring bias, a tendency to weight initial information more strongly. Both notions come with quantitative parameters that smoothly interpolate between the non-adaptive case and the fully adaptive case, allowing for a rich spectrum of intermediate analysts that are neither non-adaptive nor adversarial. Natural not only from a cognitive perspective, we show that our notions also capture standard optimization methods, like gradient descent in various settings. This gives a new interpretation to the fact that gradient descent tends to overfit much less than its adaptive nature might suggest.

paragraphs: Adaptive data analysis lets earlier results influence later questions asked of the same data. Generalization guarantees can become pessimistic when analysts are allowed to exploit every previous answer adversarially. This paper develops models of more restricted analysts, aiming to explain why ordinary adaptive analysis may behave better than that worst-case picture suggests.

The analyst is represented as an unknown dynamical system: revealed information changes its internal knowledge, which determines subsequent statistical queries. Control-theoretic restrictions describe how information persists. One models recency bias, limiting the use of distant information. Another models anchoring bias, giving greater weight to initial information. Quantitative parameters control the strength of these restrictions.

The resulting guarantees vary smoothly between non-adaptive bounds and the best-known fully adaptive bounds. This creates a spectrum of analysts with different capacities to reuse information. The authors also show that their definitions encompass gradient descent in various settings, offering an interpretation of why this adaptive optimization method can overfit less than unrestricted adaptive-analysis theory might lead one to expect.
summary.tldr: Dynamical models of analysts with recency or anchoring biases yield generalization guarantees between non-adaptive and fully adaptive extremes.

title: Natural Analysts in Adaptive Data Analysis

abstract: The representation of the approximate posterior is a critical aspect of effective variational autoencoders (VAEs). Poor choices for the approximate posterior have a detrimental impact on the generative performance of VAEs due to the mismatch with the true posterior. We extend the class of posterior models that may be learned by using undirected graphical models. We develop an efficient method to train undirected approximate posteriors by showing that the gradient of the training objective with respect to the parameters of the undirected posterior can be computed by backpropagation through Markov chain Monte Carlo updates. We apply these gradient estimators for training discrete VAEs with Boltzmann machines as approximate posteriors and demonstrate that undirected models outperform previous results obtained using directed graphical models. Our implementation is publicly available.

Our implementation is publicly available.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder relies on an approximate posterior to represent latent variables given observed data. When that approximation poorly matches the true posterior, generative performance suffers. This paper expands the available family of approximations by allowing undirected graphical models, creating another way to represent relationships among latent variables.

The central technical contribution is an efficient training method for these undirected posteriors. The authors show that gradients of the training objective with respect to posterior parameters can be obtained by backpropagating through Markov chain Monte Carlo updates. This makes the sampling procedure part of the gradient computation used to learn the posterior.

They apply the gradient estimators to discrete variational autoencoders using Boltzmann machines as approximate posteriors. In the reported experiments, these undirected models outperform earlier results using directed graphical models. The contribution therefore joins a richer posterior modeling choice with a practical way to train it, and the empirical findings demonstrate its value for the discrete generative models studied.
summary.tldr: Backpropagation through Monte Carlo updates enables undirected approximate posteriors that improve reported discrete VAE results over directed alternatives.

title: Undirected Graphical Models as Approximate Posteriors

abstract: We show that when taking into account also the image domain $[0,1]^d$, established $l_1$-projected gradient descent (PGD) attacks are suboptimal as they do not consider that the effective threat model is the intersection of the $l_1$-ball and $[0,1]^d$. We study the expected sparsity of the steepest descent step for this effective threat model and show that the exact projection onto this set is computationally feasible and yields better performance. Moreover, we propose an adaptive form of PGD which is highly effective even with a small budget of iterations. Our resulting $l_1$-APGD is a strong white-box attack showing that prior works overestimated their $l_1$-robustness. Using $l_1$-APGD for adversarial training we get a robust classifier with SOTA $l_1$-robustness. Finally, we combine $l_1$-APGD and an adaptation of the Square Attack to $l_1$ into $l_1$-AutoAttack, an ensemble of attacks which reliably assesses adversarial robustness for the threat model of $l_1$-ball intersected with $[0,1]^d$.

paragraphs: An l1-bounded image attack must respect two constraints: a total perturbation budget and valid pixel values between zero and one. The paper shows that established projected-gradient attacks are suboptimal when they fail to account for the geometry of these constraints together. The actual feasible set is their intersection, so treating the image bounds as secondary misses part of the attack problem.

The authors analyze the expected sparsity of a steepest-descent step for this combined set. They show that exact projection onto it is computationally feasible and improves attack performance. They also develop an adaptive projected-gradient method that remains highly effective with few iterations, producing the white-box attack l1-APGD.

Using this stronger attack reveals that previous work overestimated l1 robustness. The authors also use it for adversarial training and report state-of-the-art l1 robustness for the resulting classifier. Finally, they combine it with an l1 adaptation of Square Attack to create l1-AutoAttack. This ensemble is presented as a reliable assessment tool for the explicitly defined intersection of perturbation and pixel constraints.
summary.tldr: l1-APGD strengthens sparse adversarial attacks by jointly respecting perturbation budgets and pixel bounds, exposing overestimated robustness.

title: Mind the Box: $l_1$-APGD for Sparse Adversarial Attacks on Image Classifiers

abstract: Sketching is a powerful dimensionality reduction technique for accelerating algorithms for data analysis. A crucial step in sketching methods is to compute a subspace embedding (SE) for a large matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$. SE’s are the primary tool for obtaining extremely efficient solutions for many linear-algebraic tasks, such as least squares regression and low rank approximation. Computing an SE often requires an explicit representation of $A$ and running time proportional to the size of $A$. However, if $A= T_1 \Join T_2 \Join …\Join T_m$ is the result of a database join query on several smaller tables $T_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i \times d_i}$, then this running time can be prohibitive, as $A$ itself can have as many as $O(n_1 n_2 \cdots n_m)$ rows. In this work, we design subspace embeddings for database joins which can be computed significantly faster than computing the join. For the case of a two table join $A = T_1 \Join T_2$ we give input-sparsity algorithms for computing subspace embeddings, with running time bounded by the number of non-zero entries in $T_1,T_2$. This results in input-sparsity time algorithms for high accuracy regression, significantly improving upon the running time of prior FAQ-based methods for regression. We extend our results to arbitrary joins for the ridge regression problem, also considerably improving the running time of prior methods. Empirically, we apply our method to real datasets and show that it is significantly faster than existing algorithms.

paragraphs: Regression on joined database tables can become expensive before the regression algorithm even starts. A join may create a matrix with vastly more rows than the source tables contain. Standard sketching methods often need that matrix explicitly, so their dimension-reduction step can inherit the cost of constructing and reading the expanded data.

This paper designs subspace embeddings for database joins that can be computed substantially faster than forming the join. For two tables, its algorithms run in input-sparsity time, with running time bounded by the number of nonzero entries in the source tables. These embeddings enable high-accuracy regression while avoiding a computational cost tied to the full joined matrix.

The authors extend their results to arbitrary joins for ridge regression and improve the running times of previous methods. Evaluations on real datasets also show substantial speed advantages over existing algorithms. The central contribution is to make the compact source-table representation useful directly for regression computations, particularly when joining those tables would greatly expand the number of rows.
summary.tldr: New sketching algorithms enable fast regression over database joins without first constructing the potentially enormous joined matrix.

title: In-Database Regression in Input Sparsity Time

abstract: Being able to efficiently and accurately select the top-$k$ elements with differential privacy is an integral component of various private data analysis tasks. In this paper, we present the oneshot Laplace mechanism, which generalizes the well-known Report Noisy Max \cite{dwork2014algorithmic} mechanism to reporting noisy top-$k$ elements. We show that the oneshot Laplace mechanism with a noise level of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{k}/\eps)$ is approximately differentially private. Compared to the previous peeling approach of running Report Noisy Max $k$ times, the oneshot Laplace mechanism only adds noises and computes the top $k$ elements once, hence much more efficient for large $k$. In addition, our proof of privacy relies on a novel coupling technique that bypasses the composition theorems so without the linear dependence on $k$ which is inherent to various composition theorems. Finally, we present a novel application of efficient top-$k$ selection in the classical problem of ranking from pairwise comparisons.

paragraphs: Selecting the highest-scoring k elements is a common building block in data analysis. When the underlying data are private, the selection procedure must also limit what its output reveals. This paper proposes a one-shot Laplace mechanism that extends the noisy maximum-selection approach to returning multiple top elements.

The method adds noise and computes the top k elements once. A previous peeling approach instead repeatedly invokes noisy maximum selection k times. Avoiding those repeated invocations makes the proposed procedure much more efficient for large k. The authors prove approximate differential privacy with a noise level scaling like the square root of k divided by epsilon, suppressing logarithmic factors.

The privacy proof uses a coupling technique rather than relying on composition theorems, avoiding the linear dependence on k inherent in various such theorems. This is a contribution to both the algorithm and its analysis: the one-shot computation is paired with a direct privacy argument. The paper also applies efficient private top-k selection to ranking from pairwise comparisons.
summary.tldr: A one-shot noisy top-k mechanism provides approximate differential privacy while avoiding repeated maximum-selection calls.

title: Oneshot Differentially Private Top-k Selection

abstract: Although Label Distribution Learning (LDL) has witnessed extensive classification applications, it faces the challenge of objective mismatch – the objective of LDL mismatches that of classification, which has seldom been noticed in existing studies. Our goal is to solve the objective mismatch and improve the classification performance of LDL. Specifically, we extend the margin theory to LDL and propose a new LDL method called \textbf{L}abel \textbf{D}istribution \textbf{L}earning \textbf{M}achine (LDLM). First, we define the label distribution margin and propose the \textbf{S}upport \textbf{V}ector \textbf{R}egression \textbf{M}achine (SVRM) to learn the optimal label. Second, we propose the adaptive margin loss to learn label description degrees. In theoretical analysis, we develop a generalization theory for the SVRM and analyze the generalization of LDLM. Experimental results validate the better classification performance of LDLM.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning represents how strongly different labels describe an example, yet it is often used for classification. This paper identifies a mismatch between learning that distribution and achieving the classification objective. A method can therefore optimize its distribution-learning goal without being as well aligned with selecting the appropriate class as intended.

The proposed Label Distribution Learning Machine addresses the mismatch by extending margin theory to this setting. The authors define a label distribution margin and introduce a Support Vector Regression Machine to learn the optimal label. They also develop an adaptive margin loss for learning label description degrees, connecting these degrees to the broader classification-oriented approach.

The paper develops a generalization theory for the regression component and analyzes generalization for the complete method. Experiments report better classification performance for LDLM. The significance is the explicit treatment of objective alignment: when a distribution-learning method is used to classify, its training formulation should account for the classification goal as well as the label description degrees.
summary.tldr: LDLM uses margin-based learning to better align label distribution learning with classification and reports improved classification performance.

title: Label Distribution Learning Machine

abstract: Self-attention, an architectural motif designed to model long-range interactions in sequential data, has driven numerous recent breakthroughs in natural language processing and beyond. This work provides a theoretical analysis of the inductive biases of self-attention modules. Our focus is to rigorously establish which functions and long-range dependencies self-attention blocks prefer to represent. Our main result shows that bounded-norm Transformer networks "create sparse variables": a single self-attention head can represent a sparse function of the input sequence, with sample complexity scaling only logarithmically with the context length. To support our analysis, we present synthetic experiments to probe the sample complexity of learning sparse Boolean functions with Transformers.

paragraphs: Self-attention connects information across a sequence, including positions far apart. This paper asks a more specific theoretical question: which functions and long-range dependencies does the architecture favor representing? That focus concerns inductive bias, the preferences built into a model that influence what it can learn efficiently from examples.

The main result applies to Transformer networks with bounded norms. Under that condition, a single attention head can represent a sparse function of the input sequence. Here, sparsity means that the function depends on a limited part of the sequence. The associated sample complexity grows only logarithmically with context length, so the bound increases slowly as the surrounding sequence becomes longer.

The authors describe this capability as creating sparse variables: attention can form representations of selected input dependencies. Synthetic experiments examine learning sparse Boolean functions and support the theoretical analysis. The contribution gives a precise account of one useful preference of self-attention, with the bounded-norm condition and sparse-function setting central to the stated result.
summary.tldr: Bounded-norm Transformers can represent sparse sequence functions with sample complexity growing only logarithmically with context length.

title: Inductive Biases and Variable Creation in Self-Attention Mechanisms

abstract: While deep generative models have succeeded in image processing, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning, training that involves discrete random variables remains challenging due to the high variance of its gradient estimation process. Monte Carlo is a common solution used in most variance reduction approaches. However, this involves time-consuming resampling and multiple function evaluations. We propose a Gapped Straight-Through (GST) estimator to reduce the variance without incurring resampling overhead. This estimator is inspired by the essential properties of Straight-Through Gumbel-Softmax. We determine these properties and show via an ablation study that they are essential. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed GST estimator enjoys better performance compared to strong baselines on two discrete deep generative modeling tasks, MNIST-VAE and ListOps.

paragraphs: Training generative models with discrete random variables can produce high-variance gradient estimates. Reducing that variance often involves Monte Carlo resampling, which requires repeated computation and multiple function evaluations. This paper seeks a way to make the gradient estimates less variable without adding that resampling overhead.

The proposed Gapped Straight-Through estimator, or GST, draws on properties of the Straight-Through Gumbel-Softmax estimator. The authors identify properties they consider essential and investigate them through an ablation study. This connects the design of GST to an examination of which ingredients matter for the estimator's behavior.

Experiments compare GST with strong baselines on two discrete deep generative modeling tasks: MNIST-VAE and ListOps. The reported results favor GST on those tasks. The practical contribution is a gradient estimator designed to improve training while avoiding the repeated sampling used by many variance-reduction approaches. Its evidence combines an analysis of the design ingredients with task-level experiments, supporting the approach within the evaluated discrete modeling settings.
summary.tldr: The Gapped Straight-Through estimator reduces gradient-estimation variance without resampling overhead and outperforms strong baselines on two evaluated discrete modeling tasks.

title: Training Discrete Deep Generative Models via Gapped Straight-Through Estimator

abstract: Conditional generative models aim to learn the underlying joint distribution of data and labels to achieve conditional data generation. Among them, the auxiliary classifier generative adversarial network (AC-GAN) has been widely used, but suffers from the problem of low intra-class diversity of the generated samples. The fundamental reason pointed out in this paper is that the classifier of AC-GAN is generator-agnostic, which therefore cannot provide informative guidance for the generator to approach the joint distribution, resulting in a minimization of the conditional entropy that decreases the intra-class diversity. Motivated by this understanding, we propose a novel conditional GAN with an auxiliary discriminative classifier (ADC-GAN) to resolve the above problem. Specifically, the proposed auxiliary discriminative classifier becomes generator-aware by recognizing the class-labels of the real data and the generated data discriminatively. Our theoretical analysis reveals that the generator can faithfully learn the joint distribution even without the original discriminator, making the proposed ADC-GAN robust to the value of the coefficient hyperparameter and the selection of the GAN loss, and stable during training. Extensive experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of ADC-GAN in conditional generative modeling compared to state-of-the-art classifier-based and projection-based conditional GANs.

paragraphs: Conditional generators aim to produce data with a requested label while preserving the variation found within each class. The paper investigates why auxiliary classifier GANs can generate too little of that variation. Its explanation centers on a classifier that is unaware of the generator: the guidance it supplies can reduce conditional entropy instead of helping match the joint distribution of data and labels.

ADC-GAN changes the auxiliary classifier so that it distinguishes class labels for real and generated examples. This makes the classifier generator-aware and changes the information available to guide generation. The intervention targets the source of the diversity problem identified by the authors rather than simply adding another preference for varied outputs.

The theoretical analysis shows that the generator can learn the joint distribution even without the original discriminator. The authors connect this property to stable training and robustness to the weighting coefficient and GAN loss choice. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior conditional generation relative to the classifier-based and projection-based methods considered.
summary.tldr: ADC-GAN uses a generator-aware auxiliary classifier to address reduced within-class diversity in conditional GANs.

title: Conditional GANs with Auxiliary Discriminative Classifier

abstract: Modern language models are vulnerable to backdoor attacks. An injected malicious token sequence (i.e., a trigger) can cause the compromised model to misbehave, raising security concerns. Trigger inversion is a widely-used technique for scanning backdoors in vision models. It can- not be directly applied to NLP models due to their discrete nature. In this paper, we develop a novel optimization method for NLP backdoor inversion. We leverage a dynamically reducing temperature coefficient in the softmax function to provide changing loss landscapes to the optimizer such that the process gradually focuses on the ground truth trigger, which is denoted as a one-hot value in a convex hull. Our method also features a temperature rollback mechanism to step away from local optimals, exploiting the observation that local optimals can be easily determined in NLP trigger inversion (while not in general optimization). We evaluate the technique on over 1600 models (with roughly half of them having injected backdoors) on 3 prevailing NLP tasks, with 4 different backdoor attacks and 7 architectures. Our results show that the technique is able to effectively and efficiently detect and remove backdoors, outperforming 5 baseline methods. The code is available at https: //github.com/PurduePAML/DBS.

paragraphs: A backdoored language model can behave normally until a particular token sequence triggers malicious behavior. Finding that sequence through trigger inversion is difficult because text consists of discrete choices. The paper develops an optimization method for this setting, addressing the obstacle that prevents direct application of inversion techniques designed for vision models.

The method gradually lowers the temperature of a softmax function, changing the optimization landscape as the search proceeds. This process increasingly concentrates the search toward a discrete trigger, represented by a one-hot choice within a continuous convex region. A rollback mechanism can raise the temperature again to move away from local optima, exploiting their recognizability in this particular inversion problem.

The evaluation covers more than 1,600 models, approximately half with injected backdoors, across three NLP tasks, four attacks, and seven architectures. The authors report effective and efficient backdoor detection and removal, outperforming five baseline methods. The findings support dynamically changing the continuous search landscape as a practical approach to recovering discrete malicious triggers.
summary.tldr: A temperature-controlled optimization method recovers discrete NLP backdoor triggers and improves detection and removal in the reported evaluation.

title: Constrained Optimization with Dynamic Bound-scaling for Effective NLP Backdoor Defense

abstract: Weight sharing is a popular approach to reduce the training cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by reusing the weights of shared operators from previously trained child models. However, the rank correlation between the estimated accuracy and ground truth accuracy of those child models is low due to the interference among different child models caused by weight sharing. In this paper, we investigate the interference issue by sampling different child models and calculating the gradient similarity of shared operators, and observe that: 1) the interference on a shared operator between two child models is positively correlated with the number of different operators between them; 2) the interference is smaller when the inputs and outputs of the shared operator are more similar. Inspired by these two observations, we propose two approaches to mitigate the interference: 1) rather than randomly sampling child models for optimization, we propose a gradual modification scheme by modifying one operator between adjacent optimization steps to minimize the interference on the shared operators; 2) forcing the inputs and outputs of the operator across all child models to be similar to reduce the interference. Experiments on a BERT search space verify that mitigating interference via each of our proposed methods improves the rank correlation of super-pet and combining both methods can achieve better results. Our discovered architecture outperforms RoBERTa$_{\rm base}$ by 1.1 and 0.6 points and ELECTRA$_{\rm base}$ by 1.6 and 1.1 points on the dev and test set of GLUE benchmark. Extensive results on the BERT compression, reading comprehension and large-scale image classification tasks also demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of our proposed methods.

paragraphs: Weight sharing makes neural architecture search cheaper by letting candidate networks reuse trained operators. However, updates useful for one candidate can interfere with another, weakening the agreement between estimated and actual performance rankings. The paper investigates this interference by sampling candidate models and comparing the gradients they produce for shared operators.

Two observations guide the proposed fixes. Interference increases as two candidates differ in more operators, and it decreases when a shared operator receives and produces more similar representations. Accordingly, one method changes only a single operator between consecutive optimization steps. The other encourages shared operators to have similar inputs and outputs across candidate models.

Experiments in a BERT search space show that each intervention improves ranking agreement, with stronger results when combined. The discovered architecture also outperforms the reported RoBERTa and ELECTRA baselines on GLUE. Further evaluations cover BERT compression, reading comprehension, and large-scale image classification. These findings support treating interference as a practical obstacle to reliable architecture selection and show benefits from explicitly reducing it.
summary.tldr: Reducing interference between networks that share weights improves architecture rankings and the performance of architectures selected through search.

title: Analyzing and Mitigating Interference in Neural Architecture Search

abstract: Data poisoning causes misclassification of test time target examples, by injecting maliciously crafted samples in the training data. Existing defenses are often effective only against a specific type of targeted attack, significantly degrade the generalization performance, or are prohibitive for standard deep learning pipelines. In this work, we propose an efficient defense mechanism that significantly reduces the success rate of various data poisoning attacks, and provides theoretical guarantees for the performance of the model. Targeted attacks work by adding bounded perturbations to a randomly selected subset of training data to match the targets’ gradient or representation. We show that: (i) under bounded perturbations, only a number of poisons can be optimized to have a gradient that is close enough to that of the target and make the attack successful; (ii) such effective poisons move away from their original class and get isolated in the gradient space; (iii) dropping examples in low-density gradient regions during training can successfully eliminate the effective poisons, and guarantees similar training dynamics to that of training on full data. Our extensive experiments show that our method significantly decreases the success rate of state-of-the-art targeted attacks, including Gradient Matching and Bullseye Polytope, and easily scales to large datasets.

paragraphs: Targeted data poisoning inserts manipulated training examples to make a model misclassify particular inputs later. This paper studies attacks that apply bounded perturbations to a randomly selected subset of training data, aiming to match a target’s gradient or representation. Its defense focuses on identifying the poisoned examples that actually make an attack effective.

The authors show that, under bounded perturbations, only some poisons can achieve gradients sufficiently close to the target’s gradient to support a successful attack. These effective examples move away from their original class and become isolated in gradient space. The approach connects a property of effective poisoning examples to a filtering mechanism supported by theory and empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: Filtering training examples isolated in gradient space reduces targeted poisoning success by removing the poisons most capable of influencing a target.

title: Not All Poisons are Created Equal: Robust Training against Data Poisoning

abstract: It has previously been reported that the representation that is learned in the first layer of deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) is highly consistent across initializations and architectures. In this work, we quantify this consistency by considering the first layer as a filter bank and measuring its energy distribution. We find that the energy distribution is very different from that of the initial weights and is remarkably consistent across random initializations, datasets, architectures and even when the CNNs are trained with random labels . In order to explain this consistency, we derive an analytical formula for the energy profile of linear CNNs and show that this profile is mostly dictated by the second order statistics of image patches in the training set and it will approach a whitening transformation when the number of iterations goes to infinity. Finally, we show that this formula for linear CNNs also gives an excellent fit for the energy profiles learned by commonly used nonlinear CNNs such as ResNet and VGG, and that the first layer of these CNNs indeed performs approximate whitening of their inputs.

The findings connect a repeated empirical pattern to a mathematical explanation based on image statistics, with the nonlinear-network results showing how far that explanation extends in the examined models.
summary.tldr: A linear-systems analysis explains consistent first-layer CNN energy profiles through image-patch statistics and fits the approximate whitening observed in ResNet and VGG.

title: What do CNNs Learn in the First Layer and Why? A Linear Systems Perspective

abstract: In a federated learning (FL) system, distributed clients upload their local models to a central server to aggregate into a global model. Malicious clients may plant backdoors into the global model through uploading poisoned local models, causing images with specific patterns to be misclassified into some target labels. Backdoors planted by current attacks are not durable, and vanish quickly once the attackers stop model poisoning. In this paper, we investigate the connection between the durability of FL backdoors and the relationships between benign images and poisoned images (i.e., the images whose labels are flipped to the target label during local training). Specifically, benign images with the original and the target labels of the poisoned images are found to have key effects on backdoor durability. Consequently, we propose a novel attack, Chameleon, which utilizes contrastive learning to further amplify such effects towards a more durable backdoor. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Chameleon significantly extends the backdoor lifespan over baselines by $1.2\times \sim 4\times$, for a wide range of image datasets, backdoor types, and model architectures.

This paper studies why some backdoors persist longer than others. Its emphasis is durability, rather than only whether a backdoor initially succeeds.

The authors examine relationships between poisoned images and benign images from the original and target classes. They find those relationships important to persistence and introduce Chameleon, a contrastive-learning-based attack that changes the learned representation accordingly. This provides an empirical mechanism linking interactions among training examples to later backdoor behavior.

Across multiple image datasets, backdoor types, and model architectures, Chameleon extends backdoor lifespan by roughly 1.2 to 4 times relative to baselines. The security implication is that evaluating only immediate attack success can miss persistence under subsequent benign updates. The reported factors concern the tested federated settings, without establishing that the same durability holds under every aggregation rule or defense.
summary.tldr: Chameleon shows that representation relationships between benign and poisoned images can substantially increase federated-backdoor persistence.

title: Chameleon: Adapting to Peer Images for Planting Durable Backdoors in Federated Learning

abstract: Message passing neural networks (MPNNs) have been shown to suffer from the phenomenon of over-squashing that causes poor performance for tasks relying on long-range interactions. This can be largely attributed to message passing only occurring locally, over a node’s immediate neighbours. Rewiring approaches attempting to make graphs ’more connected’, and supposedly better suited to long-range tasks, often lose the inductive bias provided by distance on the graph since they make distant nodes communicate instantly at every layer. In this paper we propose a framework, applicable to any MPNN architecture, that performs a layer-dependent rewiring to ensure gradual densification of the graph. We also propose a delay mechanism that permits skip connections between nodes depending on the layer and their mutual distance. We validate our approach on several long-range tasks and show that it outperforms graph Transformers and multi-hop MPNNs.

paragraphs: Message passing neural networks can struggle when a prediction depends on distant parts of a graph. Adding connections can help, but letting distant nodes communicate immediately at every layer can weaken the useful distinction between nearby and faraway nodes.

DRew changes the communication structure gradually. Its rewiring depends on the network layer, progressively making the graph more connected as processing proceeds. A separate delay mechanism permits skip connections according to both the layer and the distance between nodes. Together, these mechanisms make distance relevant to how information travels through the model.

The framework is designed to apply to any message passing neural network architecture. On several tasks requiring long-range interactions, the authors report better performance than graph Transformers and multi-hop message passing networks. The findings support gradual rewiring and distance-dependent delays as useful ways to improve long-range communication while retaining information about the original graph’s distances.
summary.tldr: DRew improves long-range graph learning through gradual rewiring and communication delays that depend on graph distance.

title: DRew: Dynamically Rewired Message Passing with Delay

abstract: Learning in MDPs with highly complex state representations is currently possible due to multiple advancements in reinforcement learning algorithm design. However, this incline in complexity, and furthermore the increase in the dimensions of the observation came at the cost of volatility that can be taken advantage of via adversarial attacks (i.e. moving along worst-case directions in the observation space). To solve this policy instability problem we propose a novel method to detect the presence of these non-robust directions via local quadratic approximation of the deep neural policy loss. Our method provides a theoretical basis for the fundamental cut-off between safe observations and adversarial observations. Furthermore, our technique is computationally efficient, and does not depend on the methods used to produce the worst-case directions. We conduct extensive experiments in the Arcade Learning Environment with several different adversarial attack techniques. Most significantly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach even in the setting where non-robust directions are explicitly optimized to circumvent our proposed method.

The method uses a local quadratic approximation of the neural policy’s loss. This approximation captures how the loss changes near an observation, including its local curvature. The authors use it to establish a theoretical basis for distinguishing safe observations from adversarial ones. They describe the technique as computationally efficient and independent of the procedure used to construct the adversarial direction.

Experiments in the Arcade Learning Environment test the detector against several attack techniques. The reported results show effectiveness even when adversarial directions are explicitly optimized to evade the proposed method. That adaptive-attack setting is particularly relevant to the detection objective: it tests whether the method remains useful when the attacker targets the detector itself.
summary.tldr: A local quadratic analysis of policy loss detects adversarial observation directions and remains effective against tested attacks designed to evade it.

title: Detecting Adversarial Directions in Deep Reinforcement Learning to Make Robust Decisions

abstract: Moment restrictions and their conditional counterparts emerge in many areas of machine learning and statistics ranging from causal inference to reinforcement learning. Estimators for these tasks, generally called methods of moments, include the prominent generalized method of moments (GMM) which has recently gained attention in causal inference. GMM is a special case of the broader family of empirical likelihood estimators which are based on approximating a population distribution by means of minimizing a $\varphi$-divergence to an empirical distribution. However, the use of $\varphi$-divergences effectively limits the candidate distributions to reweightings of the data samples. We lift this long-standing limitation and provide a method of moments that goes beyond data reweighting. This is achieved by defining an empirical likelihood estimator based on maximum mean discrepancy which we term the kernel method of moments (KMM). We provide a variant of our estimator for conditional moment restrictions and show that it is asymptotically first-order optimal for such problems. Finally, we show that our method achieves competitive performance on several conditional moment restriction tasks.

paragraphs: Many estimation problems describe what a model should satisfy through moment restrictions: conditions on averages, sometimes conditional on other variables. Such problems arise in causal inference and reinforcement learning. The paper examines empirical likelihood approaches, including the generalized method of moments, through how they approximate an unknown population distribution from observed samples.

In the formulation discussed by the authors, using a phi-divergence to compare a candidate distribution with the empirical distribution restricts candidates to reweightings of observed data points. The proposed kernel method of moments, or KMM, replaces that comparison with maximum mean discrepancy. This change allows estimation to consider distributions beyond those obtained by merely assigning different weights to the original samples.

The authors also develop a version for conditional moment restrictions and establish asymptotic first-order optimality for that setting. This is a large-sample theoretical result about the estimator’s leading behavior. Experiments on several conditional-moment tasks show competitive performance. The main contribution is a broader distributional formulation of moment-based estimation, paired with theoretical support and empirical evidence for its conditional variant.
summary.tldr: KMM uses maximum mean discrepancy to extend moment-based estimation beyond sample reweighting, with asymptotic optimality for its conditional variant.

title: Estimation Beyond Data Reweighting: Kernel Method of Moments

abstract: We consider minimizing functions for which it is expensive to compute the (possibly stochastic) gradient. Such functions are prevalent in reinforcement learning, imitation learning and adversarial training. Our target optimization framework uses the (expensive) gradient computation to construct surrogate functions in a target space (e.g. the logits output by a linear model for classification) that can be minimized efficiently. This allows for multiple parameter updates to the model, amortizing the cost of gradient computation. In the full-batch setting, we prove that our surrogate is a global upper-bound on the loss, and can be (locally) minimized using a black-box optimization algorithm. We prove that the resulting majorization-minimization algorithm ensures convergence to a stationary point of the loss. Next, we instantiate our framework in the stochastic setting and propose the $SSO$ algorithm, which can be viewed as projected stochastic gradient descent in the target space. This connection enables us to prove theoretical guarantees for $SSO$ when minimizing convex functions. Our framework allows the use of standard stochastic optimization algorithms to construct surrogates which can be minimized by any deterministic optimization method. To evaluate our framework, we consider a suite of supervised learning and imitation learning problems. Our experiments indicate the benefits of target optimization and the effectiveness of $SSO$.

This paper proposes using an expensive gradient computation to construct a cheaper surrogate objective in a target space, such as a model's output logits. Optimizing that surrogate supports multiple parameter updates from the same costly computation.

It can be minimized locally using a black-box optimizer, and the resulting majorization-minimization algorithm converges to a stationary point. That connection supports theoretical guarantees for convex objectives. The framework allows standard stochastic methods to construct surrogates and deterministic methods to minimize them. Experiments on supervised and imitation learning problems indicate benefits from target optimization and support SSO's effectiveness, complementing the distinct full-batch and convex stochastic guarantees.
summary.tldr: Target optimization turns expensive gradients into cheaper surrogate objectives that support multiple updates, with convergence results and empirical benefits.

title: Target-based Surrogates for Stochastic Optimization

abstract: We study a distributed stochastic multi-armed bandit where a client supplies the learner with communication-constrained feedback based on the rewards for the corresponding arm pulls. In our setup, the client must encode the rewards such that the second moment of the encoded rewards is no more than $P$, and this encoded reward is further corrupted by additive Gaussian noise of variance $\sigma^2$; the learner only has access to this corrupted reward. For this setting, we derive an information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega\left(\sqrt{\frac{KT}{\mathtt{SNR} \wedge1}} \right)$ on the minimax regret of any scheme, where $\mathtt{SNR}\coloneqq \frac{P}{\sigma^2}$, and $K$ and $T$ are the number of arms and time horizon, respectively. Furthermore, we propose a multi-phase bandit algorithm, $\mathtt{UE}\text{-}\mathtt{UCB}\text{++}$, which matches this lower bound to a minor additive factor. $\mathtt{UE}\text{-}\mathtt{UCB}\text{++}$ performs uniform exploration in its initial phases and then utilizes the upper confidence bound (UCB) bandit algorithm in its final phase. An interesting feature of $\mathtt{UE}\text{-}\mathtt{UCB}\text{++}$ is that the coarser estimates of the mean rewards formed during a uniform exploration phase help to refine the encoding protocol in the next phase, leading to more accurate mean estimates of the rewards in the subsequent phase. This positive reinforcement cycle is critical to reducing the number of uniform exploration rounds and closely matching our lower bound.

Gaussian noise then corrupts that signal, so the learner must discover good actions using feedback that is both communication constrained and noisy.

It grows with the square root of the number of actions times the time horizon, with an additional penalty when the signal-to-noise ratio is below one. summary.tldr: An adaptive reward-encoding bandit algorithm nearly matches the fundamental regret limit imposed by communication constraints and Gaussian noise.

title: Communication-Constrained Bandits under Additive Gaussian Noise

abstract: Recent studies empirically demonstrate the positive relationship between the transferability of neural networks and the in-class variation of the last layer features. The recently discovered Neural Collapse (NC) phenomenon provides a new perspective of understanding such last layer geometry of neural networks. In this paper, we propose a novel metric, named Variability Collapse Index (VCI), to quantify the variability collapse phenomenon in the NC paradigm. The VCI metric is well-motivated and intrinsically related to the linear probing loss on the last layer features. Moreover, it enjoys desired theoretical and empirical properties, including invariance under invertible linear transformations and numerical stability, that distinguishes it from previous metrics. Our experiments verify that VCI is indicative of the variability collapse and the transferability of pretrained neural networks.
