paragraphs: Features from examples in the same class can become increasingly similar in a neural network’s last layer. This variability collapse is part of the neural-collapse picture of learned representations. The paper asks how to quantify it, motivated by empirical evidence linking greater within-class variation with better transferability to other tasks.

The proposed Variability Collapse Index, or VCI, is intrinsically connected to the loss of a linear probe trained on the final-layer features. It also has invariance under invertible linear transformations: changing those feature coordinates in a reversible linear way does not alter the index. The authors identify numerical stability as another desirable property distinguishing it from earlier metrics.

Experiments show that VCI is indicative of both variability collapse and the transferability of pretrained neural networks. This gives the metric a role beyond describing feature geometry: it can help characterize representations in relation to their observed transfer behavior. The stated evidence establishes an informative relationship, rather than showing that the index alone determines how well every model will transfer.
summary.tldr: VCI measures within-class feature collapse with stable, coordinate-invariant properties and empirical links to model transferability.

title: Quantifying the Variability Collapse of Neural Networks

abstract: Bayesian optimization is a powerful framework for optimizing functions that are expensive or time-consuming to evaluate. Recent work has considered Bayesian optimization of function networks (BOFN), where the objective function is given by a network of functions, each taking as input the output of previous nodes in the network as well as additional parameters. Leveraging this network structure has been shown to yield significant performance improvements. Existing BOFN algorithms for general-purpose networks evaluate the full network at each iteration. However, many real-world applications allow for evaluating nodes individually. To exploit this, we propose a novel knowledge gradient acquisition function that chooses which node and corresponding inputs to evaluate in a cost-aware manner, thereby reducing query costs by evaluating only on a part of the network at each step. We provide an efficient approach to optimizing our acquisition function and show that it outperforms existing BOFN methods and other benchmarks across several synthetic and real-world problems. Our acquisition function is the first to enable cost-aware optimization of a broad class of function networks.

paragraphs: Some expensive objectives are built from a network of functions, where intermediate outputs become inputs to later computations. Bayesian optimization can exploit this structure, but existing methods for general-purpose function networks evaluate the entire network at every iteration. That can spend resources unnecessarily when individual components are available for separate evaluation.

This paper introduces a knowledge gradient acquisition function that chooses both a node and the inputs at which to evaluate it. The choice accounts for evaluation cost, allowing each optimization step to query only part of the network. The authors also develop an efficient method for optimizing this acquisition function, addressing the computational work involved in deciding what to query.

Across several synthetic and real-world problems, the proposed approach outperforms existing function-network optimization methods and other benchmarks. Its practical significance lies in making partial evaluations part of the optimization strategy itself. The benefit applies to settings where components can actually be evaluated individually, rather than requiring every query to run the full computation.
summary.tldr: A cost-aware Bayesian optimization method chooses individual function-network components to evaluate, improving results while reducing query costs.

title: Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks with Partial Evaluations

abstract: Relationships among time series can be exploited as inductive biases in learning effective forecasting models. In hierarchical time series, relationships among subsets of sequences induce hard constraints (hierarchical inductive biases) on the predicted values. In this paper, we propose a graph-based methodology to unify relational and hierarchical inductive biases in the context of deep learning for time series forecasting. In particular, we model both types of relationships as dependencies in a pyramidal graph structure, with each pyramidal layer corresponding to a level of the hierarchy. By exploiting modern - trainable - graph pooling operators we show that the hierarchical structure, if not available as a prior, can be learned directly from data, thus obtaining cluster assignments aligned with the forecasting objective. A differentiable reconciliation stage is incorporated into the processing architecture, allowing hierarchical constraints to act both as an architectural bias as well as a regularization element for predictions. Simulation results on representative datasets show that the proposed method compares favorably against the state of the art.

paragraphs: Forecasting related time series can benefit from knowing how the series connect. Hierarchical relationships add another requirement: predictions at different levels must satisfy shared constraints. This paper develops a graph-based forecasting approach that brings ordinary relationships between series and hierarchical constraints into the same learning architecture.

The method represents these dependencies in a pyramidal graph, with each layer corresponding to a hierarchy level. Trainable graph pooling operators allow the hierarchy itself to be learned when it is not supplied beforehand. Consequently, the resulting clusters are shaped by the forecasting objective, connecting the choice of groups directly to the predictions the model must make.

A differentiable reconciliation stage incorporates hierarchical constraints into the architecture and uses them to regularize predictions during learning. This connects forecasting, grouping, and consistency within one trainable system. Simulations on representative datasets compare favorably with the state of the art. The findings support learning useful hierarchical structure alongside forecasting when that structure is not already available as prior knowledge.
summary.tldr: A trainable pyramidal graph learns time-series groups and forecasts while incorporating hierarchical consistency constraints.

title: Graph-based Time Series Clustering for End-to-End Hierarchical Forecasting

abstract: We revisit the objective perturbations framework for differential privacy where noise is added to the input $A\in \mathcal{S}$ and the result is then projected back to the space of admissible datasets $\mathcal{S}$. Through this framework, we first design novel efficient algorithms to privately release pair-wise cosine similarities. Second, we derive a novel algorithm to compute $k$-way marginal queries over $n$ features. Prior work could achieve comparable guarantees only for $k$ even. Furthermore, we extend our results to $t$-sparse datasets, where our efficient algorithms yields novel, stronger guarantees whenever $t\le n^{5/6}/\log n.$ Finally, we provide a theoretical perspective on why fast input perturbation algorithms works well in practice. The key technical ingredients behind our results are tight sum-of-squares certificates upper bounding the Gaussian complexity of sets of solutions.

paragraphs: The paper studies a differential-privacy framework that first adds noise to an input and then projects the noisy result back into the set of admissible datasets. Projection enforces the structural restrictions of that set. The authors use this framework to develop efficient algorithms for releasing useful summaries of sensitive data.

One contribution is private release of pairwise cosine similarities. Another is an algorithm for k-way marginal queries over n features, extending comparable guarantees beyond the even values of k handled by prior work. The authors also address t-sparse datasets and obtain stronger guarantees when t is at most n^(5/6)/log n.

The analysis uses tight sum-of-squares certificates to bound the Gaussian complexity of relevant solution sets. These technical bounds support the privacy framework’s guarantees and provide a theoretical explanation for why fast input-perturbation algorithms can work well in practice. The contribution combines new private-release algorithms with analysis explaining how admissible structure and sparsity can improve what these algorithms achieve.
summary.tldr: Adding noise and projecting onto admissible datasets yields efficient private similarity and marginal-query algorithms with improved sparse-data guarantees.

title: Perturb-and-Project: Differentially Private Similarities and Marginals

abstract: Many methods for estimating conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) can be expressed as weighted pseudo-outcome regressions (PORs). Previous comparisons of POR techniques have paid careful attention to the choice of pseudo-outcome transformation. However, we argue that the dominant driver of performance is actually the choice of weights. For example, we point out that R-Learning implicitly performs a POR with inverse-variance weights (IVWs). In the CATE setting, IVWs mitigate the instability associated with inverse-propensity weights, and lead to convenient simplifications of bias terms. We demonstrate the superior performance of IVWs in simulations, and derive convergence rates for IVWs that are, to our knowledge, the fastest yet shown without assuming knowledge of the covariate distribution.
originalAbstract: Many methods for estimating conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) can be expressed as weighted pseudo-outcome regressions (PORs). Previous comparisons of POR techniques have paid careful attention to the choice of pseudo-outcome transformation. However, we argue that the dominant driver of performance is actually the choice of weights. For example, we point out that R-Learning implicitly performs a POR with inverse-variance weights (IVWs). In the CATE setting, IVWs mitigate the instability associated with inverse-propensity weights, and lead to convenient simplifications of bias terms. We demonstrate the superior performance of IVWs in simulations, and derive convergence rates for IVWs that are, to our knowledge, the fastest yet shown without assuming knowledge of the covariate distribution.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimation of conditional average treatment effects: how an intervention’s average effect varies with observed characteristics. Many estimators can be written as regressions on transformed outcomes, called pseudo-outcomes, with observations receiving different weights. The authors argue that these weights can be the dominant source of performance differences, despite previous comparisons emphasizing the outcome transformation.

Their focus is inverse-variance weighting, which adjusts observations’ influence according to their variability. They show that R-Learning already has an implicit interpretation as pseudo-outcome regression with these weights. In this treatment-effect setting, inverse-variance weights reduce instability associated with inverse-propensity weighting and simplify terms appearing in the bias analysis.

Simulations demonstrate superior performance for inverse-variance weighting, and the paper derives convergence rates. The authors qualify these as the fastest they know of without assuming the covariate distribution is known. The results give both an empirical and theoretical reason to examine weighting choices carefully when comparing or constructing treatment-effect estimators, rather than attributing their behavior mainly to pseudo-outcome design.
summary.tldr: Inverse-variance weighting improves treatment-effect estimation in simulations and yields strong convergence rates without assuming a known covariate distribution.

title: Inverse-Variance Weighting for Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

abstract: Multi-layer perceptron (MLP) is a fundamental component of deep learning, and recent MLP-based architectures, especially the MLP-Mixer, have achieved significant empirical success. Nevertheless, our understanding of why and how the MLP-Mixer outperforms conventional MLPs remains largely unexplored. In this work, we reveal that sparseness is a key mechanism underlying the MLP-Mixers. First, the Mixers have an effective expression as a wider MLP with Kronecker-product weights, clarifying that the Mixers efficiently embody several sparseness properties explored in deep learning. In the case of linear layers, the effective expression elucidates an implicit sparse regularization caused by the model architecture and a hidden relation to Monarch matrices, which is also known as another form of sparse parameterization. Next, for general cases, we empirically demonstrate quantitative similarities between the Mixer and the unstructured sparse-weight MLPs. Following a guiding principle proposed by Golubeva, Neyshabur and Gur-Ari (2021), which fixes the number of connections and increases the width and sparsity, the Mixers can demonstrate improved performance.

paragraphs: MLP-Mixer architectures have performed well empirically, but their advantage over conventional multilayer perceptrons has been less clearly understood. This paper identifies sparsity as a key mechanism. It shows that a Mixer can be expressed as a wider MLP whose weights have a Kronecker-product structure.

This links an architectural explanation to a design principle: distributing a fixed connection budget across a wider, sparser model can be beneficial in the examined settings.
summary.tldr: The paper explains MLP-Mixer as a wider, structured sparse MLP and connects its performance to architectural sparsity.

title: Understanding MLP-Mixer as a wide and sparse MLP

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become pivotal in machine learning, but the impact of weight precision, such as in networks with rectified linear units (ReLU), remains underexplored. We analytically investigate the interplay of three key factors: the precision of ReLU network weights, the number of neurons, and the time of the preprocessing algorithm that generates the network description. Our study, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first formal work on weight precision, yields three main results. (1) We present an exponential time preprocessing algorithm that showcases the possibility of trading ReLU nodes for weight precision. Specifically, our method achieves an exponential reduction in neuron count when computing any function of high complexity with boolean input encoding. What is the implication of the above result in theoretical and practical works? (2) In theory of computing, in general, there is no free lunch. In our case, if you significantly reduce the number of neurons then you should pay the cost in weight precision. To address this, we introduce a notion of network size that considers weight precision in addition to the network’s number of neurons. We establish that under this redefined notion of network size, it is generally impossible to exchange neurons for weight precision in ReLU networks of the same (redefined) size. (3) In practice, we show that high weight precision alone cannot help in reducing the neuron count. If instead of our exponential time preprocessing algorithm one uses any polynomial time algorithm, then it is impossible to non-trivially reduce the neuron count, regardless of the high weight precision.

paragraphs: Counting neurons alone may hide another resource used by a neural network: the precision needed to represent its weights. This paper analyzes how weight precision, neuron count, and the preprocessing time required to construct a ReLU network interact. Its results distinguish representational possibilities from the cost of producing and describing those representations.

An exponential-time preprocessing construction demonstrates that greater weight precision can buy an exponential reduction in neuron count when computing high-complexity functions with Boolean input encoding. The authors then introduce a network-size measure that includes both neurons and weight precision. Under this accounting, exchanging neurons for precision generally cannot preserve the same total size.

The final result concerns construction time. With polynomial-time preprocessing, arbitrarily high weight precision alone cannot deliver a nontrivial reduction in neuron count in the studied framework. Together, the results show why a compact neuron count can be misleading: the apparent saving may depend on expensive weight descriptions and an expensive procedure for constructing the network.
summary.tldr: Higher weight precision can reduce ReLU neuron counts through expensive preprocessing, but the savings change when precision and construction time are counted.

title: The Effect of Weight Precision on the Neuron Count in Deep ReLU Networks

abstract: In this paper, we explore a new generative approach for learning visual representations. Our method, DARL, employs a decoder-only Transformer to predict image patches autoregressively. We find that training with Mean Squared Error (MSE) alone leads to strong representations. To enhance the image generation ability, we replace the MSE loss with the diffusion objective by using a denoising patch decoder. We show that the learned representation can be improved by using tailored noise schedules and longer training in larger models. Notably, the optimal schedule differs significantly from the typical ones used in standard image diffusion models. Overall, despite its simple architecture, DARL delivers performance remarkably close to state-of-the-art masked prediction models under the fine-tuning protocol. This marks an important step towards a unified model capable of both visual perception and generation, effectively combining the strengths of autoregressive and denoising diffusion models.

paragraphs: DARL explores whether predicting image content can also teach a model useful visual representations. It uses a decoder-only Transformer to predict image patches autoregressively, with each prediction made in sequence. The authors first find that training this architecture with mean squared error alone produces strong representations, making a simple generative objective a useful starting point.

To improve image generation, they replace that loss with a diffusion objective implemented through a denoising patch decoder. They then study how the noise schedule and training affect representation quality. Tailored schedules and longer training in larger models improve the learned representations, and the best schedule differs substantially from schedules typically used in standard image diffusion models.

Under a fine-tuning evaluation protocol, DARL performs close to leading masked prediction models despite its simple architecture. The findings support combining autoregressive prediction with denoising as a route toward models that serve both visual perception and generation. They also show that choices suited to conventional diffusion generation may need adjustment when representation learning is a central goal.
summary.tldr: DARL combines autoregressive image-patch prediction with denoising to learn visual representations that approach leading masked prediction models under fine-tuning.

title: Denoising Autoregressive Representation Learning

abstract: Preserving details and avoiding high computational costs are the two main challenges for the High-Resolution Salient Object Detection (HRSOD) task. In this paper, we propose a two-stage HRSOD model from the perspective of evolution and succession, including an evolution stage with Low-resolution Location Model (LrLM) and a succession stage with High-resolution Refinement Model (HrRM). The evolution stage achieves detail-preserving salient objects localization on the low-resolution image through the evolution mechanisms on supervision and feature; the succession stage utilizes the shallow high-resolution features to complement and enhance the features inherited from the first stage in a lightweight manner and generate the final high-resolution saliency prediction. Besides, a new metric named Boundary-Detail-aware Mean Absolute Error (${MAE}_{{BD}}$) is designed to evaluate the ability to detect details in high-resolution scenes. Extensive experiments on five datasets demonstrate that our network achieves superior performance at real-time speed (49 FPS) compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: High-resolution salient object detection needs to locate prominent objects while preserving fine details. Processing a large image also raises computational cost. ESNet addresses these demands with a two-stage design that distributes localization and high-resolution refinement across different parts of the network.

The first stage uses a low-resolution location model. Mechanisms acting on supervision and features help it retain detail-relevant information while finding salient objects. The second stage inherits those features and supplements them with shallow features from the high-resolution image. This lightweight refinement produces the final high-resolution saliency prediction without assigning all of the work to a single high-resolution stage.

The paper also introduces Boundary-Detail-aware Mean Absolute Error, a metric intended to evaluate detail detection in high-resolution scenes. Across five datasets, the authors report superior performance relative to state-of-the-art methods at a real-time speed of 49 frames per second. The combined contribution addresses both prediction and evaluation: a staged model preserves details efficiently, while the proposed metric specifically assesses the detail quality that motivates the architecture.
summary.tldr: ESNet combines low-resolution localization with lightweight high-resolution refinement, reporting strong detail preservation and real-time salient object detection.

title: ESNet: Evolution and Succession Network for High-Resolution Salient Object Detection

abstract: Selecting appropriate thresholds for anomaly detection in online, unsupervised settings is a challenging task, especially in the presence of data distribution shifts. Addressing these challenges is critical in many practical large scale systems, such as infrastructure monitoring and network intrusion detection. This paper proposes an algorithm that connects online thresholding with constructing confidence sequences achieving (1) adaptive online threshold selection robust to distribution shifts, (2) statistical guarantees on false positive and false negative rates without any distributional assumptions, and (3) improved performance when given relevant offline data to warm-start the online algorithm, while having bounded degradation if the offline data is irrelevant. We complement our theoretical results by empirical evidence that our method outperforms commonly used baselines across synthetic and real world datasets.

paragraphs: Online anomaly detection needs a threshold that decides when an observation should trigger an alert. Choosing that threshold is especially difficult without supervision and when the incoming data distribution changes. This paper connects threshold selection to the construction of confidence sequences, bringing a statistical framework into the process of updating thresholds over time.

The proposed algorithm adapts its threshold online and is designed to remain robust to distribution shifts. The authors establish guarantees on both false positives and false negatives without imposing distributional assumptions. These two kinds of error correspond to raising an alert unnecessarily and failing to flag an anomaly, so the theory addresses both sides of threshold selection.

The algorithm can also begin with offline data. Relevant historical data improves performance, while irrelevant historical data causes only bounded degradation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show better performance than commonly used baselines. Together, the results support an approach that combines ongoing adaptation, statistical error guarantees, and a controlled way to benefit from information available before monitoring begins.
summary.tldr: Confidence-sequence-based thresholding adapts to distribution shifts, provides false-positive and false-negative guarantees, and can safely benefit from relevant historical data.

title: Online Adaptive Anomaly Thresholding with Confidence Sequences

abstract: Non-IID transfer learning on graphs is crucial in many high-stakes domains. The majority of existing works assume stationary distribution for both source and target domains. However, real-world graphs are intrinsically dynamic, presenting challenges in terms of domain evolution and dynamic discrepancy between source and target domains. To bridge the gap, we shift the problem to the dynamic setting and pose the question: given the label-rich source graphs and the label-scarce target graphs both observed in previous $T$ timestamps, how can we effectively characterize the evolving domain discrepancy and optimize the generalization performance of the target domain at the incoming $T+1$ timestamp? To answer it, we propose a generalization bound for dynamic non-IID transfer learning on graphs, which implies the generalization performance is dominated by domain evolution and domain discrepancy between source and target graphs. Inspired by the theoretical results, we introduce a novel generic framework named EvoluNet. It leverages a transformer-based temporal encoding module to model temporal information of the evolving domains and then uses a dynamic domain unification module to efficiently learn domain-invariant representations across the source and target domains. Finally, EvoluNet outperforms the state-of-the-art models by up to 12.1%, demonstrating its effectiveness in transferring knowledge from dynamic source graphs to dynamic target graphs.

paragraphs: EvoluNet studies knowledge transfer between graph domains that change over time and have different data distributions. Its setting provides label-rich source graphs and label-scarce target graphs for the previous T timestamps. The goal is to improve prediction in the target domain at timestamp T+1, accounting for both evolving graphs and changing differences between domains.

The authors derive a generalization bound that highlights domain evolution and source–target discrepancy as major influences on target performance. This motivates two parts of the framework. A transformer-based temporal encoder represents how the domains evolve, while a dynamic domain-unification module learns representations that are invariant across the source and target domains.

The approach therefore treats temporal change and transfer mismatch as connected problems. Its reported improvements over state-of-the-art models reach up to 12.1%, supporting the effectiveness of transferring knowledge between dynamic graphs in the evaluated settings. The theoretical contribution explains why both kinds of change deserve attention, while the framework turns that guidance into a concrete representation-learning strategy.
summary.tldr: EvoluNet combines temporal modeling and domain-invariant representations to transfer knowledge between changing source and target graphs.

title: EvoluNet: Advancing Dynamic Non-IID Transfer Learning on Graphs

abstract: In federated learning (FL), data heterogeneity is the main reason that existing theoretical analyses are pessimistic about the convergence rate. In particular, for many FL algorithms, the convergence rate grows dramatically when the number of local updates becomes large, especially when the product of the gradient divergence and local Lipschitz constant is large. However, empirical studies can show that more local updates can improve the convergence rate even when these two parameters are large, which is inconsistent with the theoretical findings. This paper aims to bridge this gap between theoretical understanding and practical performance by providing a theoretical analysis from a new perspective on data heterogeneity. In particular, we propose a new and weaker assumption compared to the local Lipschitz gradient assumption, named the heterogeneity-driven pseudo-Lipschitz assumption. We show that this and the gradient divergence assumptions can jointly characterize the effect of data heterogeneity. By deriving a convergence upper bound for FedAvg and its extensions, we show that, compared to the existing works, local Lipschitz constant is replaced by the much smaller heterogeneity-driven pseudo-Lipschitz constant and the corresponding convergence upper bound can be significantly reduced for the same number of local updates, although its order stays the same. In addition, when the local objective function is quadratic, more insights on the impact of data heterogeneity can be obtained using the heterogeneity-driven pseudo-Lipschitz constant. For example, we can identify a region where FedAvg can outperform mini-batch SGD even when the gradient divergence can be arbitrarily large. Our findings are validated using experiments.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients perform local training before combining their updates. Existing theory can predict substantially worse convergence when clients take more local steps and their objectives differ strongly. Yet experiments sometimes show that additional local training helps even in those circumstances. This paper develops a different mathematical description of heterogeneity to help explain that mismatch.

The authors introduce a heterogeneity-driven pseudo-Lipschitz assumption that is weaker than the usual local gradient smoothness assumption. Combined with a gradient divergence assumption, it yields convergence bounds for FedAvg and extensions. A potentially much smaller heterogeneity-dependent constant replaces the local Lipschitz constant, reducing the bound without changing its asymptotic order.

For quadratic local objectives, the analysis also identifies a region where FedAvg can outperform mini-batch SGD despite arbitrarily large gradient divergence. This conditional finding shows why gradient disagreement alone can give an overly pessimistic picture. Experiments support the analysis, which sharpens how existing algorithms are understood rather than claiming that more local updates always help.
summary.tldr: A weaker description of client heterogeneity yields tighter federated optimization bounds and helps explain when additional local training can help.

title: A New Theoretical Perspective on Data Heterogeneity in Federated Optimization

abstract: How to explain temporal models is a significant challenge due to the inherent characteristics of time series data, notably the strong temporal dependencies and interactions between observations. Unlike ordinary tabular data, data at different time steps in time series usually interact dynamically, forming influential patterns that shape the model’s predictions, rather than only acting in isolation. Existing explanatory approaches for time series often overlook these crucial temporal interactions by treating time steps as separate entities, leading to a superficial understanding of model behavior. To address this challenge, we introduce FDTempExplainer, an innovative model-agnostic explanation method based on functional decomposition, tailored to unravel the complex interplay within black-box time series models. Our approach disentangles the individual contributions from each time step, as well as the aggregated influence of their interactions, in a rigorous framework. FDTempExplainer accurately measures the strength of interactions, yielding insights that surpass those from baseline models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a wide range of time series applications, including anomaly detection, classification, and forecasting, showing its superior performance to the state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: A time-series model can respond to a pattern formed by several observations together. Explaining each time step separately can therefore miss a major part of its behavior: how observations interact over time. The paper argues that this omission makes existing explanations superficial when temporal relationships strongly influence predictions.

FDTempExplainer addresses the problem through functional decomposition. It separates the contribution associated with each time step from the combined influence of interactions between time steps. The method is model-agnostic, making its explanation framework applicable to black-box temporal models. Its purpose is to expose both individual effects and the additional influence that arises when observations act together.

The authors report that the method accurately measures interaction strength and provides insights beyond those obtained from baseline approaches. Evaluations span anomaly detection, classification, and forecasting, with superior performance relative to state-of-the-art algorithms in the studied applications. The practical significance is that an explanation can account for a model's use of temporal patterns, rather than leaving their contribution hidden inside separate time-step importance scores.
summary.tldr: FDTempExplainer explains black-box time-series predictions by separating individual time-step contributions from the influence of temporal interactions.

title: Explain Temporal Black-Box Models via Functional Decomposition

abstract: Contextual optimization problems are prevalent in decision-making applications where historical data and contextual features are used to learn predictive models that inform optimal actions. However, practical applications often suffer from model misspecification due to incomplete knowledge of the underlying data-generating process, leading to suboptimal decisions. Existing approaches primarily address the well-specified case, leaving a critical gap in handling misspecified models. In this paper, we propose a novel Integrated Learning and Optimization (ILO) framework that explicitly accounts for model misspecification by introducing a tractable surrogate loss function with strong theoretical guarantees on generalizability, tractability, and optimality. Our surrogate loss aligns with the true decision performance objective, ensuring robustness to misspecification without imposing restrictive assumptions. The proposed approach effectively mitigates the challenges of non-convexity and non-smoothness in the target loss function, leading to efficient optimization procedures. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis and experimental validation, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our work offers a principled solution to the practically relevant challenge of model misspecification in contextual optimization.

paragraphs: Contextual optimization uses historical observations and information about the current situation to choose an action. A predictive model informs that choice, but the model may misrepresent the process generating the data. This mismatch can lead to poor decisions, even when the learning procedure is otherwise well designed. The paper makes this model misspecification central to its approach.

The authors propose an Integrated Learning and Optimization framework built around a tractable surrogate loss. A surrogate replaces a difficult training objective with one that is easier to optimize. Here, it is designed to align with actual decision performance while accounting for misspecification. This addresses the non-convexity and non-smoothness that can make the original decision loss computationally challenging.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees concerning generalization, tractability, and optimality, and reports experimental improvements over state-of-the-art methods. Its significance is the connection between efficient model training and the quality of the actions that follow. The framework targets reliable decision performance even when the predictive model does not correctly describe the underlying data-generating process.
summary.tldr: An integrated learning-and-optimization framework uses a tractable surrogate loss to improve decisions under model misspecification.

title: Contextual Optimization Under Model Misspecification: A Tractable and Generalizable Approach

abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance, MLLM-based virtual agents have demonstrated remarkable performance. However, existing benchmarks face significant limitations, including uncontrollable task complexity, extensive manual annotation, and a lack of multidimensional evaluation. In response to these challenges, we introduce OmniBench, a self-generating, graph-based benchmark with an automated pipeline for synthesizing tasks of controllable complexity through subtask composition. To evaluate the diverse capabilities of virtual agents on the graph, we further present OmniEval, a multidimensional evaluation framework that includes subtask-level evaluation, graph-based metrics, and comprehensive tests across 10 capabilities. Our synthesized dataset contains 36k graph-structured tasks across 20 scenarios, achieving a 91% human acceptance rate. Training on our graph-structured data shows that it improves generalization across environments. We conduct multidimensional evaluations for virtual agents, revealing their performance across various capabilities and paving the way for future advancements. Our project is available at https://omni-bench.github.io.

paragraphs: Evaluating virtual agents requires tasks with meaningful differences in difficulty and measurements that reveal their individual capabilities. Existing benchmarks can make complexity hard to control, require extensive manual annotation, and provide limited evaluation dimensions. OmniBench addresses these issues with an automated process for generating tasks represented as graphs.

The benchmark composes subtasks to produce tasks with controllable complexity. Its companion framework, OmniEval, evaluates performance at the subtask level, uses graph-based metrics, and tests ten capabilities. This combination connects the structure used to generate tasks with the structure used to assess agent behavior, providing more detailed information than an undifferentiated overall result.

The generated dataset contains 36,000 graph-structured tasks across 20 scenarios and achieves a 91% human acceptance rate. Training on this data improves generalization across environments in the reported experiments. The multidimensional evaluations also reveal differences across agent capabilities. Together, these findings support automated task composition as both an evaluation resource and a source of training data for virtual agents.
summary.tldr: OmniBench automatically generates controllable graph-structured tasks, while OmniEval measures virtual agents across subtasks and ten capabilities.

title: What Limits Virtual Agent Application? OmniBench: A Scalable Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Essential Virtual Agent Capabilities

abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) can generalize to implications of facts that they are finetuned on. For example, if finetuned on "John Doe lives in Tokyo," LMs correctly answer "What language do the people in John Doe’s city speak?” with "Japanese”. However, little is known about the mechanisms that enable this generalization or how they are learned during pretraining. We introduce extractive structures as a framework for describing how components in LMs (e.g., MLPs or attention heads) coordinate to enable this generalization. The structures consist of informative components that store training facts as weight changes, and upstream and downstream extractive components that query and process the stored information to produce the correct implication. We hypothesize that extractive structures are learned during pretraining when encountering implications of previously known facts. This yields two predictions: a data ordering effect where extractive structures can be learned only if facts precede their implications, and a weight grafting effect where extractive structures can be grafted to predict counterfactual implications. We empirically show these effects in the OLMo-7b, Llama 3-8b, Gemma 2-9b, and Qwen 2-7b models. Of independent interest, our results also indicate that fact learning can occur at both early and late layers, which lead to different forms of generalization.

These observations support the proposed mechanism without turning the pretraining hypothesis into a universal explanation. The results also indicate that facts can be learned in early or late layers, with different resulting forms of generalization.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes and empirically investigates cooperating model components that let pretrained language models derive implications from finetuned facts.

title: Extractive Structures Learned in Pretraining Enable Generalization on Finetuned Facts

abstract: State-Space Models (SSMs), and particularly Mamba, have recently emerged as a promising alternative to Transformers. Mamba introduces input selectivity to its SSM layer (S6) and incorporates convolution and gating into its block definition. While these modifications do improve Mamba’s performance over its SSM predecessors, it remains largely unclear how Mamba leverages the additional functionalities provided by input selectivity, and how these interact with the other operations in the Mamba architecture. In this work, we demystify the role of input selectivity in Mamba, investigating its impact on function approximation power, long-term memorization, and associative recall capabilities. In particular: (i) we prove that the S6 layer of Mamba can represent projections onto Haar wavelets, providing an edge over its Diagonal SSM (S4D) predecessor in approximating discontinuous functions commonly arising in practice; (ii) we show how the S6 layer can dynamically counteract memory decay; (iii) we provide analytical solutions to the MQAR associative recall task using the Mamba architecture with different mixers — Mamba, Mamba-2, and S4D. We demonstrate the tightness of our theoretical constructions with empirical results on concrete tasks. Our findings offer a mechanistic understanding of Mamba and reveal opportunities for improvement.

Together, these results provide mechanistic accounts of representational power, memory, and retrieval, clarifying how architectural components can support observed capabilities and revealing opportunities for further improvement.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how Mamba’s input selectivity supports discontinuous-function approximation, resistance to memory decay, and associative recall.

title: Understanding Input Selectivity in Mamba: Impact on Approximation Power, Memorization, and Associative Recall Capacity

abstract: We develop a novel optimization method for quantization-aware training (QAT). Specifically, we show that convex, piecewise-affine regularization (PAR) can effectively induce neural network weights to cluster towards discrete values. We minimize PAR-regularized loss functions using an aggregate proximal stochastic gradient method (AProx) and prove that it enjoys last-iterate convergence. Our approach provides an interpretation of the straight-through estimator (STE), a widely used heuristic for QAT, as the asymptotic form of PARQ. We conduct experiments to demonstrate that PARQ obtains competitive performance on convolution- and transformer-based vision tasks.

We minimize PAR-regularized loss functions using an aggregate proximal stochastic gradient method (AProx) and prove that it enjoys last-iterate convergence. Our approach provides an interpretation of the straight-through estimator (STE), a widely used heuristic for QAT, as the asymptotic form of PARQ. paragraphs: Quantization-aware training prepares neural network weights to take discrete values. PARQ approaches this through the training objective: it adds a convex, piecewise-affine regularizer that encourages weights to cluster near discrete values. The paper shows that this kind of regularization can effectively create the clustering needed for quantization, making the optimization formulation central to the method.

The authors minimize the regularized objective using an aggregate proximal stochastic gradient method called AProx and prove last-iterate convergence. That guarantee concerns the endpoint of the optimization sequence. They also show that the straight-through estimator, a common heuristic in quantization-aware training, can be interpreted as an asymptotic form of PARQ, connecting the proposed method to an established practical technique.

Experiments on vision tasks with convolutional and transformer-based models show competitive performance. The contribution combines a mechanism for encouraging discrete weight values, a convergence result for the optimization method, and a theoretical interpretation of the straight-through estimator. The empirical finding supports the approach’s practical relevance without claiming that it dominates other quantization methods.
summary.tldr: PARQ encourages quantized weights through piecewise-affine regularization, provides last-iterate convergence, and interprets the straight-through estimator as its asymptotic form.

title: PARQ: Piecewise-Affine Regularized Quantization

abstract: Transforming complex actions into discrete skill abstractions has demonstrated strong potential for robotic manipulation.Existing approaches mainly leverage latent variable models, e.g., VQ-VAE, to learn skill abstractions through learned vectors (codebooks), while they suffer from codebook collapse and modeling the causal relationship between learned skills. To address these limitations, we present Skill Training with Augmented Rotation (STAR), a framework that advances both skill learning and composition to complete complex behaviors. Specifically, to prevent codebook collapse, we devise rotation-augmented residual skill quantization (RaRSQ).It encodes relative angles between encoder outputs into the gradient flow by rotation-based gradient mechanism. Points within the same skill code are forced to be either pushed apart or pulled closer together depending on gradient directions.Further, to capture the casual relationship between skills, we present causal skill transformer (CST) which explicitly models dependencies between skill representations through an autoregressive mechanism for coherent action generation.Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of STAR on both LIBERO benchmark and realworld tasks, with around 12% improvement over the baselines.

paragraphs: Representing complex robot actions as discrete skills can make manipulation easier to organize. Existing approaches learn a codebook of skill vectors, but can suffer from codebook collapse and difficulty modeling relationships between skills. STAR addresses both the diversity of the learned skill representations and their composition into coherent behavior.

Its rotation-augmented residual skill quantization mechanism incorporates relative angles between encoder outputs into gradient flow. Depending on gradient direction, points assigned to the same skill code are pushed apart or pulled together. This mechanism is designed to prevent codebook collapse. A separate causal skill transformer models dependencies between skill representations autoregressively, using preceding skill information to support coherent action generation.

The authors evaluate STAR on the LIBERO benchmark and real-world tasks, reporting around 12% improvement over the baselines. The findings support treating skill learning and skill sequencing as connected problems. Maintaining diverse representations provides the skill vocabulary, while explicit dependency modeling helps combine that vocabulary into more complex robot behavior.
summary.tldr: STAR combines rotation-based skill quantization with autoregressive skill composition, reporting around 12% improvement over baselines in robotic tasks.

title: STAR: Learning Diverse Robot Skill Abstractions through Rotation-Augmented Vector Quantization

abstract: The critical challenge of semi-supervised semantic segmentation lies in how to fully exploit a large volume of unlabeled data to improve the model’s generalization performance for robust segmentation. Existing methods mainly rely on confidence-based scoring functions in the prediction space to filter pseudo labels, which suffer from the inherent trade-off between true and false positive rates. In this paper, we carefully design an agent construction strategy to build clean sets of correct (positive) and incorrect (negative) pseudo labels, and propose the Agent Score function (AgScore) to measure the consensus between candidate pixels and these sets. In this way, AgScore takes a step further to capture homogeneous patterns in the embedding space, conditioned on clean positive/negative agents stemming from the prediction space, without sacrificing the merits of confidence score, yielding better trad-off. We provide theoretical analysis to understand the mechanism of AgScore, and demonstrate its effectiveness by integrating it into three semi-supervised segmentation frameworks on Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, and COCO datasets, showing consistent improvements across all data partitions.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised semantic segmentation uses unlabeled images to help learn pixel-level predictions. A central decision is which model-generated labels to trust during training. Confidence thresholds provide one signal, but accepting more useful labels can also admit more incorrect ones. The paper seeks a better balance by adding information from learned feature representations.

The authors construct clean reference sets of correct and incorrect pseudo labels, called positive and negative agents. Their Agent Score, or AgScore, measures agreement between candidate pixels and these sets. It uses patterns in embedding space while conditioning on agents obtained from prediction space, retaining the benefits of confidence information and adding evidence about feature similarity.

The paper provides theoretical analysis of this scoring mechanism and tests it within three semi-supervised segmentation frameworks. Evaluations on Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, and COCO show consistent improvements across all tested data partitions. The results support using structured agreement with positive and negative references to improve pseudo-label selection, making unlabeled data more useful for the downstream segmentation task.
summary.tldr: AgScore improves pseudo-label selection for segmentation by combining confidence information with agreement against positive and negative feature references.

title: Beyond Confidence: Exploiting Homogeneous Pattern for Semi-Supervised Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Language Models (LMs) have advanced diagnosis prediction by leveraging the semantic understanding of medical concepts in Electronic Health Records (EHRs). Despite these advancements, existing LM-based methods often fail to capture the structures of medical concepts (e.g., hierarchy structure from domain knowledge). In this paper, we propose BoxLM, a novel framework that unifies the structures and semantics of medical concepts for diagnosis prediction. Specifically, we propose a structure-semantic fusion mechanism via box embeddings, which integrates both ontology-driven and EHR-driven hierarchical structures with LM-based semantic embeddings, enabling interpretable medical concept representations. Furthermore, in the box-aware diagnosis prediction module, an evolve-and-memorize patient box learning mechanism is proposed to model the temporal dynamics of patient visits, and a volume-based similarity measurement is proposed to enable accurate diagnosis prediction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BoxLM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, especially achieving strong performance in few-shot learning scenarios, showcasing its practical utility in real-world clinical settings.

paragraphs: Language models can represent the meanings of medical concepts in electronic health records, but those meanings do not fully capture how concepts are organized. Medical concepts also belong to hierarchies, including relationships supplied by domain knowledge. BoxLM brings these structural relationships into the same framework as language-based representations for diagnosis prediction.

The framework uses box embeddings to combine hierarchies derived from medical ontologies and patient records with semantic embeddings from a language model. This fusion produces interpretable concept representations. A separate patient-modeling mechanism updates and retains information across visits, allowing the patient representation to reflect changes over time. Diagnosis prediction then uses a similarity measure based on box volumes.

The reported experiments show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, with particularly strong results when few training examples are available. These findings support combining the organization of medical knowledge with its textual meaning, while also accounting for a patient's visit history. The demonstrated outcome is improved diagnosis prediction in the experiments, which the authors present as evidence of potential practical clinical utility.
summary.tldr: BoxLM combines medical hierarchies, language-based meaning, and changing patient histories through box embeddings to improve diagnosis prediction.

title: BoxLM: Unifying Structures and Semantics of Medical Concepts for Diagnosis Prediction in Healthcare

abstract: Despite their success in specific scenarios, existing foundation agents still struggle to generalize across various virtual scenarios, mainly due to the dramatically different encapsulations of environments with manually designed observation and action spaces. To handle this issue, we propose the General Computer Control (GCC) setting to restrict foundation agents to interact with software through the most unified and standardized interface, i.e., using screenshots as input and keyboard and mouse actions as output. We introduce Cradle, a modular and flexible LMM-powered framework, as a preliminary attempt towards GCC. Enhanced by six key modules, Information Gathering, Self-Reflection, Task Inference, Skill Curation, Action Planning, and Memory, Cradle is able to understand input screenshots and output executable code for low-level keyboard and mouse control after high-level planning and information retrieval, so that Cradle can interact with any software and complete long-horizon complex tasks without relying on any built-in APIs. Experimental results show that Cradle exhibits remarkable generalizability and impressive performance across four previously unexplored commercial video games (Red Dead Redemption 2, Cities:Skylines, Stardew Valley and Dealer’s Life 2), five software applications (Chrome, Outlook, Feishu, Meitu and CapCut), and a comprehensive benchmark, OSWorld. With a unified interface to interact with any software, Cradle greatly extends the reach of foundation agents thus paving the way for generalist agents.

paragraphs: Computer agents often encounter environments with separately designed observation and action interfaces. The paper identifies these differences as a major obstacle to generalization. It proposes General Computer Control, a setting in which the agent sees screenshots and acts through the keyboard and mouse. This supplies a common interaction interface across software.

Cradle is a preliminary framework for this setting, powered by a large multimodal model. Its six modules handle information gathering, self-reflection, task inference, skill curation, action planning, and memory. Together, they connect visual observations and high-level planning to executable code for low-level input control. The framework is designed to carry out complex, extended tasks without relying on software-specific built-in APIs.

Experiments cover four commercial games, five software applications, and the OSWorld benchmark. The authors report strong performance and generalization across these environments. The significance is the breadth achievable through one interface: the same screenshot-and-input arrangement supports interaction with varied software. These results present Cradle as a step toward general computer agents, with the framework's general-purpose interface demonstrated across the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Cradle combines multimodal reasoning, planning, and memory to operate varied software through screenshots and keyboard-and-mouse actions.

title: Cradle: Empowering Foundation Agents towards General Computer Control

abstract: Randomized response (RR) mechanisms constitute a fundamental and effective technique for ensuring label differential privacy (LabelDP). However, existing RR methods primarily focus on the response labels while overlooking the influence of covariates and often do not fully address optimality. To address these challenges, this paper explores optimal LabelDP procedures using RR mechanisms, focusing on achieving optimal estimation and inference in binary response models. We first analyze the asymptotic behaviors of RR binary response models and then optimize the procedure by maximizing the trace of the Fisher Information Matrix within the $\varepsilon$- and $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-LabelDP constraints. Our theoretical results indicate that the proposed methods achieve optimal LabelDP guarantees while maintaining statistical accuracy in binary response models under mild conditions. Furthermore, we develop private confidence intervals with nominal coverage for statistical inference. Extensive simulation studies and real-world applications confirm that our methods outperform existing approaches in terms of precise estimation, privacy protection, and reliable inference.

paragraphs: Binary response models analyze outcomes with two possible labels. Randomized response protects those labels by introducing randomness, but that protection also changes the information available for estimation. This paper studies how to design the randomization while accounting for covariates, the accompanying variables that help explain an outcome. Its goal is to combine label privacy with accurate estimation and dependable statistical inference.

The authors first analyze how randomized-response models behave as the amount of data grows. They then optimize the procedure by maximizing the trace of the Fisher information matrix, a criterion for the statistical information retained. This optimization operates within both epsilon label differential privacy and its epsilon-delta variant, explicitly linking the information objective to privacy constraints.

Under mild conditions, the theoretical results establish the stated optimal privacy guarantees while preserving statistical accuracy. The authors also construct private confidence intervals with nominal coverage. Simulations and real-world applications show improvements over existing approaches in estimation, privacy protection, and inference, supporting the benefit of designing randomization around the response model.
summary.tldr: This work optimizes randomized response for binary outcomes to balance label privacy, estimation accuracy, and reliable confidence intervals.

title: Differentially Private Analysis for Binary Response Models: Optimality, Estimation, and Inference

abstract: Improving the generalization of multi-camera 3D object detection is essential for safe autonomous driving in the real world. In this paper, we consider a realistic yet more challenging scenario, which aims to improve the generalization when only single source data available for training, as gathering diverse domains of data and collecting annotations is time-consuming and labor-intensive. To this end, we propose the Fourier Cross-View Learning (FCVL) framework including Fourier Hierarchical Augmentation (FHiAug), an augmentation strategy in the frequency domain to boost domain diversity, and Fourier Cross-View Semantic Consistency Loss to facilitate the model to learn more domain-invariant features from adjacent perspectives. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees via augmentation graph theory. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to explore generalizable multi-camera 3D object detection with a single source. Extensive experiments on various testing domains have demonstrated that our approach achieves the best performance across various domain generalization methods.

paragraphs: Multi-camera 3D object detectors need to work beyond the conditions represented in their training data. Collecting and labeling many different domains is expensive, so this paper studies generalization when training data comes from only one source. The goal is to improve performance on other domains without requiring a collection of diverse training sources.

The proposed Fourier Cross-View Learning framework has two components. Fourier Hierarchical Augmentation modifies data in the frequency domain to increase training diversity. A cross-view semantic consistency loss encourages the detector to learn features that remain meaningful across neighboring camera perspectives and are less tied to a particular domain.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees using augmentation graph theory and evaluate the framework across multiple testing domains. Their experiments report the best performance among the domain generalization methods compared. The approach connects two sources of training information: variation created through augmentation and semantic agreement across camera views. The results support this combination as a way to improve generalization under the stated single-source training constraint.
summary.tldr: Fourier augmentation and cross-view consistency improve multi-camera 3D detection across testing domains when training uses only one source.

title: Generalizable Multi-Camera 3D Object Detection from a Single Source via Fourier Cross-View Learning

abstract: The remarkable capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) can be mainly attributed to their massive training datasets, which are often scraped from the internet without respecting data owners’ intellectual property rights. Dataset Inference (DI) offers a potential remedy by identifying whether a suspect dataset was used in training, thereby enabling data owners to verify unauthorized use. However, existing DI methods require a private set—known to be absent from training—that closely matches the compromised dataset’s distribution. Such in-distribution, held-out data is rarely available in practice, severely limiting the applicability of DI. In this work, we address this challenge by synthetically generating the required held-out set. Our approach tackles two key obstacles: (1) creating high-quality, diverse synthetic data that accurately reflects the original distribution, which we achieve via a data generator trained on a carefully designed suffix-based completion task, and (2) bridging likelihood gaps between real and synthetic data, which is realized through post-hoc calibration. Extensive experiments on diverse text datasets show that using our generated data as a held-out set enables DI to detect the original training sets with high confidence, while maintaining a low false positive rate. This result empowers copyright owners to make legitimate claims on data usage and demonstrates our method’s reliability for real-world litigations. Our code is available at https://github.com/sprintml/PostHocDatasetInference.

paragraphs: Dataset inference investigates whether a collection of data was used to train a model. Existing methods require comparison data that matches the suspected dataset’s distribution but is known to have been excluded from training. Such a private held-out collection is often unavailable, limiting the ability to investigate training-data use after the fact.

The authors replace that missing comparison collection with synthetic data. A generator trained on a specially designed suffix-completion task produces diverse text intended to reflect the original distribution. Post-hoc calibration then addresses likelihood differences between real and generated examples. Both components matter: matching the content distribution alone does not resolve the scoring gap between synthetic and real data.

Across diverse text datasets, experiments show that the generated comparison sets enable high-confidence detection of original training datasets while maintaining a low false positive rate. The findings support a more practical route to post-hoc dataset inference when suitable held-out data was never reserved. The authors position this capability as evidence that could help data owners substantiate claims about unauthorized training use.
summary.tldr: Synthetic comparison data and post-hoc calibration enable dataset inference without a preexisting private held-out set, with strong reported detection and low false positives.

title: Unlocking Post-hoc Dataset Inference with Synthetic Data

abstract: Test-time compute scaling allocates inference computation uniformly, uses fixed sampling strategies, and applies verification only for reranking. In contrast, we propose a verifier-guided adaptive framework treating reasoning as iterative trajectory generation and selection. For each problem, the agent runs multiple inference iterations. In each iteration, it optionally produces a high-level plan, selects a set of reasoning tools and a compute strategy together with an exploration parameter, and then generates a candidate reasoning trajectory. A process reward model (PRM) serves as a unified control signal: within each iteration, step-level PRM scores are aggregated to guide pruning and expansion during generation, and across iterations, aggregated trajectory rewards are used to select the final response. Across datasets, our dynamic, PRM-guided approach consistently outperforms direct test-time scaling, yielding large gains on MATH-500 and several-fold improvements on harder benchmarks such as AIME24 and AMO-Bench. We characterize efficiency using theoretical FLOPs and a compute intensity metric penalizing wasted generation and tool overhead, demonstrating that verification-guided allocation concentrates computation on high-utility reasoning paths.
originalAbstract: Test-time compute scaling allocates inference computation uniformly, uses fixed sampling strategies, and applies verification only for reranking. In contrast, we propose a verifier-guided adaptive framework treating reasoning as iterative trajectory generation and selection. For each problem, the agent runs multiple inference iterations. In each iteration, it optionally produces a high-level plan, selects a set of reasoning tools and a compute strategy together with an exploration parameter, and then generates a candidate reasoning trajectory. A process reward model (PRM) serves as a unified control signal: within each iteration, step-level PRM scores are aggregated to guide pruning and expansion during generation, and across iterations, aggregated trajectory rewards are used to select the final response. Across datasets, our dynamic, PRM-guided approach consistently outperforms direct test-time scaling, yielding large gains on MATH-500 and several-fold improvements on harder benchmarks such as AIME24 and AMO-Bench. We characterize efficiency using theoretical FLOPs and a compute intensity metric penalizing wasted generation and tool overhead, demonstrating that verification-guided allocation concentrates computation on high-utility reasoning paths.

paragraphs: Spending more computation at inference time raises a second question: which reasoning paths deserve that effort? This paper proposes an adaptive framework that uses verification throughout an iterative reasoning process. A process reward model supplies a shared signal for controlling generation and choosing the final answer.

An iteration may include a high-level plan, selects reasoning tools and a compute strategy with an exploration parameter, and generates a candidate trajectory. Aggregated step-level reward scores guide pruning and expansion within generation. Aggregated trajectory rewards then guide selection across iterations.

Across the evaluated datasets, the method consistently outperforms direct test-time scaling, with large gains on MATH-500 and several-fold improvements on harder benchmarks including AIME24 and AMO-Bench. The authors assess efficiency using theoretical FLOPs and a compute-intensity measure that penalizes wasted generation and tool overhead. Their results support using verification to direct computation toward useful reasoning paths, connecting answer quality with how inference effort is allocated.
summary.tldr: A verifier-guided framework adaptively selects, expands, and prunes reasoning paths to improve how test-time computation is spent.

title: What If We Allocate Test-Time Compute Adaptively?

abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) depend on in-context learning (ICL) for rapid task adaptation, but their scalability is severely limited by finite context windows and the growing cost of key–value (KV) caches in long multi-modal sequences. Existing memory compression approaches typically rely on rigid token removal or sample-dependent importance estimation, which introduces bias, disrupts semantic structure—particularly for visual representations—and yields static memories that cannot adapt to new queries. We introduce TASM (Task-Aware Structured Memory), a training-free framework that addresses these limitations through task-aware, structure-preserving, and dynamically accessible memory construction. TASM employs Task-Vector Guided Compression to replace sample-specific signals with a task-level direction that captures shared relevance across demonstrations. To preserve the underlying information manifold, it further applies Semantics-Aware Token Merging, formulating compression as a Bipartite Graph Matching problem that merges tokens without destructive pruning. Finally, TASM organizes compressed representations into a multi-resolution hierarchy consisting of a compact Core Memory and a Latent Bank, enabling Query-Adaptive Dynamic Activation and Dynamic Retrieval at inference time. Empirical evaluations show that TASM sustains strong multi-modal ICL performance under high compression ratios, demonstrating an effective balance between efficiency, adaptability, and semantic fidelity.

The training-free framework first identifies a task-level direction that captures relevance shared across demonstrations. This combines guidance about what matters for the task with a mechanism for consolidating information without destructive pruning.

Query-adaptive activation and retrieval make additional stored information accessible during inference as needed. Evaluations report strong multimodal in-context learning performance under high compression ratios. The findings support memory designs that combine compact storage with dynamic access, balancing efficiency, adaptability, and preservation of meaning.
summary.tldr: TASM compresses multimodal demonstrations into structured memory that preserves semantics and retrieves information according to the current query.

title: Task-Aware Structured Memory for Dynamic Multi-modal In-Context Learning

abstract: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery couples kilometer-scale context with query-critical evidence that may occupy only a few pixels. Such vast spatial scale leads to a quadratic explosion of visual tokens and hinders the extraction of information from small objects. Previous works utilize direct downsampling, dense tiling, or global top-K pruning, which either compromise query-critical image details or incur unpredictable compute. In this paper, we propose UHR-BAT, a query-guided and region-faithful token compression framework to efficiently select visual tokens under strict context budget. Specifically, we leverage text-guided, multi-scale importance estimation for visual tokens, effectively tackling the challenge of achieving precise yet low-cost feature extraction. Furthermore, by introducing region-wise preserve and merge strategies, we mitigate visual token redundancy, further driving down the computational budget. The experimental results show that UHR-BAT achieves state-of-the-art performance across various benchmarks.

paragraphs: Ultra-high-resolution remote sensing images combine enormous spatial coverage with crucial details that may occupy only a few pixels. Feeding all that visual information into a vision-language model creates a large token burden. Downsampling, dense tiling, and global token pruning can lose query-relevant details or make computational demands difficult to control.

UHR-BAT compresses visual tokens under a strict context budget, using the text query to guide selection. It estimates token importance at multiple spatial scales, allowing the requested information to influence what is retained. Region-wise preservation and merging then reduce redundant tokens while respecting the regional structure of the image. These components address both the search for small relevant evidence and the cost of representing the broader scene.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks. The stated result supports combining query guidance with regional compression for this setting, where the largest visual structures need not contain the most useful evidence. Budget awareness is part of the framework’s design, tying token selection directly to the available context capacity while seeking to preserve the details needed to answer the query.
summary.tldr: UHR-BAT uses query-guided, multiscale token selection and regional merging to process huge remote sensing images within a strict context budget.

title: UHR-BAT: Budget-Aware Token Compression Vision-Language model for Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing

abstract: Interactive world models continually generate video by responding to a user’s actions, enabling open-ended generation capabilities. However, existing models typically lack a 3D representation of the environment, meaning 3D consistency must be implicitly learned from data, and spatial memory is restricted to limited temporal context windows. This results in an unrealistic user experience and presents significant obstacles to downstream tasks such as training agents. To address this, we present PERSIST, a new paradigm of world model which simulates the evolution of a latent 3D scene: environment, camera, and renderer. This allows us to synthesise new frames with persistent spatial memory and consistent geometry. Both quantitative metrics and a qualitative user study show substantial improvements in spatial memory, 3D consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing methods, enabling coherent, evolving 3D worlds. We further demonstrate novel capabilities, including synthesising diverse 3D environments from a single image, as well as enabling fine-grained, geometry-aware control over generated experiences by supporting environment editing and specification directly in 3D space.

paragraphs: Interactive world models generate video as a user takes actions. PERSIST instead models an evolving latent 3D scene, including the environment, camera, and renderer. New frames are synthesized from this persistent state. The approach gives the model a continuing spatial representation to work with as the experience changes, connecting visual generation to an underlying scene rather than only to a history of pixels.

Quantitative evaluation and a user study report substantial improvements in spatial memory, geometric consistency, and stability over long interactions compared with existing methods. The authors also demonstrate generating diverse 3D environments from one image and controlling experiences through direct editing and specification in 3D space. These capabilities show how persistent scene state can support both visual continuity and more precise, geometry-aware user control.
summary.tldr: PERSIST maintains an evolving 3D scene to improve spatial memory, geometric consistency, and control in interactive video generation.

title: Beyond Pixel Histories: World Models with Persistent 3D State

abstract: Significant progress has been made in the field of Instruction-based Image Editing Models (IIEMs). However, while these models demonstrate plausible adherence to instructions and strong reasoning ability on current benchmarks, their ability to edit small objects remains underexplored, despite its importance for precise local editing and refining details in both real and generated images. In this paper, we introduce DeepLookEditBench (DLEBench), the first benchmark dedicated to assessing the abilities of IIEMs in editing small-scale objects. Specifically, we construct a challenging testbed comprising 1889 samples across seven instruction types. In these samples, target objects occupy only 1%-10% of the image area, covering complex scenarios such as partial occlusion and multi-object editing. To ensure robust evaluation on this benchmark, we propose an evaluation protocol with refined score rubrics to minimize subjectivity and ambiguity in two criteria: Instruction Following and Visual Consistency. This protocol also introduces a dual-mode evaluation framework (Tool-driven and Oracle-guided Modes) addressing the misalignment between LMM-as-a-Judge and human judgments on DLEBench. Empirical results on 10 IIEMs reveal significant performance gaps in small-scale object editing, highlighting the need for specialized benchmarks to advance this ability.

paragraphs: DLEBench evaluates whether instruction-based image editors can reliably change small objects. Existing benchmarks show strong instruction following and reasoning, but those successes leave precise local editing underexplored. The new benchmark focuses on objects occupying only 1%–10% of an image, making the requested changes concern a small part of the overall scene.
