These results show why dedicated evaluation matters: plausible performance on broader editing tasks does not fully characterize the ability to make accurate changes to fine details.
summary.tldr: DLEBench exposes gaps in small-object image editing through a dedicated testbed and evaluation protocol addressing automated-judge disagreement.

title: DLEBench: Evaluating Small-scale Object Editing Ability for Instruction-based Image Editing Model

abstract: We study in-context universal approximation and compositional generalization in frozen softmax Transformers as prompt-programmable computation. We prove in-context universality via in-context emulation: a fixed-weight Transformer emulates target computations specified by the prompt and hence approximates a broad class of continuous sequence-to-sequence functions. Building on this view, we establish one-pass and multi-pass composition theorems: prompts associated with simple “subprograms” let the same fixed Transformer execute their composition and thereby synthesize more complex programs on-the-fly. These results support a principled view of prompts as programs and fixed-weight Transformers as program interpreters. They also provide concrete mechanisms by which GPT-style models execute and assemble algorithms in context. Please see arXiv for the full version.

Building on this view, we establish one-pass and multi-pass composition theorems: prompts associated with simple “subprograms” let the same fixed Transformer execute their composition and thereby synthesize more complex programs on-the-fly. These results support a principled view of prompts as programs and fixed-weight Transformers as program interpreters. They also provide concrete mechanisms by which GPT-style models execute and assemble algorithms in context. Please see arXiv for the full version.

paragraphs: This paper studies what a softmax Transformer can compute through its prompt while its weights remain fixed. The central perspective treats prompts as specifications of computations and the Transformer as an interpreter. This gives a mathematical way to examine how in-context behavior can implement algorithms without updating model parameters.

The authors prove in-context universality through emulation: a fixed-weight Transformer can emulate computations supplied in its prompt and thereby approximate a broad class of continuous sequence-to-sequence functions. The result connects approximation ability to a mechanism for executing prompt-specified computations, rather than treating that ability as an isolated property.

They also establish composition theorems for one-pass and multi-pass execution. Prompts describing simpler subprograms allow the same fixed Transformer to execute their composition and assemble more complex programs in context. These are theoretical results about computational capability. They provide concrete mechanisms for understanding algorithm execution and composition in GPT-style models within the framework studied.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that fixed-weight softmax Transformers can emulate prompt-specified computations and compose simpler programs in context.

title: In-Context Universal Approximation, Compositional Generalization, and Algorithm Emulation

abstract: Standard RLHF relies on transitive scalar rewards, failing to capture the cyclic nature of human preferences. While some approaches like the General Preference Model (GPM) address this, we identify a theoretical limitation: their implicit formulation entangles hierarchy with cyclicity, failing to guarantee dominant solutions. To address this, we propose the Hybrid Reward-Cyclic (HRC) model, which utilizes game-theoretic decomposition to explicitly disentangle preferences into orthogonal transitive (scalar) and cyclic (vector) components. Complementing this, we introduce Dynamic Self-Play Preference Optimization (DSPPO), which treats alignment as a time-varying game to progressively guide the policy toward the Nash equilibrium. Synthetic data experiments further validate HRC’s structural superiority in mixed transitive–cyclic settings, where HRC converges faster and achieves higher accuracy than GPM. Experiments on RewardBench 2 demonstrate that HRC consistently improves over both BT and GPM baselines (e.g., +1.23% on Gemma-2B-it). In particular, its superior performance in the Ties domain empirically validates the model’s robustness in handling complex, non-strict preferences. Extensive downstream evaluations on AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard-v0.1, and MT-Bench confirm the efficacy of our framework. Notably, when using Gemma-2B-it as the base preference model, HRC+DSPPO achieves a peak length-controlled win-rate of 44.75% on AlpacaEval 2.0 and 46.8% on Arena-Hard-v0.1, significantly outperforming SPPO baselines trained with BT or GPM. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/lab-klc/Hybrid-Reward-Cyclic.

title: Transitivity Meets Cyclicity: Explicit Preference Decomposition for Dynamic Large Language Model Alignment

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models achieve impressive visual fidelity, yet they remain unreliable in multi-object generation. Despite extensive empirical evidence of these failures, the underlying causes remain unclear. We begin by asking how much of this limitation arises from the data itself. To disentangle data effects, we consider two regimes across different dataset sizes: (1) concept generalization, where each individual concept is observed during training under potentially imbalanced data distributions, and (2) compositional generalization, where specific combinations of concepts are systematically held out. To study these regimes, we introduce mosaic (Multi-Object Spatial relations, AttrIbution, Counting), a controlled framework for dataset generation. By training diffusion models on mosaic, we find that scene complexity plays a dominant role rather than concept imbalance, and that counting is uniquely difficult to learn in low-data regimes. Moreover, compositional generalization collapses as more concept combinations are held out during training. These findings highlight fundamental limitations of diffusion models and motivate stronger inductive biases and data design for robust multi-object compositional generation.

paragraphs: Visually convincing generated images can still contain the wrong objects, relationships, or counts. This paper investigates how training data contributes to such multi-object failures. The authors introduce mosaic, a controlled dataset-generation framework covering spatial relations, attribution, and counting, so they can vary data conditions and study their effects on diffusion models.

The study separates two regimes across different dataset sizes. Concept generalization includes every individual concept during training but permits imbalanced frequencies. Compositional generalization systematically withholds particular combinations of concepts. This separation helps distinguish difficulty learning from uneven concept exposure from difficulty assembling familiar concepts into combinations absent from the training data.

In the controlled experiments, scene complexity plays a more dominant role than concept imbalance, while counting is especially difficult when data is scarce. Compositional generalization collapses as more combinations are withheld. These findings point to substantial weaknesses in the studied models’ multi-object generation and motivate stronger inductive biases and more deliberate data design. They also show why balancing individual concepts alone may not address the central difficulties.
summary.tldr: Controlled experiments identify scene complexity, low-data counting, and withheld concept combinations as major obstacles to multi-object diffusion generation.

title: When Do Diffusion Models Learn to Generate Multiple Objects?

abstract: Verification of model outputs is rapidly emerging as a key primitive for both training and real-world deployment of large language models (LLMs). In practice, this often involves using imperfect LLM judges and reward models since ground truth acquisition can be time-consuming and expensive. We introduce Fully Unsupervised Score Ensembling (FUSE), a method for improving verification quality by ensembling verifiers without access to ground truth correctness labels. The key idea behind FUSE is to control conditional dependencies between verifiers in a manner that improves the unsupervised performance of a class of spectral algorithms from the ensembling literature. Despite requiring zero ground truth labels, FUSE typically matches or improves upon semi-supervised alternatives in test-time scaling experiments with diverse sets of generator models, verifiers, and benchmarks. In particular, we validate our method on both conventional academic benchmarks such as GPQA Diamond and on frontier, unsaturated benchmarks such as Humanity’s Last Exam and IMO Shortlist questions.

paragraphs: Checking language-model answers often depends on other imperfect models, such as judges or reward models. Combining several verifiers could improve those judgments, but learning how to combine them usually benefits from known correct and incorrect answers. Obtaining those labels can be expensive, especially for difficult questions whose answers are hard to establish.

Fully Unsupervised Score Ensembling, or FUSE, combines verifiers without ground-truth correctness labels. Its central idea is to control conditional dependencies between the verifiers. These relationships matter because the usefulness of multiple judgments depends on how their information overlaps. FUSE manages those dependencies to improve the unsupervised performance of spectral ensembling algorithms.

In test-time scaling experiments spanning different answer-generating models, verifiers, and benchmarks, FUSE typically matches or improves upon semi-supervised alternatives. Evaluations include GPQA Diamond, Humanity’s Last Exam, and IMO Shortlist questions. These findings suggest that carefully handling relationships among imperfect verifiers can yield useful combined judgments even without labeled examples for fitting the ensemble.
summary.tldr: FUSE combines imperfect verifiers without correctness labels and typically matches or exceeds semi-supervised alternatives in the reported evaluations.

title: FUSE: Ensembling Verifiers with Zero Labeled Data

abstract: Molecular representation learning has achieved remarkable progress in molecular property prediction, yet out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains challenging. In practice, training data typically cover only a limited portion of the chemical space, causing models to rely on environment-dependent factors that fail to transfer when scaffold structures or functional compositions shift. To address this issue, we propose MoSIR, a framework for learning molecular semantic invariant representation with prototype constraint, which projects entangled molecular embeddings into a learnable semantic prototype space to extract semantic invariant representation while isolating environment-sensitive variations. Building upon this decomposition, we optimize a bi-level min-max objective that introduces representation perturbations to simulate plausible environment shifts and enforce semantic stability. We further provide theoretical guarantees for MoSIR by deriving an OOD generalization bound under distribution shifts. Extensive experiments on multiple molecular OOD benchmarks demonstrate that MoSIR consistently outperforms strong baselines across diverse shift settings, and qualitative analyses confirm that the learned prototypes capture meaningful chemical semantics.

paragraphs: Molecular property predictors often learn from a limited part of chemical space. When molecular scaffolds or functional compositions change, patterns that helped during training may stop being useful. MoSIR addresses this problem by separating molecular information intended to remain stable across environments from variations that are sensitive to the training environment.

The framework projects mixed molecular embeddings into a learnable space of semantic prototypes. This decomposition supports a bi-level min-max objective that perturbs representations to simulate plausible environmental changes and encourages semantic stability under those changes. The prototypes provide a structured space in which the model can distinguish transferable chemical meaning from environment-sensitive variation.

The authors derive an out-of-distribution generalization bound and evaluate MoSIR on multiple molecular benchmarks with different kinds of distribution shift. It consistently outperforms strong baselines in those experiments. Qualitative analyses also indicate that the prototypes capture meaningful chemical semantics. Together, the results support combining prototype-based separation with perturbation-based training to improve transfer beyond the chemical environments represented in training.
summary.tldr: MoSIR learns molecular prototypes and trains for semantic stability under simulated shifts to improve out-of-distribution property prediction.

title: Learning Molecular Semantic Invariant Representation with Prototype Constraint

abstract: Macro placement is a fundamental step in modern VLSI physical design, determining the solution quality of high-dimensional combinatorial optimization problems. Despite recent advancements in machine learning for spatial coordinate determination, the temporal dimension of placement sequencing remains largely governed by static heuristics. In this work, we demonstrate that the placement sequence is not merely a preprocessing step but a decisive factor in optimization, where suboptimal early decisions trigger irreversible domino effects that constrain the solution space. To harness this unexplored dimension, we propose OrderPlace, a novel framework that automates the discovery of macro placement strategies via proxy-guided Large Language Model (LLM) evolution. Unlike existing methods that rely on manual rules like area or connectivity, OrderPlace leverages LLMs to evolve generalizable, code-level ordering strategies—ranging from static metrics to dynamic, physics-inspired mechanisms. To mitigate the prohibitive cost of evaluating sequences, we introduce a lightweight proxy evaluation mechanism that efficiently filters candidates using a deterministic greedy probe. Experimental results on the standard ISPD 2005 benchmarks demonstrate that OrderPlace discovers novel ordering strategies. Compared with WireMask-EA and the state-of-the-art method EGPlace, OrderPlace reduces wirelength by 34.04% and 14.08%, respectively.

It argues that early choices can trigger irreversible downstream effects, restricting later options, so the ordering strategy is itself an important optimization variable rather than a routine preliminary step.

OrderPlace uses language models to evolve executable ordering strategies. The discovered strategies can range from fixed scoring rules to dynamic, physics-inspired mechanisms, expanding beyond manually chosen rules based on area or connectivity. Evaluating many candidate sequences would be costly, so a lightweight proxy uses a deterministic greedy placement probe to filter candidates efficiently.

On the ISPD 2005 benchmarks, the framework discovers novel ordering strategies and reduces wirelength by 34.04% relative to WireMask-EA and 14.08% relative to EGPlace. These results show that improving the decision sequence can materially improve the eventual layout in the evaluated setting. The broader contribution is a search procedure that combines language-generated strategy code with inexpensive preliminary evaluation to explore this consequential design choice.
summary.tldr: OrderPlace evolves chip macro-placement ordering strategies with language models and cheap proxy evaluations, reducing benchmark wirelength.

title: Order Matters: Unveiling the Hidden Impact of Macro Placement Sequences via Proxy-Guided LLM Evolution

abstract: Despite significant progress in multi-modal Re-Identification (ReID), existing methods tend to emphasize low-frequency cues. Consequently, they focus on attributes such as color, illumination, and coarse appearance, while overlooking mid- and high-frequency structures that encode geometric, textural, and identity-discriminative details. This imbalance leads to incomplete spectral representations and unstable cross-modal alignment. To overcome these limitations, we introduce FUSE, a frequency-domain framework that reformulates multi-modal ReID as a two-stage process of spectral disentanglement and energy alignment. The proposed Spectral Decomposition Module (SDM) adaptively partitions features into low, mid, and high-frequency subspaces, enabling hierarchical spectral modeling. The Cross-Modal Alignment Module (CAM) further enforces energy alignment and subspace complementarity across modalities via frequency-consistency regularization. In addition, FUSE incorporates learnable frequency modulation to enhance robustness under varying illumination and heterogeneous sensor conditions. Extensive experiments on RGBNT201, RGBNT100, and MSVR310 show that FUSE achieves 9.1% mAP and 9.5% Rank-1 improvements, establishing an interpretable frequency-domain paradigm for multi-modal representation learning.

summary.tldr: FUSE separates and aligns visual information across frequency ranges to improve multi-modal object re-identification.

title: FUSE: Frequency-domain Unification and Spectral Energy Alignment for Multi-modal Object Re-Identification

abstract: We propose a training-free conditional sampling method for flow matching models based on importance sampling. Because a naïve application of importance sampling suffers from weight degeneracy in high-dimensional settings, we modify and incorporate a resampling technique in sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) during intermediate stages of the generation process. To encourage the generated samples to diverge along distinct trajectories, we derive a stochastic flow with adjustable noise strength to replace the deterministic flow at the intermediate stage. Our framework requires no additional training, while providing theoretical guarantees of asymptotic accuracy. Experimentally, our method significantly outperforms existing approaches on conditional sampling tasks for MNIST and CIFAR-10. We further demonstrate the applicability of our approach in higher-dimensional, multimodal settings through text-to-image generation experiments on CelebA-HQ.

paragraphs: TFTF aims to draw samples satisfying a condition from flow-matching models without additional training. It starts from importance sampling, but a direct application encounters weight degeneracy in high dimensions: useful sampling weight becomes concentrated among too few candidates. The method changes the generation process to address this concentration.

The authors adapt a resampling technique from sequential Monte Carlo and apply it at intermediate generation stages. They also derive a stochastic flow with adjustable noise to replace the deterministic flow at an intermediate stage. This encourages candidates to follow distinct trajectories, supporting diversity as resampling directs computation toward the conditional target.

The framework comes with theoretical guarantees of asymptotic accuracy, which concern its limiting behavior. Experiments show substantial improvements over existing conditional-sampling approaches on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Text-to-image experiments on CelebA-HQ further demonstrate applicability in a higher-dimensional, multimodal setting. The contribution is a sampling procedure that combines intermediate selection and stochastic exploration while leaving model training unchanged.
summary.tldr: TFTF combines intermediate resampling and stochastic flows for conditional generation without extra training, with asymptotic accuracy guarantees.

title: TFTF: Training-Free Targeted Flow for Conditional Sampling

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) finds a least-cost transport plan between two probability distributions. Unlike standard OT, which infers unstructured pointwise mappings, low-rank optimal transport explicitly constrains the rank of the transport plan to infer latent structure. This improves statistical robustness, yields sharper parametric rates for estimating Wasserstein distances, and generalizes $K$-means to co-clustering. However, these advantages come at the cost of a non-convex and NP-hard optimization problem. We introduce Transport Clustering, an algorithm to compute a low-rank OT plan that reduces low-rank OT to a clustering problem on correspondences obtained from a full-rank transport registration step. We prove that this reduction yields polynomial-time, constant-factor approximation algorithms for low-rank OT: specifically, a $(1+\gamma)$ approximation for negative-type metrics, a $(1+\gamma+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,)$ approximation for kernel costs, and a $(1+\gamma+\rho)$ approximation for general metrics satisfying the triangle inequality. Here, $\gamma \in [0,1]$ is the cost ratio of the optimal full-rank to low-rank solutions, and $\rho\in[0,1]$ is an asymmetry coefficient on the cluster variances. Numerically, Transport Clustering outperforms existing solvers on synthetic benchmarks and large-scale datasets.

Constraining the transport plan to low rank makes latent structure explicit and offers statistical advantages, including more robust estimation. It also creates a non-convex, NP-hard optimization problem. This paper introduces Transport Clustering to obtain efficiently computable approximations to that structured matching problem.

The authors prove polynomial-time, constant-factor approximation guarantees for this reduction. summary.tldr: Transport Clustering reduces low-rank optimal transport to clustering and provides polynomial-time constant-factor approximation guarantees.

title: Transport Clustering: Solving Low-Rank Optimal Transport via Clustering

abstract: Predicting model performance at larger scales enables the design of training strategies and architectures tailored to specific performance targets. Empirical scaling law research identifies functional forms to aid this prediction task. These describe the relationship between loss and compute using a loss-compute frontier defined by learning curves. Due to the empirical nature of this approach, the computational burden is substantial, making strategic resource allocation essential – yet it remains surprisingly underexplored. In this work, we address this shortcoming by exploring the suitability of Successive Halving (SH) and SH combined with parametric and non-parametric surrogate models. In addition to enabling a more systematic allocation of a given compute budget, our findings show that SH paired with surrogate models yields a set of learning curves that includes one with a lower loss-compute value than what naive uniform allocation or an SH-only approach can obtain. Our experiments demonstrate mean relative improvements of up to $2.84%$ and $5.47%$ on real-world and synthetic learning curve datasets. This strategic resource allocation enables us to obtain accurate scaling laws at significantly reduced computational costs, saving up to $98.7%$ over the traditional exhaustive approach.

paragraphs: Scaling laws help predict how model loss changes as training compute increases. Estimating them can itself be expensive because researchers must collect learning curves across training configurations. This paper studies how to distribute a fixed compute budget so that the resulting curves reveal the loss-compute frontier more efficiently.

The authors investigate Successive Halving, a procedure that progressively removes less promising candidates, both alone and combined with surrogate models. These surrogates provide parametric or non-parametric estimates to guide resource allocation. The aim is to spend more of the available budget on curves that are useful for identifying strong performance at a given computational cost.

In the reported experiments, combining Successive Halving with surrogates finds a set containing a better loss-compute curve than uniform allocation or Successive Halving alone. title: Active Budget Allocation for Efficient Scaling Law Estimation via Surrogate-Guided Pruning

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are the two dominant paradigms for enhancing Large Language Model (LLM) performance on downstream tasks. While RL generally preserves broader model capabilities (retention) better than SFT, it comes with significant costs: complex reward engineering, instability, and expensive on-policy sampling. In contrast, SFT is efficient but brittle, often suffering from catastrophic forgetting due to $\textbf{Supervision Mismatch}$: the divergence between the model’s evolving policy and static training labels. We address this trade-off with $\textbf{Trajectory-Mixed Supervision (TMS)}$, a reward-free framework that approximates the on-policy benefits of RL by creating a dynamic curriculum from the model’s own historical checkpoints. TMS minimizes $\textit{Policy-Label Divergence (PLD)}$, preventing the mode collapse that drives forgetting in standard SFT. Experiments across reasoning (MATH, GSM8K) and instruction-following benchmarks demonstrate that TMS effectively shifts the accuracy-retention Pareto frontier. While RL remains the gold standard for retention, TMS significantly outperforms standard and iterative SFT, bridging the gap to RL without requiring reward models or verifiers. Mechanistic analysis confirms that PLD drift accurately predicts forgetting, and that TMS successfully mitigates this drift.

Reinforcement learning generally retains broader capabilities better, but introduces reward-design, stability, and sampling costs.

This reward-free self-distillation framework seeks to reduce Policy-Label Divergence, the discrepancy between the evolving policy and its supervision. It significantly outperforms standard and iterative supervised fine-tuning, although reinforcement learning remains strongest for retention. Mechanistic analysis finds that divergence drift predicts forgetting and that TMS reduces this drift. The findings support adapting supervision over training as a way to approach RL’s retention benefits without reward models or verifiers.
summary.tldr: TMS uses historical model checkpoints to adapt supervision, improving task learning and capability retention without rewards or verifiers.

title: TMS: Trajectory-Mixed Supervision for On-Policy Self Distillation

abstract: We study the MaxECC problem, where given an edge-colored hypergraph with $k$ colors and edge size $r$, we seek to color the vertices of the graph in order to maximize the number of satisfied edges (edges having the same color as their extremities): this is an effective mechanism for clustering (coloring) objects based on their multi-way interactions with one another in a system, providing significant applications in machine learning, clustering, and data mining. We exponentially improve upon the approximation ratio of an existing algorithm to $\frac{1}{r+1}$, present another novel dependent-rounding algorithm with an approximation ratio of $1/ \lceil \frac{k}{2}\rceil$, and modify the initial algorithm via analytical scaling techniques in order to achieve an approximation factor of $(1-e^{-r})/r$. We then apply our scaling algorithm to graph MaxECC and improve the best-known approximation factor for all hypergraphs: in particular, our algorithm provides an approximation factor of $0.43$ as opposed to the previously-known $0.38$ factor for graphs.

paragraphs: MaxECC describes a clustering problem in which interactions already have colors and the objects involved must be assigned colors. An interaction counts as satisfied when all its participating objects receive its color. Hyperedges allow an interaction to involve more than two objects, making the formulation suitable for clustering based on relationships among whole groups.

The paper develops approximation algorithms, which provide guarantees relative to the best achievable number of satisfied edges. For edge size r, one algorithm achieves a ratio of 1/(r+1), exponentially improving an existing algorithm's ratio. A separate dependent-rounding method achieves 1/ceil(k/2), where k is the number of colors. The guarantees therefore capture different structural aspects of the problem.

Analytical scaling further improves the first approach to a factor of (1-exp(-r))/r. Applying the scaling approach to ordinary graphs yields a factor of 0.43, compared with the previously known 0.38. These are algorithmic approximation guarantees rather than reported prediction accuracies. The results improve how much of an optimal clustering objective can be guaranteed when exact optimization is not supplied.
summary.tldr: New rounding and scaling algorithms improve approximation guarantees for clustering with colored multi-way interactions, including a 0.43 guarantee for graphs.

title: Edge-colored Clustering in Hypergraphs: A MaxECC Approximation

abstract: Federated Continual Learning (FCL) enables the continuous acquisition of knowledge from streaming tasks, but inherently struggles with the temporal dynamics of client data distributions. These dynamics naturally induce asynchronous concept drift, where distribution shifts occur independently across clients at unsynchronized times and with varying magnitudes. Such asynchrony generates conflicting updates that destabilize global convergence and exacerbate catastrophic forgetting. However, existing FCL research focuses on static or incremental settings, typically treating all incoming updates uniformly, which obscures concept drift under divergent distributions and fails to adapt to the evolution of learned concepts. To address these limitations, we propose RC-FCL, a retrospective calibration framework for FCL that can effectively distinguish asynchronous concept drift and adjust the learning strategy adaptively. Specifically, RC-FCL leverages a conditional generative model to synthesize class-conditional reference distributions of previously learned concepts for local drift detection. It calibrates local adaptation using a weighting mechanism driven by the local discriminator to prioritize informative samples, and executes a global aggregation strategy based on drift magnitude. Our experimental results demonstrate that RC-FCL achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: In federated continual learning, different clients keep learning as their data changes over time. Those changes need not happen together or have the same magnitude. The resulting asynchronous concept drift can produce conflicting updates, destabilize the shared model, and worsen forgetting of earlier knowledge.

RC-FCL uses retrospective calibration to detect and respond to these differences. A conditional generative model synthesizes reference distributions for previously learned classes, providing a basis for local drift detection. A weighting mechanism driven by the local discriminator then prioritizes informative samples during adaptation. This coordinates two decisions that uniform update handling overlooks: how each client should learn from its current data and how its update should contribute to the shared model. The experiments report competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods. The findings support explicitly recognizing clients' different stages of distribution change, while the stated performance claim is competitiveness rather than universal superiority.
summary.tldr: RC-FCL uses generated reference distributions and drift-aware weighting to adapt federated learning when clients' data changes at different times.

title: RC-FCL: Combating Asynchronous Concept Drift in Federated Continual Learning via Retrospective Calibration

abstract: Ride-hailing platforms must balance passenger waiting times with overall system efficiency under highly uncertain supply–demand conditions. Adaptive delayed matching, which controls the holding intervals for batched sets of requests and vehicles, exposes an inherent trade-off between matching and pickup delays. The non-stationary nature of request arrivals and dynamic congestion exposes a key limitation of existing methods, which rely on shallow encoders that cannot capture these spatio-temporal regime shifts. We introduce the Regime-Aware Spatio-Temporal Mixture-of-Experts (RAST-MoE) framework, which formalizes adaptive delayed matching as a regime-aware Markov Decision Process and equips RL agents with a self-attention Mixture-of-Experts encoder, letting different experts specialize automatically across operational regimes while keeping per-sample computation modest. On real-world TNC trajectory data from San Francisco, our 12M-parameter model reduces average matching delay by 10% and pickup delay by 15%, trains stably without reward hacking, generalizes zero-shot to two additional cities, and exhibits clear expert specialization across demand regimes. These results demonstrate the value of MoE-enhanced RL for large-scale decision-making tasks with complex spatio-temporal dynamics.

paragraphs: Ride-hailing platforms can hold requests briefly before matching passengers and vehicles in batches. Choosing the holding interval involves a trade-off between time spent waiting for a match and time spent waiting for pickup. Changing demand and congestion make this decision difficult, particularly when a model cannot represent shifts across places and times.

RAST-MoE frames delayed matching as a decision process that accounts for changing operational regimes. Its reinforcement-learning agent uses a self-attention mixture-of-experts encoder, allowing different experts to specialize automatically in different conditions. These findings support regime-sensitive representations for coordinating decisions under changing supply and demand.
summary.tldr: RAST-MoE uses specialized experts to adapt ride-hailing matching decisions to changing conditions, reducing both matching and pickup delays in the reported evaluation.

title: RAST-MoE-RL: A Regime-Aware Spatio-Temporal MoE Framework for Deep Reinforcement Learning in Ride-Hailing

abstract: Reasoning is a core capability of language models (LMs), yet it remains unclear how much model capacity is necessary to support reasoning during pretraining. In this work, we study the minimal parameter budget required for implicit reasoning, defined as the ability to infer new facts from learned knowledge without explicit chain-of-thought supervision. To isolate this phenomenon, we pretrain LMs from scratch in a controlled synthetic environment that mimics the structure and distribution of real-world knowledge graphs, and evaluate their ability to complete missing edges via multi-hop inference. From both a theoretical and an empirical perspective, we identify a scaling law linking this optimal parameter budget to a graph search entropy measure. Across a wide range of model sizes, training steps, and graph complexities, we show that an optimally sized language model can reliably reason over approximately 0.008 bits of information per parameter at most. Our results characterize the minimal sufficient capacity for implicit reasoning during pretraining. Our findings provide principled guidance for matching model size to data complexity and offer new insights into the scaling behavior of reasoning in large language models.

title: Finding the Minimal Parameter Budget for Implicit Reasoning: A Data Complexity Driven Scaling Law for Language Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize sensitive facts, motivating unlearning methods that remove targeted knowledge without costly retraining. However, unlearning research remains heavily English-centric. We study multilingual unlearning by extending the TOFU benchmark to five languages, and fine-tune, unlearn and query our models with different permutations of languages. We find that unlearning transfer – the ability of an unlearned model to "forget" facts in languages other than the unlearning language – is highly variable: e.g., it is strongest between languages sharing scripts and families, and we show that the unlearning language predicts which query languages are most likely to yield the strongest transfer. Layer-wise analysis reveals that unlearning leaves the shared cross-lingual latent space largely intact in early layers, instead operating primarily in later decoding layers. This suggests that unlearning does not truly erase knowledge, but rather induces superficial suppression. Exploiting this structure, a single inference-time steering direction reverses much of this suppression across languages, recovering 50% (Qwen) and 90% (Gemma) of the unlearned knowledge.

The authors interpret this pattern as evidence suggesting suppression of knowledge rather than its genuine erasure.

A subsequent intervention uses a single direction to steer the model during inference and reverses much of that suppression across languages. It recovers 50% of the unlearned knowledge in Qwen and 90% in Gemma. These findings make both cross-language testing and reversibility relevant to assessing unlearning: reduced answers after an update may coexist with recoverable internal knowledge.
summary.tldr: Multilingual tests find uneven unlearning transfer and substantial reversibility, suggesting that the studied methods often suppress rather than erase knowledge.

title: Multilingual Unlearning in LLMs: Transfer, Dynamics, and Reversibility

abstract: This paper studies second-order methods for nonconvex-strongly-convex bilevel optimization. We propose a novel fully second-order bilevel approximation method (FSBA) that achieves an iteration complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-1.5})$ for finding the $(\epsilon, \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon}))$ second-order stationary point of the hyper-objective function. Our results demonstrate that second-order methods can achieve an accelerated convergence rate than first-order methods in bilevel optimization. To address the heavy computational cost associated with the second-order oracle, we introduce a lazy variant of FSBA, called LFSBA, which reuses second-order information across several iterations. We prove that LFSBA exhibits better computational complexity than FSBA by a factor of $\sqrt{d}$, where $d$ is the dimension of the problem. We also apply a similar idea to nonconvex strongly-concave minimax optimization and propose the lazy minimax cubic-regularized Newton (LMCN) method with better computational complexity compared to existing second-order methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems with an inner optimization task nested inside an outer one. Its setting allows the outer objective to be nonconvex while requiring strong convexity in the inner problem. The proposed Fully Second-Order Bilevel Approximation method uses second-order information to accelerate progress toward a second-order stationary point of the resulting hyper-objective.

FSBA achieves an iteration complexity of approximately ε^−1.5, with logarithmic factors suppressed, for an (ε, O(√ε)) second-order stationary point. This is a stationarity guarantee, rather than a claim of finding a global optimum. Within the studied setting, the analysis shows that second-order methods can achieve faster convergence rates than first-order bilevel methods.

Because obtaining second-order information is expensive, the authors introduce a lazy variant, LFSBA, that reuses it over several iterations. They prove a computational complexity improvement by a factor of √d relative to FSBA, where d is the problem dimension. The paper also applies this reuse idea to nonconvex, strongly concave minimax optimization, producing LMCN with better computational complexity than existing second-order methods.
summary.tldr: Second-order bilevel methods obtain accelerated stationarity guarantees, while reusing curvature information reduces their theoretical computational cost.

title: Second-Order Bilevel Optimization with Accelerated Convergence Rates

abstract: Transformers integrate information from multiple past positions through sparse attention patterns that copy from specific locations. We study how these patterns form during training in a high-order Markov-chain setting, where the next token depends on several groups of past positions with differing statistical importance. Learning proceeds in discrete stages, each marked by the emergence of a sparse attention pattern for the next most important group. The dynamics are initially competitive, with all attention heads focusing on the dominant pattern, but later become cooperative, with different heads specializing in distinct patterns. For a tractable surrogate, the dynamics reduce to those of a tensor factorization problem, enabling us to prove stagewise convergence. Empirically, the number of stages completed depends on training set size, suggesting a form of implicit complexity control through early stopping. Overall, we give a theoretical account of how structured attention patterns and head specialization emerge without an explicit curriculum.

paragraphs: Transformer attention heads often specialize in copying information from particular past positions. This paper studies how that structure emerges during training in high-order Markov chains, where different groups of positions have different predictive importance. The goal is to explain the learning sequence rather than impose head specialization explicitly.

Learning occurs in stages: the most important pattern emerges first, followed by progressively weaker patterns. Heads initially compete for the dominant pattern, then become cooperative as they specialize. For a tractable surrogate, the dynamics reduce to tensor factorization, allowing a proof of stagewise convergence.

Experiments show that training-set size affects how many stages are completed, suggesting implicit complexity control through early stopping. The contribution is a theoretical account of structured attention and specialization without an explicit curriculum. Its formal setting is the analyzed Markov-chain surrogate, so the result does not claim that every attention head in a general language model follows the same exact progression.
summary.tldr: Sparse attention patterns emerge in importance-ordered stages, with heads shifting from competition to specialization in the studied model.

title: Incremental Learning of Sparse Attention Patterns in Transformers

abstract: Existing online change-point detection (CPD) methods rely on fixed-dimensional Euclidean summaries, implicitly assuming that distributional changes are well captured by moment-based or feature-based representations. They can obscure important changes in distributional shape or geometry. We propose an intrinsic distribution-valued CPD framework that treats streaming batch data as a stochastic process on the 2-Wasserstein space. Our method detects changes in the law of this process by mapping each empirical distribution to a tangent space relative to a pre-change Fréchet barycenter, yielding a reference-centered local linearization of 2-Wasserstein space. This representation enables sequential detectors by adapting classical multivariate monitoring statistics to tangent fields. We provide theoretical guarantees and demonstrate, via synthetic and real-world experiments, that our approach detects complex distributional shifts with reduced detection delay at matched $\mathrm{ARL}_0$ compared with moments-based and model-free baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/yyzeng43/IDD-icml.

paragraphs: Online change-point detection asks when incoming data begin behaving differently. Many methods represent each batch using a fixed set of numbers, such as moments or extracted features. These summaries can hide changes in the shape or geometry of a distribution. This paper instead treats each incoming batch as an empirical probability distribution.

The method places these distributions in 2-Wasserstein space, a setting for comparing distributions through their geometry. It builds a reference from a pre-change Fréchet barycenter and maps each distribution into a tangent space around that reference. This creates a local linear representation in which classical multivariate monitoring statistics can operate sequentially.

The contribution connects distribution-aware representations with established monitoring tools, allowing detectors to track changes beyond those visible in simple summaries. The authors provide theoretical guarantees and evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world data. They report shorter detection delays for complex shifts than moments-based and model-free baselines at matched average run length before a false alarm. That comparison matters because faster detection is assessed under comparable false-alarm behavior.
summary.tldr: This method monitors entire data distributions through Wasserstein geometry, detecting complex shifts faster at matched false-alarm behavior in experiments.

title: Beyond Euclidean Summaries: Online Change Point Detection for Distribution-Valued Data

abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable success on complex multi-modal tasks. However, it remains insufficiently explored whether they exhibit modality preference, a tendency to favor one modality over another when processing multi-modal contexts. To study this question, we introduce $MC^2$ benchmark, which constructs controlled evidence-conflict scenarios to systematically evaluate modality preference in decision-making. Extensive experiments reveal that all 20 tested MLLMs generally demonstrate clear modality preferences, and such preferences are statistically associated with performances of downstream taks for MLLMs. Further analysis shows that modality preference can be controlled by instruction guidance and captured within the latent representations of MLLMs. Built on these insights, we propose a probing and steering method based on representation engineering to explicitly control modality preference without requiring additional fine-tuning. This method effectively amplifies modality preference toward a desired direction and demonstrates promising improvements across multiple multi-modal understanding and reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: A multimodal model may favor one kind of input when different modalities provide conflicting evidence. This paper makes that preference measurable through the MC² benchmark, which constructs controlled evidence conflicts. The setup allows researchers to examine which source a model follows when its inputs disagree.

Across 20 tested models, the authors find that all generally display clear modality preferences. Those preferences are statistically associated with downstream task performance. Further analysis shows that instructions can influence the preferences and that information about them is present in internal model representations. The findings connect observable choices under conflict with signals inside the models.

The authors use those internal signals to develop a representation-engineering method that probes and steers preference without additional fine-tuning. It strengthens preference in a chosen direction and shows promising improvements on several multimodal understanding and reasoning tasks. The contribution therefore combines a controlled evaluation of input preference with a way to adjust it, while the reported performance relationship remains an association rather than a universal rule about which modality to favor.
summary.tldr: The paper measures modality preferences under conflicting evidence and steers those preferences through internal representations without additional fine-tuning.

title: Evaluating and Steering Modality Preferences in Multi-modal LLMs

abstract: Parameter-free stochastic optimization aims to design algorithms that are agnostic to the underlying problem parameters while still achieving convergence rates competitive with optimally tuned methods. While some parameter-free methods do not require the specific values of the problem parameters, they still rely on prior knowledge, such as the lower or upper bounds of them. We refer to such methods as "partially parameter-free". In this work, we target achieving "fully parameter-free" methods, i.e., the algorithmic inputs do not need to satisfy any unverifiable condition related to the true problem parameters. We propose a powerful and general grid search framework, named GRASP, with a novel self-bounding analysis technique that effectively determines the search ranges of parameters, in contrast to previous work. Our method demonstrates generality in: (i) the non-convex case, where we propose a fully parameter-free method that achieves near-optimal convergence rate, up to logarithmic factors; (ii) the convex case, where our parameter-free methods are competitive with strong performance in terms of acceleration and universality. Finally, we contribute a sharper guarantee for the model ensemble, a final step of the grid search framework, under interpolated variance characterization.

paragraphs: An optimizer may avoid needing exact problem parameters yet still require a valid upper or lower bound on them. This paper calls such methods partially parameter-free. Its stronger goal is to remove algorithmic input requirements that depend on unverifiable conditions about the true problem parameters, while retaining convergence competitive with well-tuned methods.

GRASP approaches this through a general grid-search framework and a self-bounding analysis that determines parameter search ranges. Choosing those ranges is central: a search is not fully free of hidden parameter knowledge if its boundaries must already be supplied correctly. The analysis is designed to address that dependency.

For non-convex problems, the authors establish a fully parameter-free method with a near-optimal convergence rate up to logarithmic factors. For convex problems, they report competitive guarantees involving acceleration and universality. They also sharpen the guarantee for the model-ensemble step under an interpolated variance characterization. The contribution is both an optimization framework and an analysis of how search can avoid relying on unverifiable prior bounds.
summary.tldr: GRASP uses grid search and self-bounding analysis to pursue strong optimization guarantees without unverifiable prior bounds on problem parameters.

abstract: Tensorial data are frequently encountered in various machine learning tasks today and dimensionality reduction is one of their most important applications. This paper extends the classical principal component analysis (PCA) to its multilinear version by proposing a novel dimensionality reduction algorithm for tensorial data, named as uncorrelated multilinear PCA (UMPCA). UMPCA seeks a tensor-to-vector projection that captures most of the variation in the original tensorial input while producing uncorrelated features through successive variance maximization. We evaluate the proposed algorithm on a second-order tensorial problem, face recognition, and the experimental results show its superiority, especially in low-dimensional spaces, through the comparison with three other PCA-based algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper extends principal component analysis to tensorial data through an algorithm called uncorrelated multilinear PCA, or UMPCA. The task is dimensionality reduction: converting a tensor input into a smaller vector representation while capturing much of the variation in the original data.

UMPCA seeks a tensor-to-vector projection that produces uncorrelated features. It does this through successive variance maximization, making the variation captured by the representation and the lack of correlation between its features central design goals. The method therefore adapts the variance-focused idea of classical PCA to a multilinear setting with an explicit feature-correlation requirement.

The authors evaluate UMPCA on face recognition using second-order tensor data and compare it with three other PCA-based algorithms. The experiments show superior performance, particularly when the resulting representation has few dimensions. That finding supports the method for the evaluated face-recognition problem and highlights its effectiveness under strong dimensionality reduction. The main contribution is the combination of tensor-to-vector projection, successive variance maximization, and uncorrelated output features.
summary.tldr: UMPCA extracts uncorrelated features from tensor data and outperforms three PCA-based alternatives in face recognition, especially at low dimensions.

title: Uncorrelated multilinear principal component analysis through successive variance maximization

abstract: Given a weighted and complete graph G = (V, E), V denotes the set of n objects to be clustered, and the weight d(u, v) associated with an edge (u, v) belonging to E denotes the dissimilarity between objects u and v. The diameter of a cluster is the maximum dissimilarity between pairs of objects in the cluster, and the split of a cluster is the minimum dissimilarity between objects within the cluster and objects outside the cluster. In this paper, we propose a new criterion for measuring the goodness of clusters:?the ratio of the minimum split to the maximum diameter, and the objective is to maximize the ratio. For k = 2, we present an exact algorithm. For k >= 3, we prove that the problem is NP-hard and present a factor of 2 approximation algorithm on the precondition that the weights associated with edges of G satisfy the triangle inequality. The worst-case runtime of both algorithms is O(n3). We compare the proposed algorithms with the Normalized Cut by applying them to image segmentation. The experimental results on both natural and synthetic images demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

The diameter of a cluster is the maximum dissimilarity between pairs of objects in the cluster, and the split of a cluster is the minimum dissimilarity between objects within the cluster and objects outside the cluster. In this paper, we propose a new criterion for measuring the goodness of clusters:?the ratio of the minimum split to the maximum diameter, and the objective is to maximize the ratio. For k = 2, we present an exact algorithm. For k >= 3, we prove that the problem is NP-hard and present a factor of 2 approximation algorithm on the precondition that the weights associated with edges of G satisfy the triangle inequality. The worst-case runtime of both algorithms is O(n3). We compare the proposed algorithms with the Normalized Cut by applying them to image segmentation. The experimental results on both natural and synthetic images demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper defines clustering quality by balancing separation between groups against spread within them. Objects form a complete weighted graph, where edge weights express dissimilarity. A cluster's diameter is its largest internal dissimilarity; its split is the smallest dissimilarity connecting it to an outside object.

The proposed objective maximizes the minimum split divided by the maximum diameter across clusters. This judges the clustering through its weakest separation and largest internal spread. For two clusters, the authors provide an exact algorithm. For three or more, they prove the problem is NP-hard and give a factor-of-two approximation under the explicit condition that dissimilarities satisfy the triangle inequality.

Both algorithms have worst-case runtime O(n³), with n denoting the number of objects. The authors compare them with Normalized Cut on image segmentation using natural and synthetic images, reporting results that demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution combines an interpretable clustering objective with algorithms whose guarantees distinguish the two-cluster case from the harder setting with more clusters.
summary.tldr: A separation-to-diameter clustering objective admits an exact two-cluster algorithm and a conditional factor-of-two approximation for larger cluster counts.

title: Clustering to Maximize the Ratio of Split to Diameter
